docs.title: Get started
docs.text: Wodby deploys and manages web applications on Kubernetes. A stack defines the services your application needs; app environments let you deploy those services separately for development, staging, and production.

docs.title: Deploy your first application
docs.text:
1. Create or choose an organization and a project.
  2. Choose a cluster option: use your cloud account, connect your own server, or let Wodby create and manage the cluster.
  3. Create an application from a catalog stack, configure its first environment, and deploy it. You can create a Wodby Cloud cluster during app creation.

For a temporary test, enable Demo when creating a Wodby Cloud cluster. Demo clusters and their applications are deleted automatically after 24 hours.

If the catalog does not include what you need, create a custom stack. You can create or import services to add to it.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
To work through an AI client, start with MCP. It covers connection, read-only verification, permissions, and migration, staging, and troubleshooting workflows.

  • Apps, app environments, and app services
  • Stacks and services
  • Providers and integrations
  • Glossary

docs.title: Access control
docs.text:
Wodby access is layered. A user can have:

  • an organization role
  • one or more team memberships
  • one or more direct project memberships
  • project access inherited from teams

These layers answer different questions:

  • Can the user enter the organization?
  • Can the user administer organization-wide settings?
  • Can the user see, create, or change resources in a project?
  • Can the user use a resource that belongs to another project or to the organization?
  • Can the user reveal a stored credential as readable text?

docs.title: Organization roles
docs.text:
Organization membership is the top-level access gate. A user must have an active organization membership before any project or resource access can apply.

Role Meaning Owner Full access to organization resources and billing. Owners can manage other owners. Admin Full access to organization resources, projects, teams, and org-owned resources. Admins do not manage billing, termination protection, owners, or other admins. Member Works through project access. Members do not receive organization-wide resource access by default.

Organization owners and admins have full resource access across the organization. Project roles matter most for organization members.

docs.title: Membership management
docs.text:
Organization membership changes follow role hierarchy rules.

  • Owners can manage owners, admins, and members.
  • Admins can manage members, but not owners or other admins.
  • Members cannot manage organization memberships.

An invitation sets only the email address and the organization role. Give access to projects and teams afterwards from the member's page, Organization > Members > [Member]:

  • Projects lists the member's direct and team project access, with the role and where it comes from. Owners and admins have access to every project whether or not it is listed. They can add the member to a project, change a direct role, or remove direct access. Access through a team is changed on the team or on the project.
  • Teams lists the member's teams and their role in each. Owners and admins can add, remove, or change them.
  • Edit changes the organization role or removes the member.

Invited people can be added to teams right away. Direct project access can be added once they accept the invitation.

When an organization membership is removed, Wodby also removes that membership from teams and direct project memberships.

docs.title: Teams
docs.text:
Teams are reusable groups of organization members. Use teams when the same people need the same project access in several places.

Team roles are:

Role Meaning Member Receives the project access given to the team. Team leader Receives the project access given to the team, and can see the team and its members.

Organization owners and admins can create, update, and delete teams. They also manage team members and team leaders.

A team can hold any project role except roles that manage the project: the system Admin role, and custom roles with the Manage project permission. Project administration is only granted directly to specific organization members.

docs.title: Project roles
docs.text:
Projects are the main day-to-day permission boundary. Project access can be granted:

  • directly to an organization member
  • indirectly through one or more teams

A project role is a set of permissions. Some permissions apply to the whole project. The others apply per environment type, so one role can, for example, deploy to staging while only viewing production. Every organization has the environment types Production, Staging, Test, Development, and Feature.

Organization owners and admins have every permission in every project. Project roles matter for organization members.

docs.title: Project permissions
docs.text: Permission Allows View project Seeing the project and the resources owned by or shared with it. Every project role includes it. Manage resources Creating and changing the project's apps, clusters, stacks, services, integrations, providers, and databases, and using Modify/Delete shares. Manage project Changing project settings and project access. Teams cannot hold roles with this permission.

docs.title: Environment permissions
docs.text:
Environment permissions apply to app environments of the matching type. Preview environments use the environment type configured for the app's previews.

Some actions need Manage resources and an environment permission together:

  • Creating an app also needs Create for the type of its first environment.
  • Deleting an app also needs Delete in every environment of the app.
  • Turning on preview environments, or changing their base environment or environment type, also needs Configure and Shell on the base environment and Create for the type of previews.
  • For a database that belongs to an environment, creating a DB and adding, changing, or deleting database users also need Configure in that environment type. Deleting a DB needs Delete.

For a database that belongs to an environment, environment permissions also decide backups, restores, deletion, and secret reveal. Creating a database, changing its other settings, app-wide settings, and other project resources need Manage resources only.

Permission Allows View Seeing status, settings, deployments, metrics, and tasks. Logs Reading application logs. Deploy Running builds and deployments, redeploying, and cancelling them. Operate Restarting, pausing, maintenance mode, and running actions and crons. Configure Changing settings, variables, Helm values, resources, routes, ports, endpoint auth, tokens, links, integrations, and when cron jobs run. Upgrade Upgrading and reconciling the stack, changing stack auto-upgrade, and moving the environment to another cluster. Shell Opening the web terminal, running commands, setting the commands of cron jobs, controlling workspaces, and using workspace agents. A shell exposes the credentials the workload receives. Back up Creating and downloading backups, importing the environment's backups elsewhere, seeding preview environments from it, managing backup presets, and voiding backup files. Restore Importing data, which replaces existing data. Create Creating environments of this type. Delete Deleting environments and databases of this type. Reveal secrets Revealing app tokens, endpoint auth passwords, the shared preview password, and database user passwords. Reveal master passwords Revealing database master passwords.

Every project member can see the project's environments and read their logs, so every role includes View and Logs in every environment type.

docs.title: System roles
docs.text:
Every organization has five system roles. They cannot be changed.

Role Project permissions Production Other environment types Read View project View, logs View, logs Developer (non-production) View project View, logs View, logs, deploy, operate, configure, create, shell Developer View project View, logs, deploy, operate, configure, create View, logs, deploy, operate, configure, create, shell Write View project, manage resources Every permission except secret reveal Every permission except secret reveal Admin All All All

Write, Developer, and Developer (non-production) memberships also have a Reveal secrets switch. See Secret reveal permissions.

Organization > Project roles lists every role with exactly what it allows in each environment type.

docs.title: Custom project roles
docs.text:
Organization owners and admins can define their own project roles in Organization > Project roles:

  1. Open a role that is close to what you need and select Copy, or select New project role.
  2. Set a title and a name. The name uses lowercase letters, digits, dashes, or underscores, and cannot be a system role name.
  3. Choose the project permissions, and the environment permissions for each environment type.
  4. Save the role. It can now be chosen on any project's Access page and on member pages.

Changing a custom role changes access at once for every member and team that holds it. A role cannot be deleted while any project membership holds it; give those members and teams another role first. A role that teams hold cannot get the Manage project permission.

Custom roles grant Reveal secrets and Reveal master passwords per environment type, so memberships with a custom role have no separate Reveal secrets switch. New projects start with a system role for their first members; custom roles can be given on the project's Access page afterwards.

docs.title: Combining access
docs.text:
A user who receives project access in more than one way gets every permission that any of those memberships grants, for each environment type.

Example:

  • direct project membership is Developer (non-production)
  • team project membership is a custom role that can deploy and upgrade production
  • the user can work in staging, development, test, and feature environments, and deploy and upgrade production

Team access never includes managing the project. Even if older data contains an admin role for a team, Wodby treats that team role as Write during access checks.

docs.title: Managing project access
docs.text:
Project access is managed from Organization > Projects > [Project] > Access. Organization owners and admins can also manage it per member from Organization > Members > [Member] > Projects.

Organization owners/admins and members whose role includes Manage project can:

  • add organization members
  • add teams
  • assign direct user roles
  • assign team roles
  • change roles later
  • remove project memberships

In the dashboard, only organization owners and admins can pick any member or team to add. Others with Manage project can change or remove existing memberships and add teams they lead.

Members with Manage project can only give, change, or remove roles that grant no more than they hold in the project themselves. For example, a member whose custom role manages the project but cannot deploy to production cannot make anyone an Admin, and cannot change or remove an Admin membership. The system Admin role holds every permission, so this limit only affects custom roles. Organization owners and admins are not limited.

docs.title: Secret reveal permissions
docs.text:
Changing an app and seeing the secrets Wodby stores for it are separate permissions. This lets a developer manage and deploy an app without automatically receiving every credential that Wodby stores for it.

For project-owned resources, direct secret reveal follows this table:

Effective access Reveal secrets Reveal master passwords Organization owner or admin Allowed Allowed Project Admin Allowed Allowed Project Write, Developer, or Developer (non-production) with Reveal secrets turned on Allowed in environment types the role can configure Not allowed The same roles with Reveal secrets turned off Not allowed Not allowed Project Read Not allowed Not allowed Custom role As set for each environment type As set for each environment type

Reveal secrets currently covers app-service tokens, app endpoint-auth passwords, the shared preview environment password, and database-user passwords. Reveal master passwords covers database master or root passwords. Organization-owned secrets can be revealed only by organization owners and admins.

The Reveal secrets switch is set per membership, on the project's Access page or the member's page. If a user has several memberships in the same project, secret reveal is allowed when at least one of them allows it. Access through a project that merely shares the resource does not grant direct reveal—the permission is evaluated through the resource's owner project.

Existing Write assignments may initially have Reveal secrets turned on to preserve their previous access. Project administrators should review those assignments from the project's Access page and turn it off where it is not needed.

Every direct reveal also requires an interactive user session with a recent login or step-up confirmation. Depending on the account, Wodby asks for a password, authenticator/recovery code, or a code sent to the verified primary email. See Secret reveal confirmation.

Runtime access is broader than the reveal button

Secret reveal permission controls whether Wodby displays a stored value through its dashboard/API reveal operation. It does not prevent an authorized workload from receiving its configured credentials. A user who can deploy or configure an app, or open a web terminal, may be able to inspect credentials already injected into that runtime. Give deploy, configure, and shell permissions only to trusted application operators, even when direct secret reveal is disabled.

docs.title: Permission meanings
docs.text:
Wodby uses the same basic permission meanings across resource types.

Permission Meaning Typical requirement Read/use View, select, or reference an existing resource in supported workflows Any project role on the owner project or a project with Read/Use or Modify/Delete sharing, or org-wide view access where the resource is organization-owned Create in project Create a new project-owned resource A project role with Manage resources, or organization owner/admin Create in organization Create a new organization-owned resource Organization owner/admin Modify/delete Change or remove the resource itself Organization owner/admin for organization-owned resources. For project-owned resources, Manage resources in the owner project, or the matching environment permission for app environments and their databases Ownership & sharing Change the resource owner or project access list See Resource ownership. The requirement depends on whether the resource is organization-owned or project-owned Manage project Rename, delete, or manage project access A project role with Manage project, or organization owner/admin Manage organization/team Manage org settings, teams, team members, team leaders, and custom project roles Organization owner/admin Manage termination protection Change organization-wide deletion safeguards Organization owners only Manage org members Invite, change roles, or remove organization members Owners can manage owners/admins/members. Admins can manage members only Manage billing Change subscription, billing details, invoices, or spending limits Organization owners only

docs.title: What read means
docs.text:
In Wodby, read access is not only inspection. For reusable resources, read access also means use access.

For example, if a user can create an app in Project A and Project A can read a cluster, stack, integration, service, provider, or database, that resource can be selected where the workflow allows it.

Typical read/use examples:

  • deploy an app to a visible Kubernetes cluster
  • create an app from a visible stack
  • attach a visible integration to an app service
  • use a visible service, provider, or database in a supported workflow

The user still needs write access to the target object they are creating or modifying. For example, deploying an app requires write access in the app's project even if the selected cluster only needs read/use access.

Resource-specific checks still apply. A resource may need to be in an OK status, belong to the same organization, provide the right integration type, or satisfy stack/service compatibility rules.

Read/use access for the user is necessary but does not by itself make an organization/project-scoped resource a valid dependency. A project-owned target can reference resources owned by or shared with its owner project, and organization-owned resources that are available to all projects. An organization-owned target can reference only organization-owned resources in the same organization. See Sharing.

docs.title: Resource ownership
docs.text:
Resources can be owned at either organization scope or project scope.

Supported owned resource types include:

  • apps
  • Kubernetes clusters
  • databases
  • integrations
  • providers
  • services
  • stacks

docs.title: Organization-owned resources
docs.text:
Organization-owned resources belong to the organization rather than to one owner project.

Access rules:

Action Allowed users Read/use Organization owners, admins, or users who can access a project with Read/Use or Modify/Delete access. Every organization member when the resource is available to all projects Modify/delete Organization owners and admins Ownership & sharing Organization owners and admins

Regular organization members do not automatically see organization-owned resources. They can see and use an organization-owned resource only when it is shared with a project they can access or when it is available to all projects.

docs.title: Project-owned resources
docs.text:
Project-owned resources have one owner project. The owner project always has Modify/Delete access, and additional projects can receive either Read/Use or Modify/Delete access through sharing.

Access rules:

Action Allowed users Read/use Users who can access the owner project or any shared project Modify/delete Users whose role in the owner project includes Manage resources, plus organization owners/admins. App environments and their databases follow the environment permissions Ownership & sharing Organization owners/admins. For project-owned resources that remain project-owned, users with owner-scope write access can update sharing or owner project when they also have project Admin access to every affected project

Sharing a project-owned resource to another project does not move ownership. A Read/Use share grants visibility and use only. A Modify/Delete share includes read/use and marks the project-resource link as write-capable for project-scoped ACL checks, but direct resource update/delete mutations still require access through the owner project or organization admin/owner access.

docs.title: Sharing
docs.text:
Sharing makes a resource visible or usable outside its owner scope. A Modify/Delete share also marks the project-resource link as write-capable for workflows that check project-resource access.

Use sharing when:

  • several projects should deploy to the same Kubernetes cluster
  • several projects should use the same integration
  • one project should consume a stack, service, provider, or database owned elsewhere
  • an organization-owned resource should be available to selected project members

Sharing does not grant project administration rights and does not transfer ownership.

Project access entries have two access levels:

  • Read/Use lets the target project view, select, or reference the resource.
  • Modify/Delete includes Read/Use and marks the project-resource link as write-capable for workflows that check project-resource access.

For organization-owned resources, only organization owners and admins can change the resource owner or project access list. Changing any resource to organization ownership also requires organization owner/admin access. For project-owned resources that remain project-owned, a user must have resource write access through the owner scope and Admin access to each project whose share or owner is changed. Organization owners and admins satisfy these checks across the organization.

See Sharing for the user-facing sharing workflow.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
Tasks inherit access from the resources and projects they reference.

  • Project-linked tasks are visible through their linked projects.
  • A task linked to several projects is visible if the user can access at least one linked project.
  • Project-linked tasks can be repeated by organization owners/admins and project members who can access at least one linked project.
  • Project-linked tasks can be cancelled or otherwise modified only by organization owners and admins.
  • Project-linked tasks do not fall back to general organization membership if the user cannot access any linked project.
  • Tasks without project links are treated as organization-scoped tasks.

Organization-scoped tasks can be read by roles with organization-wide visibility. They can be repeated, cancelled, or otherwise modified only by organization owners and admins.

docs.title: Apps and app environments
docs.text:
Apps can be organization-owned or project-owned. In the dashboard, the app creation Owner field accepts either Organization <organization> or Project <project>. Creating an organization-owned app requires organization owner/admin access. Creating a project-owned app requires write/admin access in the owner project, or organization owner/admin access.

During app creation, referenced resources such as clusters, stacks, integrations, services, providers, and databases generally require read/use access, not modify access. A shared cluster can therefore be a valid deployment target for a project-owned app without granting cluster write access, provided the cluster is shared with the app's owner project. Organization/project-scoped dependencies for an organization-owned app must be organization-owned in the same organization.

App environments do not have a separate project owner. They belong to the app and use the app's ownership and sharing settings. Container-based databases created for app services follow the same rule: their owner and project access list stay synchronized with the app and cannot be changed independently. Managed databases keep their own ownership and sharing settings.

Changing an existing app, app environment, app service, deployment, build source, environment variables, tokens, annotations, routes, ports, auth settings, and similar app-owned configuration requires modify access to the app or app environment.

docs.title: Shared cluster
docs.text:
Project Platform owns a Kubernetes cluster. Project Web can read/use that cluster through a Read/Use share.

  • A Project Web writer can deploy an app from Project Web to the shared cluster.
  • The same user cannot scale or delete the cluster unless they also have write/admin access to the owner project or organization admin/owner access.
  • The same user cannot change ownership or sharing unless they have owner-scope write access and Admin access to the affected projects, or organization admin/owner access. Changing the cluster to organization ownership requires organization admin/owner access.

docs.title: Organization-owned integration
docs.text:
An organization admin creates a GitHub integration at organization scope and shares it with Project API as Read/Use.

  • Project API users can select the integration in supported workflows.
  • Only organization owners and admins can modify or delete the integration.

docs.title: Team access
docs.text:
A Developers team is added to Project App with Write.

  • Team members can create and update resources inside Project App.
  • Team leaders can view the Developers team, but organization owners/admins manage team membership.
  • The team cannot be project admin. Project admin must be granted directly to specific users.

docs.title: Production changes by a few people
docs.text:
Only system administrators should deploy to and patch production. Core developers work outside production and only look at production. One team works on a single project, and its leads manage that project's access.

  1. Create a custom role Sys admin by copying Read and adding Deploy, Operate, Configure, Upgrade, Back up, and Restore in Production. Give it to a Sys admins team in every project.
  2. Give a Core developers team the Developer (non-production) role in the same projects. Leave Delete out by using the system role, or copy it into a custom role to fine-tune it.
  3. Give a Team X team the Developer or Developer (non-production) role in Team X's project only.
  4. Give Team X's leads a custom role with Manage project directly in that project, so they can manage its access. Teams cannot hold that permission. Leads can then also give themselves any role in that project, including production access.

docs.title: Automation time windows
docs.text:
Automation time windows define when Wodby may start scheduled automation. Upgrade windows restrict changes to running workloads, while backup windows restrict when an automatic backup may begin.

Time windows are available for:

  • automatic app environment stack upgrades
  • automatic cluster infrastructure version upgrades
  • automatic cluster infrastructure app stack upgrades
  • automatic cluster Kubernetes version upgrades
  • automatic backups from app, database, and organization-wide backup presets

Each supported upgrade setting has its own window. For example, a cluster can use different windows for infrastructure version, infrastructure app, and Kubernetes version upgrades, and app environments that share a stack can use different upgrade windows.

Catalog operations that do not change running workloads do not use time windows. Git auto-updates of services and stacks, automatic stack service revision updates, and automatic sync of copied stacks with their origin can create new catalog revisions at any time. An app environment's time window still controls when its running workload may be upgraded to one of those revisions.

docs.title: Configure a window
docs.text:
For an automatic upgrade, enable Time window in its automation settings. For a backup preset, enable Auto backups. Then select a start time, end time, time zone, and one or more days. All seven days are selected by default. The Every day, Weekdays, and Weekends shortcuts provide quick ways to change the selection.

New app environments and clusters receive enabled 02:00 to 04:00 windows in the organization's default time zone for each applicable automatic upgrade. The organization creation form preselects the creator's browser time zone and lets them change it before creation; if browser detection is unavailable, Wodby uses UTC. Owners and admins can change it under Organization > Settings > General.

New backup presets created in the dashboard default to a three-hour 02:00 to 05:00 window in the organization's default time zone. Their backup timeout also defaults to three hours. The timeout is separate from the window: the window controls when a backup may start, while the timeout limits how long the backup task may run.

The organization time zone is a creation default, not a live link. Changing it does not rewrite existing resource or backup-preset windows, and each window can use a different time zone. Resources created before a default window was assigned keep their existing setting.

The searchable selector lists available IANA time zone names and follows daylight-saving changes for the selected location. API clients that provide an explicit window without a time zone use UTC; clients that omit the days use every day. Existing windows saved before day selection was introduced also continue to use every day.

A valid window:

  • uses 24-hour HH:mm times
  • includes the start time and excludes the end time
  • is at least one hour long
  • has different start and end times
  • selects at least one day

When the end time is later than the start time, the window is within one day. For example, 02:00 to 04:00 allows automation from 02:00 up to, but not including, 04:00. When the end time is earlier, the window crosses midnight. For example, 22:00 to 02:00 starts at 22:00 and ends at 02:00 the next day.

For a window that crosses midnight, the selected day is the day on which the window starts. For example, a Monday 22:00 to 02:00 window remains open until 02:00 on Tuesday. Selecting Tuesday instead would open the next window at 22:00 on Tuesday.

docs.title: What the window controls
docs.text:
An upgrade window controls when Wodby may dispatch an automatic upgrade task. A task that starts inside the window continues normally if it runs past the end time. Manual upgrades are never restricted by an automation time window.

If an eligible automatic operation is detected outside its window, Wodby defers it quietly. It does not create an update task, mark the resource as failed, or send a success or failure notification for that deferred check. Periodic reconciliation checks the resource again and can start the operation during a later window.

Cluster upgrades preserve their required order. When both a cluster infrastructure version upgrade and an infrastructure app upgrade are pending, Wodby waits for the infrastructure version upgrade first. An open infrastructure app window does not bypass a closed infrastructure version window.

For an automatic backup, Wodby schedules the occurrence for the beginning of the selected window. If processing is delayed, the backup may still start later while the window is open. If the window has already closed, Wodby skips that occurrence and advances to the next selected day; it does not queue the missed backup for replay. A backup that starts inside the window may continue after it closes, subject to its backup timeout. Manual backups are not restricted by the window.

docs.title: Pausing automatic backups
docs.text: Auto backups is the only schedule state control in the dashboard. Turning it off on an existing preset pauses the schedule but preserves its window, timeout, and override setting. Turning it on again resumes the saved schedule. A new preset saved with Auto backups off has no automatic schedule.

docs.title: Existing backup presets
docs.text:
Backup schedules created by the previous dashboard used an exact UTC launch time. Wodby converts the daily and single-weekday schedules generated by that dashboard into three-hour UTC windows beginning at the same launch time. The selected day, backup timeout, and paused or enabled state are preserved. For example, a Monday 02:00 UTC schedule becomes a Monday 02:00 to 05:00 UTC window.

Custom cron expressions that do not match the previous dashboard's daily or single-weekday format remain on the legacy exact-time schedule and are not reinterpreted in an organization's time zone.

docs.title: Notification emails
docs.text: Success and failure emails for automatic app stack upgrades, cluster infrastructure version upgrades, and cluster infrastructure app upgrades include the time when the upgrade task started. When a time window is configured, the email shows the start time in that window's time zone together with the configured interval and selected days. When no window is configured, the email shows the start time in UTC and explicitly notes that the upgrade could run at any time.

docs.title: App
docs.text: The top-level application object in Wodby. All app environments of the same app share one stack and app identity, but the app itself is not the running deployment.

docs.title: App environment
docs.text: One isolated, deployed copy of an app. Each app environment has a fixed environment type and its own services, routes, builds, and configuration.

docs.title: App service
docs.text: One service inside one app environment. An app service is the app-level representation of a stack service for that specific deployed app copy.

docs.title: Backup preset
docs.text: A reusable backup configuration that stores storage destination settings and can optionally schedule automatic backups.

docs.title: Demo
docs.text: The temporary Wodby Cloud option for testing. Demo clusters are deleted automatically after 24 hours, and applications deployed to them are deleted with them.

docs.title: Endpoint
docs.text: A network entry point exposed by an app service. In practice, endpoints back HTTP routes and published ports.

docs.title: Environment type
docs.text: A fixed deployment classification chosen from prod, staging, test, dev, or feature. App environments, clusters, databases, integration policies, and backup presets use the same enum.

docs.title: Integration
docs.text: A configured connection to a third-party service, created from a provider.

docs.title: K3s
docs.text: A lightweight Kubernetes distribution used for self-hosted clusters connected from your own server.

docs.title: Main route
docs.text: The main HTTP route for the whole app environment. The main route is always also primary.

docs.title: Managed Kubernetes
docs.text: A Kubernetes cluster created in your own cloud account through a supported provider integration.

docs.title: Organization
docs.text: The top-level workspace boundary for users, teams, projects, billing, and shared settings.

docs.title: Preview environment
docs.text: A temporary app environment that Wodby creates automatically for a pull request, copied from a base environment and deleted when the pull request closes or has been idle for a configured period.

docs.title: Primary route
docs.text: The default HTTP route for a specific app service endpoint.

docs.title: Private App Access
docs.text: An app environment setting that publishes the entire app or selected HTTP endpoints through a supported access provider while suppressing the corresponding ordinary public routes.

docs.title: Project
docs.text: The main resource and access boundary inside an organization.

docs.title: Provider
docs.text: Wodby's definition of how to work with a third-party service, including fields, kinds, and exposed variables.

docs.title: Resource owner
docs.text: The organization or project that owns a resource. The owner determines the direct write/delete boundary, while sharing controls which other projects can read or use the resource.

docs.title: Route
docs.text: An HTTP entrypoint for an app service endpoint. A route matches a hostname and path, then sends traffic to an app service endpoint or redirects the request.

docs.title: Service
docs.text: Wodby's representation of one piece of software, a Helm-based workload, or a workflow. Most services deploy containers; external services represent software that runs outside Wodby.

docs.title: Sharing
docs.text: The project access list for a resource. Sharing can grant Read/Use or Modify/Delete access without changing the resource owner.

docs.title: Stack
docs.text: The blueprint from which an app is created.

docs.title: Stack draft revision
docs.text: An unpublished version of stack configuration. Stack edits update the draft until it is either published as a stack revision or discarded.

docs.title: Stack revision
docs.text: A published versioned snapshot of the stack configuration. App environments can be upgraded between stack revisions.

docs.title: Stack service
docs.text: A service as included in a stack, tied to a specific service revision plus stack-level configuration such as options, settings, links, integrations, and defaults.

docs.title: Team
docs.text: A reusable group of organization members used to assign project access more efficiently.

docs.title: Variable integration
docs.text: An integration whose main purpose is to inject reusable environment variables into apps or stacks.

docs.title: Variable provider
docs.text: A provider that exposes environment variables instead of, or in addition to, infrastructure actions.

docs.title: Wodby Cloud
docs.text: Wodby's managed Kubernetes offering. Wodby Cloud clusters can be created from the Clusters page or during the new app flow.
