docs.title: App environments
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph App["<div style='margin-top:10px; white-space: nowrap;'>App</div>"]
        subgraph group[ ]
            Dev["Dev environment"]
            Staging["Staging environment"]
            Prod["Production environment"]
        end
        style group fill:none,stroke:none,stroke-width:0px          
    end

    KubernetesA["Kubernetes Cluster A"]
    KubernetesB["Kubernetes Cluster B"]

    Dev --> KubernetesB
    Staging --> KubernetesB
    Prod --> KubernetesA

An app environment is one isolated deployment of your application on a Kubernetes cluster. It was previously called an app instance; both terms refer to the same resource.

Each app environment has its own:

  • Environment type, such as prod, staging, or dev
  • Stack revision
  • Endpoints to configure HTTP routes and published ports
  • Maintenance mode to temporarily replace public HTTP routes with a maintenance response
  • Cluster migration to move the environment and supported persistent data to another cluster
  • Private App Access to choose public, identity-protected, or private-network HTTP access
  • Builds and deploys, when the stack has services with build configuration
  • CI provider and container registry selections
  • Backups and imports, when the stack provides those capabilities
  • App services used to override stack configuration for this specific environment
  • Metrics, when cluster monitoring is enabled
  • live log streaming
  • Cron schedules and jobs
  • Tasks history

Wodby can also create temporary preview environments for pull requests automatically.

All environments of the same app share the same stack, but different environments can run on different clusters and different stack revisions.

App environments do not have a separate project owner. They belong to the app and use the app's ownership and sharing settings.

The environment machine name is permanent and must follow the general Kubernetes name rules. The generated namespace, <app-name>-<environment-name>, must be 63 characters or shorter, unique in the cluster and not reserved. See App environment namespaces.

You add or remove environments from Apps > [App] > Environments.

New environments start with the organization's default CI provider and container registry. These values are copied at creation time rather than inherited dynamically: changing an organization default affects future environments only. An environment retains its selection even when it currently has no enabled service with build configuration, so the same provider is ready if a buildable service is enabled or added later.

To change an existing environment, open Apps > [App] > [Environment] > Settings > CI/CD. The tab remains available when the environment has no active buildable services, and saves the selection for services that are enabled or added later. Changes apply to future builds. Existing builds keep the CI provider, registry, and registry repository recorded when those builds were created.

docs.title: Development workspaces
docs.text: For persistent code editing over SSH, set Deployment mode to Development workspace when creating an environment. This mode is separate from the environment type and cannot be changed after creation. Workspace environments use an editable Git checkout instead of the normal image build and deployment workflow.

docs.title: Copying configuration to a new environment
docs.text:
When you add an environment to an existing app, Step 4 shows Copy configuration from. Select another environment of the same app and confirm to prefill compatible configuration for the new environment:

  • CI and container registry selections
  • public build boilerplate selections and connected Git repositories
  • service settings and integrations
  • volume sizes
  • existing database selections for compatible external database services

Only fields supported by the selected stack revision and integrations available to you are copied. Review both App settings and Services before creating the environment. Private App Access, imports, backups, volume data, and database data are not copied.

When the source environment was created by cloning a boilerplate into your Git account, the new environment connects to that resulting repository. It does not clone the boilerplate into another repository. A public boilerplate source remains a public boilerplate when the same boilerplate is available in the selected stack revision.

Warning

This warning appears in the dashboard only when the stack has an enabled external database service. If the source environment uses an existing database, copying its configuration can select that same database for the new environment. Both environments would connect to one database; Wodby does not clone its data. To keep the environments isolated, review the Databases section and select a different database server or choose Create new in the DB field.

docs.title: Pausing and resuming an environment
docs.text:
Pausing and maintenance mode serve different purposes. Maintenance mode keeps workloads running and temporarily replaces public HTTP routes with a maintenance response. Pause an environment when you want its application workloads and scheduled jobs to stop.

Open an app environment's Settings tab. Settings opens on Edit by default; select Pause & Resume, then Pause app environment, when you want to stop the environment temporarily without deleting its configuration or data. Pausing is available on paid plans. Resuming remains available so you can leave the paused state before a downgrade.

The status in this tab is Running during normal operation. It changes to Pausing while workloads are being stopped, Paused after Kubernetes verifies the pause, and Resuming while workloads are being restored.

Pausing cancels active work for the environment, then:

  • scales Deployments and StatefulSets to zero
  • stops scheduled jobs and removes other active Kubernetes workload resources
  • releases the workloads' requested compute and memory back to the cluster
  • leaves routes, configuration, secrets, persistent volumes, and Helm releases in place

Automatic cron jobs and backups that become due while the environment is Pausing, Paused, or Resuming are skipped. Wodby advances each schedule to its next run instead of queueing the missed execution for after resume. Managed technical-domain certificates can still renew through DNS validation while the environment is paused, but renewal does not restore or redeploy application workloads. On infrastructure version 4.0.0 or newer, routing changes made while the environment is paused remain pending and are applied after its workloads are restored.

The environment's endpoints do not respond while it is paused. Persistent volumes and their data remain provisioned so the environment can be resumed later. A pause has no automatic expiration.

After Kubernetes verifies that the workloads have stopped, the environment moves to paused. Select Resume app environment from the same Pause & Resume tab to make its services count toward plan usage again and restore the workloads and endpoints. Infrastructure app environments cannot be paused independently.

docs.title: Billing while paused
docs.text:
An environment continues to count toward app-service plan usage while the pause is in progress. After Kubernetes verifies the pause, its enabled app services no longer count toward that usage. They count again before workloads are restored when the environment resumes. Pausing does not cancel the organization's subscription, and the Team plan's $48 monthly minimum still applies. A paid subscription cannot be downgraded while an environment is Pausing or Paused: wait for any pause in progress to finish, resume every paused environment, then retry the downgrade. See Billing.

For environments running on Wodby Cloud, persistent storage and cluster infrastructure are billed separately. Pausing an environment does not itself resize or stop its cluster, although the freed workload capacity may allow a scalable cluster to reduce its node count. This Wodby Cloud infrastructure note does not apply to clusters in your own cloud account, where infrastructure costs are determined by your provider.

docs.title: Deleting an environment
docs.text:
Deleting an app environment marks it as deleting immediately and blocks new builds and deployments from starting.

Before Kubernetes cleanup begins, the deletion task cancels active builds, deployments, and post-deployment script tasks for the environment and waits for each task to stop. It then removes the environment's Kubernetes resources and other generated resources. Follow the deletion task logs to see which active tasks were canceled and whether cleanup completed.

Deleting an app applies the same process to all of its environments. It needs the Delete permission in every environment of the app.

docs.title: Errored environments
docs.text:
An app environment can move to errored when Wodby cannot finish creating it or cannot finish deletion cleanup.

Errored environments remain visible so you can inspect task logs and delete the environment. Operations that would create new runtime work or change deployable configuration are blocked, including new builds and deployments, stack upgrades, service configuration changes, route and auth changes, app-scoped backups, cron jobs, shell sessions, live logs, pod queries, and container-backed database changes. Automatic app-scoped backups and cron jobs skip errored environments. Managed technical-domain certificates can still renew through DNS validation, without deploying application workloads.

Review the failed task to find the cause. After fixing the underlying problem, delete the errored environment and create a new one.

docs.title: Application high availability
docs.text: High availability depends on more than one layer. To make an app highly available, look at the cluster, the app services themselves, and the storage they depend on.

docs.title: Kubernetes cluster high availability
docs.text:
Start with the cluster. A common baseline is:

  • at least two worker nodes
  • nodes spread across at least two availability zones when the provider supports that
  • a highly available control plane, which is often included by default or offered as an option

docs.title: Stateless app services
docs.text: Stateless app services are usually the easiest part of HA. In practice, you normally want at least two replicas so one pod can continue serving traffic if another fails.

docs.title: Stateful app services
docs.text:
Stateful services need service-specific HA support. Single-node and highly available deployments often differ significantly in architecture, operational complexity, and required resources.

For some stateful components, it can be simpler to rely on managed services such as managed databases.

docs.title: Distributed storage
docs.text:
Not every distributed storage system is highly available by itself. If your app depends on shared storage, make sure the storage layer also meets your HA requirements.

In some cases, a managed distributed-storage service such as AWS EFS is a better HA fit than a container-based storage service inside the cluster.

docs.title: Application imports
docs.text:
If an application's stack includes services that provide import functionality, you can run imports for the corresponding app service.

There are two main import methods.

The source can be an uploaded archive, a public URL, or a completed backup from a compatible app service. When the source app service has a usable backup preset, Wodby can also create a fresh backup to use for the import.

docs.title: Importing from another app
docs.text:
A backup-based import must stay within the destination app's ownership boundary:

  • the source and destination apps must belong to the same organization
  • an organization-owned destination can import only from an organization-owned source
  • for a project-owned destination, the source app must be owned by or shared with the destination's owner project, including when the source app is organization-owned

Your access to both apps through separate projects does not combine their resource boundaries. Share the source app with the destination project before starting the import. You also need the Back up permission on the source environment, both to use one of its existing backups and to create a fresh one.

docs.title: 1. Simple files import
docs.text:
Wodby imports files directly into the running volume by unpacking the provided tar archive to the specified path. The import replaces the volume's content: files that aren't in the archive are removed.

This method is not transactional.

docs.title: 2. Through init volume
docs.text:
Wodby mounts the import archive into the init volume provided by the service, and a container performs the import during startup. This pattern is commonly used for databases.

This method is transactional. Wodby starts a copy of the app service with a new persistent volume. If the import succeeds, Wodby redeploys the service using the new volume that contains the imported data.

For a container-based database service, Wodby provisions the app's database user on the replacement volume and reapplies its managed database grants before redeployment. A missing user is created, and an existing user is accepted when it already uses the expected credentials. If an uploaded dump creates a same-named user or role with different credentials, the import task reports a credential conflict instead of replacing that account. Database dumps intended for this workflow should normally contain the application database schema and data, not server-level user or role definitions.

docs.title: K3s storage capacity preflight
docs.text:
Before an app-service import runs on K3s, its task checks the capacity of the destination volume.

For a transactional init-volume import using the default local-path provisioner, Wodby accounts for the replacement data volume and the temporary 10 GiB import volume while the current volume still exists. The import stops before creating replacement claims when known available capacity is insufficient or the backing node reports DiskPressure.

For an in-place files import, the service contract does not declare the incoming archive's expanded size. Wodby still checks disk pressure, but reports byte capacity as unverified and continues. The same warning behavior applies when Kubernetes volume statistics or a provisioner-specific capacity resolver are unavailable.

When the import source is a pending app-service backup, Wodby checks the destination before creating that backup, checks the source backup volume through its own preflight, and checks the destination again before import provisioning. Storage operations are serialized for every involved K3s cluster.

External database imports do not use this Kubernetes volume preflight.

docs.title: Maintenance mode
docs.text:
App environment maintenance mode temporarily replaces enabled public HTTP and HTTPS routes with a Wodby maintenance response. Use it when visitors should see a consistent maintenance page while you continue running deployments, migrations, or other work inside the application.

Maintenance mode changes routing only. It does not stop application workloads or change the app environment lifecycle status.

docs.title: Enable maintenance mode
docs.text:
1. Open Apps > [App] > [Environment] > Settings > Maintenance.
  2. Select Enable maintenance mode.
  3. Review the affected traffic and confirm.
  4. Follow the routing task if the dashboard opens it.

The maintenance status moves from Off to Enabling while Wodby applies the routing change, then to Active after the public edge confirms it. The app environment keeps its normal lifecycle status, such as running, deploying, awaiting, or errored. Environment headers and lists show a separate maintenance badge.

Enabling maintenance mode requires a non-infrastructure app environment with ready platform-managed routing. You can change maintenance mode while the environment is running, awaiting a deployment, errored, or deploying. The cluster must support the direct-response routing capability used for the fixed page. If the capability is unavailable, the dashboard leaves maintenance mode off and explains the requirement.

docs.title: Traffic behavior
docs.text:
While maintenance mode is active, every enabled public Wodby HTTP or HTTPS route for the app environment returns the same fixed page with:

  • HTTP status 503 Service Unavailable
  • Retry-After: 300, asking clients to retry after five minutes
  • Cache-Control: no-store
  • search-engine no-index headers

The page is served at the public edge and does not depend on an application container. It is fixed and cannot be customized. Existing hostname and path matching, TLS certificates, HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects, and HTTP basic authentication remain in place.

Maintenance mode also covers public redirect routes. A route configured to redirect to another destination returns the maintenance response until maintenance mode is disabled.

The following traffic is not replaced:

  • routes marked private
  • routes suppressed because Private App Access publishes them through a protected or private provider path
  • published TCP or UDP ports

With Selected endpoints Private App Access, any ordinary public routes outside the selected scope still receive the maintenance response. Provider-managed protected or private endpoints continue using their normal provider path.

docs.title: Workloads, tasks, and billing
docs.text:
Application workloads remain running. Scheduled jobs, builds, deploys, backups, and other application operations continue according to their normal rules. Maintenance mode does not reduce app-service plan usage or infrastructure costs.

A workload deployment and a maintenance request can overlap. When necessary, Wodby waits for the workload deployment before applying the pending routing change. Follow the routing task to see its progress or failure details.

You cannot pause an app environment while maintenance mode is requested or active. Disable maintenance mode and wait for its status to return to Off, then use Settings > Pause & Resume. See Pausing and resuming an environment.

docs.title: Disable or reverse maintenance mode
docs.text:
Open Settings > Maintenance and select Disable maintenance mode. The status changes to Disabling while Wodby restores application backends to the public routes, then returns to Off after the public edge confirms the change. Visitors may continue to receive the maintenance response during this transition.

You can reverse a pending request. For example, select Disable maintenance mode while the status is Enabling, or select Enable maintenance mode while it is Disabling. Wodby finishes or supersedes the in-progress routing change and converges on the latest requested state.

If a routing task fails, the requested and active states can differ. The dashboard continues to show Enabling or Disabling instead of reporting a completed change. Review the task logs, correct the routing or cluster problem, and retry the failed routing task.

docs.title: Maintenance mode compared with pausing
docs.text:
Behavior Maintenance mode Paused environment Public HTTP and HTTPS routes Fixed 503 maintenance response Do not respond Application workloads Continue running Stop Scheduled jobs Continue normally Stop and skip runs that become due Builds and deploys Continue normally Cannot start Persistent data Remains provisioned Remains provisioned App-service plan usage Unchanged Stops after pause completes TCP and UDP ports Unchanged Do not respond with the stopped workloads

Use maintenance mode when the application must keep running behind a temporary public response. Use pause when the environment is not needed and its workloads should release compute and memory.

docs.title: App environment cluster migration
docs.text:
App environment cluster migration moves an existing environment and its persistent data from one Kubernetes cluster to another cluster in the same Wodby organization. The app environment keeps its identity and configuration; Wodby deploys its services on the target cluster, restores supported data, and switches its managed technical routes.

This is a cold migration. Wodby stops source writers before creating the final backups, and the environment remains unavailable while its data is backed up, restored, and deployed on the target. Plan a maintenance window whose length allows for the size of your data and the deployment time of your services.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Before starting a migration, make sure:

  • You have Write access to the app.
  • The app environment is a standard application environment, not an infrastructure app environment.
  • The environment has an active deployment, has status OK, uses platform-managed routing, and is not in maintenance mode.
  • The source and target clusters have status OK, belong to the same organization, and the target cluster is available to the app's owner project when the app is project-owned.
  • The target cluster allows the environment's type. See Cluster environments.
  • No other app environment on the target cluster uses the same Kubernetes namespace. The environment keeps its namespace when it moves. See App environment namespaces.
  • The source cluster supports the maintenance response required to freeze public traffic, and the target cluster supports the current app-owned routing resources. Upgrade cluster infrastructure first if the migration reports a missing routing capability.
  • Wodby Blob Storage is available. Migration backups always use Wodby Blob Storage, which requires a paid subscription.
  • Every app service that owns a persistent volume provides matching backup and import operations. A disabled data service with a migration backup/import operation must be enabled first.
  • Every build-backed app service has an active build that Wodby can reuse on the target cluster.

The first version of cluster migration supports only managed technical routes. Before migrating:

  • remove Private App Access
  • remove private routes
  • remove or disable custom routes
  • unpublish TCP and UDP ports

You can recreate these access and endpoint settings after the migration completes.

Create or connect the target cluster before opening the migration form. The target must be different from the current cluster. A cluster that still contains a retained source from an earlier migration cannot be reused as a target until that retained source is cleaned up.

docs.title: Start a migration
docs.text:
1. Open Apps > [App] > [Environment] > Settings > Migration.
  2. Review any prerequisite warnings and resolve every blocker.
  3. Select the target cluster.
  4. For each root persistent volume, select the storage class that should receive the restored data on the target. Wodby selects the target cluster's single default class automatically when one is available.
  5. Select Review migration.
  6. Review the downtime and target-cluster confirmation, then select Start migration.

Changing the target cluster clears and revalidates the storage-class selections. Shared volumes and volumes that reuse another volume do not need an independent mapping; their owning storage service or source volume controls the class.

The environment status changes to Migrating, and operations that could change its configuration or runtime are blocked until the migration completes or the source is restored. The source and target clusters also serialize conflicting app and storage work while the task is running.

docs.title: What Wodby does
docs.text:
The migration task performs these steps in order:

  1. Enable a maintenance response on managed public routes, drain active app work, and stop source writers.
  2. Create final service-native backups in Wodby Blob Storage.
  3. Stop the remaining workloads on the source cluster.
  4. Deploy the environment on the target cluster and restore each migration backup.
  5. Switch the environment's managed technical routing and DNS to the target cluster.
  6. Return the environment to normal operation and retain the stopped source runtime for seven days.

Open the migration's task to follow detailed logs. The Migration page also shows the current phase and migration status. Expand a migration-history row to inspect the backup and restore created for each data component.

docs.title: Failure and rollback
docs.text:
If the migration task fails before completion, Wodby automatically attempts to:

  • remove the staged target runtime
  • restore the environment's source-cluster, deployment, storage, and database references
  • reinstall the source service releases
  • restore source routing without the maintenance response
  • point managed technical DNS back to the source cluster

A migration shows Rolled back when recovery completes. If automatic recovery cannot finish, the migration remains Failed or Rollback failed; correct the underlying cluster, storage, or deployment problem, then select Roll back from the migration history.

Do not treat a successful migration as a reversible failover. After cutover, the target may accept new writes, so a completed migration cannot be rolled back to the retained source. To move back, first clean up the retained source and then start a new forward migration with the former source cluster as the new target.

docs.title: Retained source and cleanup
docs.text:
After a successful cutover, Wodby keeps the stopped source namespace for seven days. It does not receive traffic or new writes, but its Kubernetes resources and persistent volumes can continue to incur infrastructure and storage costs.

Wodby schedules cleanup after the retention time expires. The cleanup job runs hourly, so deletion may begin after the displayed retention deadline rather than at the exact minute. To remove the retained source earlier, select Clean up source in migration history and confirm the permanent deletion.

Source cleanup does not delete the migration backups. Those backups remain available according to the normal backup destination and retention behavior.

While either cluster is still required by a migration or retained source, Wodby blocks operations that could make recovery unsafe, including deleting the app environment, deleting either cluster, or changing cluster sharing in a way that removes required access.

docs.title: Kubernetes resources monitoring
docs.text:
When cluster monitoring is enabled, Wodby collects metrics at several levels:

  • Kubernetes cluster and node metrics
  • Kubernetes namespace metrics
  • app environment runtime metrics
  • app service runtime metrics
  • pod and container runtime metrics

Cluster-level metrics are shown from Clusters > [Cluster] > Metrics.

That page also includes namespace-level usage details, including namespace type, related app environment, pod and container counts, restart totals, CPU and memory usage, and persistent volume storage usage per namespace.

docs.title: Monitoring with third-party service
docs.text: You can also monitor your app with third-party services. For example, you can attach a New Relic integration.

docs.title: Live logs
docs.text:
For a deployed app environment, you can stream live container logs from Apps > [App] > [Environment] > Logs. Live logs remain available while a deployment is in progress, including as pods are added or replaced during a rollout.

You choose the app service first. If that service exposes more than one workload or container, you can select the target explicitly. Otherwise Wodby uses the primary workload and its first container automatically.

Live logs follow the selected container across all current replicas by default, including replicas added while the stream is open. When a workload has multiple pods, you can keep All replicas selected or narrow the stream to one pod. All-replica streams prefix every line with its pod name so interleaved messages remain attributable to the replica that produced them. A stream narrowed to one pod does not add that prefix.

If a selected pod is replaced, its stream stops instead of silently switching to the replacement pod. Choose the new pod or switch back to All replicas to continue following the workload through scaling and rolling updates.

Logs for deployments, builds, cron jobs, and actions are available in the related tasks.

docs.title: Persistent log storage
docs.text:
Wodby streams container logs but does not retain them as searchable historical application logs. Use a logging service or cluster-level log collector when you need long-term retention, search, or alerting for container output.

Task-step logs are stored separately and remain available from the related deployment, build, cron, action, or other task. Task logs are an operation history; they are not a persistent copy of the application's container logs.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
App environment metrics are available from Apps > [App] > [Environment] > Metrics.

That page shows:

  • CPU and memory usage, with its share of the limit, or of the request when only a request is set
  • persistent volume storage usage and capacity for the app environment namespace
  • pod and container readiness
  • a row for each Kubernetes workload, with its service, pods, containers, CPU, memory, and storage usage

Derivative services are listed under their main service. A workload name is shown only for services that run more than one workload. See Resources management for how requests and limits work.

App service metrics are available from Apps > [App] > [Environment] > Stack > App services > [Service] > Metrics.

That page shows:

  • aggregated CPU and memory usage for the service, with its share of the limit, or of the request when only a request is set
  • persistent volume storage usage and capacity for volumes associated with the service
  • pod readiness
  • per-pod and per-container metrics such as requests, limits, restarts, node placement, and lifecycle timestamps

Storage metrics come from Kubernetes PVC stats. They are available at app environment, app service, and namespace levels. Per-pod and per-container tables do not show separate storage usage because PVC usage is reported for volumes rather than individual containers.

If cluster monitoring is disabled, app environment and app-service metrics pages are not available.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks
docs.text: The catalog stacks for application runtimes include an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default: ASP.NET Core, Astro, Django, Drupal, FastAPI, Flask, Go, Java, Kotlin, Laravel, Next.js, Node.js, Nuxt, PHP, Python, Rails, Ruby, Rust, Spring Boot, Strapi, SvelteKit, Symfony, TanStack Start, and WordPress. The Collector runs in the same app environment as your application and has no public domain. It forwards traces, metrics, and logs to the destinations its links name: usually the Collector of an Observability app, or a hosted OpenTelemetry backend.

docs.title: See your application's telemetry in Grafana
docs.text:
The Collector in your app only forwards data. To store and view it, send it to an app created from the Observability stack, which has Grafana. One Observability app can collect data from many apps and environments.

  1. Create an app from the Observability stack. See Creating New Application. On the same cluster as your app, data stays on the cluster's private network; on another cluster it goes to the Observability Collector's public domain.
  2. In your app's environment, open the otel-collector app service, then Connections > Links. Set Upstream to the Collector of the Observability app, listed with the other apps you can link to. See Links tab.
  3. Under Configuration > General, enable the service, then deploy the app environment so your application gets the variables below.
  4. Add an OpenTelemetry SDK or agent to your code and set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, for example to the app and environment name. See What your application gets.
  5. Open the Observability app's Grafana and find the data in Explore. See View telemetry in Grafana.

Repeat steps 2 and 3 in each environment you want to see. Environments created before the stack included the Collector get it with a stack upgrade.

docs.title: Destinations
docs.text:
The Collector has four links. At least one must be set before the Collector can be enabled, so set its links first.

Link Sends Can point at Upstream Every signal, unless one of the links below is set A Collector, or a custom target Traces Traces A Collector, Grafana Tempo, or a custom target Metrics Metrics A Collector, VictoriaMetrics, or a custom target Logs Logs A Collector, Grafana Loki, or a custom target

A signal with no destination is dropped. For a hosted backend, choose Custom and enter its OTLP/HTTP base URL, without a path, and the Authorization header it expects, for example Bearer <key>. Backends that need another header name are not supported by these fields; edit the Collector config under Configuration > Configs instead.

Use Traces, Metrics, or Logs to split signals, for example traces to a hosted backend and logs to your Observability app. The Collector of a Grafana Tempo, Grafana Loki, or VictoriaMetrics app accepts only its own signal, so link it with the matching link, not with Upstream.

docs.title: What your application gets
docs.text:
While the Collector is enabled, the application service, and worker services such as Celery or Sidekiq, get the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables:

Variable Value OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT http://otel-collector:4318 OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL http/protobuf OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS The Collector's ingest token, as a secret

Wodby does not instrument your code. Add an OpenTelemetry SDK or agent for your language that reads these variables, and set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME to name the application in traces. While the Collector is disabled, the variables are absent, so start the instrumentation only when OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT is set.

docs.title: PHP applications
docs.text:
In the PHP, Laravel, Symfony, WordPress, and Drupal stacks, the PHP service also gets OTEL_PHP_AUTOLOAD_ENABLED=true while the Collector is enabled. The OpenTelemetry PHP extension is already in the image. Add the SDK, the OTLP exporter, and an HTTP client to your project with Composer:

composer require open-telemetry/sdk open-telemetry/exporter-otlp php-http/guzzle7-adapter

The SDK then sets itself up from the variables when your application loads Composer's autoloader, with no code changes. Add instrumentation packages for what you want to trace, for example open-telemetry/opentelemetry-auto-laravel, open-telemetry/opentelemetry-auto-symfony, open-telemetry/opentelemetry-auto-wordpress, or open-telemetry/opentelemetry-auto-pdo for database queries. While the Collector is disabled, the variables are absent and the SDK stays off.

docs.title: Preview environments
docs.text:
A preview environment is a temporary app environment that Wodby creates for a pull request. When a pull request is opened against the branch your base environment follows, Wodby copies that environment, builds the pull request branch, seeds the services you selected with data from the base environment, and posts the result back to the pull request. With Wodby CI, every push to the pull request rebuilds the preview. With a third-party CI system, your pipeline starts the builds. Wodby deletes the preview when the pull request is closed or merged, or after it has been idle for a configurable number of days.

Preview environments require an active paid subscription. They are disabled by default and configured per app. They work with GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket. This page says pull request for what GitLab calls a merge request.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The base environment must be a standard environment, not a development workspace, with at least one enabled service connected to a Git branch through a GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket integration. Pull requests are matched against that branch, so an environment following main creates previews for pull requests into main.
  • The integration needs enough access to the repository:
    • GitHub: the GitHub App installation needs write access to Pull requests, Commit statuses, and Issues, and the Pull request and Issue comment events. With Wodby CI, it also needs the Push event. GitHub asks the installation owner to approve these when they are missing. See GitHub.
    • GitLab: the Maintainer role on the project and, for an access token, the api scope. See GitLab.
    • Bitbucket: the Admin permission on the repository. See Bitbucket.
  • The base environment must not use Private App Access. Environments with Public or Basic Auth access are supported.
  • Database services of the base environment must run as containers in the environment. Environments that use an existing database server are not supported yet.
  • The cluster of the base environment must allow the environment type chosen for previews. See Environment types.

docs.title: After a downgrade
docs.text:
Previews do not block a downgrade. Once a downgrade is scheduled, and on the Developer plan:

  • You can't turn previews on or create or recreate a preview. A new pull request gets a failed wodby/preview status and a comment that says why.
  • Existing previews keep following their pull requests and count toward your plan limits until the pull requests close or the previews go idle.
  • You can turn previews off at any time. If you leave them on, your settings stay, and new pull requests get previews again after you upgrade.

docs.title: Enabling preview environments
docs.text:
For a new application, open the Preview environments section in step 4 of the new application form and set Pull request previews to Enabled. The environment you are creating becomes the base environment. The option is available when a service has a build source and the deployment mode is CI/CD. You choose which services are seeded with data after the application is created.

For an existing application, open Apps > [App] > Settings > Preview environments. You need permission to modify the app.

Turning previews on, choosing another base environment, or changing the environment type of previews also needs these environment permissions:

  • Configure and Shell on the base environment. Previews are copies of it, with its variables and secrets, and the pull request's code runs with them.
  • Create for the environment type of previews.

Other preview settings, such as Concurrent previews or Idle expiry (days), need only permission to modify the app.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Description Pull request previews Turns preview environments on or off for the app. Turning them off does not delete existing previews; they are still removed when their pull requests close. Base environment The environment whose configuration is copied into every preview and whose services provide seed data. Only standard environments of the app are offered. Choosing a production environment shows a warning: previews copy its variables and secrets, and seeded services get its data. Environment type The environment type of created previews. feature is the default; prod is not allowed. Run cron jobs Whether previews run the base environment's cron jobs. Disabled by default: cron jobs are copied but turned off, so previews don't send duplicate emails or run scheduled tasks twice. You can still turn on a single cron job in a preview. Draft pull requests Whether draft pull requests get previews. Disabled by default; a preview is created when the draft is marked ready for review. Concurrent previews The maximum number of preview environments the app keeps at the same time, up to 50. Pull requests beyond the limit are skipped until a preview is deleted. The default is 5. Idle expiry (days) Deletes a preview whose pull request had no activity for this many days. The default is 7 and the maximum is 90; 0 disables idle expiry. Basic Auth Protects every preview with basic auth. Enabled by default. All previews of the app share one generated password. See Basic auth. Seed data Base environment services that support both imports and backups. Select a service to restore a fresh backup of it into every new preview, and choose the import and backup when the service offers more than one.

Seeding a service requires a backup preset for the chosen backup in the base environment. Services without one are listed with a No backup preset tag and cannot be selected until a preset exists; the tag links to the base environment's presets.

Selecting or changing seed data needs the Back up permission on the base environment, because every new preview receives a copy of its data.

If seeding a selected service is not possible when a preview is created, the preview is still created and that service starts without data. This happens when the preset was deleted, or the service was removed, disabled, or not in OK status in the base environment. Wodby reports it on the pull request (see Pull request feedback). Deleting a backup preset that previews seed from finishes with a warning that explains this.

Changes to these settings apply to previews created afterwards, and existing previews keep running until their pull request closes or they expire. The exception is Idle expiry (days), which also applies to existing previews, so lowering it can delete previews soon after you save.

docs.title: What a preview contains
docs.text:
Each preview is created from the base environment at the moment the pull request is picked up:

  • Service configuration is copied: enabled services and versions, settings, environment variables, volume sizes, integrations, cron schedules, and service links. Secret values are copied as well, so pull request code can reach the same external services as the base environment.
  • Every service runs one replica, with autoscaling turned off. CPU and memory requests and limits stay as in the base environment.
  • Backup presets are not copied, so previews make no scheduled backups. You can still back up a preview manually.
  • Cron jobs are turned off unless Run cron jobs is enabled.
  • The service connected to the pull request repository follows the pull request branch instead of the base branch.
  • Container database services get their own database.
  • Only the services selected in Seed data get data. They are seeded from a fresh backup of the base environment taken at creation time. The backup is restored during the preview's first deployment, so a large database delays the first successful deployment.
  • Custom domains, TLS certificates, and Private App Access are not copied. The preview is reached through its generated technical domain.
  • Service basic auth entries and exemptions are copied with their passwords. With Basic Auth enabled, the shared preview password replaces the base environment's environment-wide entry. With it disabled, that entry is copied as it is. Entries and exemptions for a single domain are not copied.

The environment machine name is pr-<number>, the title shows the pull request number and title, and the technical domain follows the usual *.pr-<number>.[app-name].[org-name].wodby.app pattern. Previews count toward app-service plan usage like any other environment while they exist.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Event Result Pull request opened, reopened, or marked ready for review A preview is created when the pull request targets the base environment's branch and no preview exists yet. A push to a pull request without a preview also creates one, for example after enabling previews for an open pull request. Push to the pull request branch With Wodby CI, the preview is rebuilt and redeployed with the new commit, and a push that arrives while a deployment is running is built after that deployment finishes. With a third-party CI system, your pipeline starts the build. Pull request closed or merged The preview is deleted. If deletion cannot start, for example while a build is running, Wodby retries it automatically. No activity for the idle expiry period The preview is deleted. Pull request from a fork No preview is created. Forks could run untrusted code with the app's configuration. Draft pull request No preview is created unless Draft pull requests is enabled. Concurrent preview limit reached The pull request is skipped and gets a failed wodby/preview status. It gets a preview on its next push once a preview has been deleted.

Wodby also checks open pull requests every 15 minutes, in case it missed a notification from your Git provider. A preview whose pull request was closed or merged is deleted. An open pull request that should have a preview gets one, for example right after you enable previews for an app with open pull requests. A pull request whose latest commit already has a wodby/preview status is left alone, so a preview you deleted is not recreated until the next push.

Automatic preview deletion is not blocked by the organization's termination protection. You can also delete a preview manually from the app's environments list; the next push to the pull request creates a new one.

docs.title: Basic auth
docs.text:
With Basic Auth enabled, every preview asks visitors for a username and password. All previews of the app share one password, which Wodby generates when previews are enabled, so reviewers learn it once. The username is wodby.

On Apps > [App] > Settings > Preview environments you can:

  • reveal the password. This requires secret reveal permission in the environment type used for previews, and a recent secret reveal confirmation. Each reveal is recorded as a task.
  • regenerate the password. Every existing preview switches to the new password, and reviewers need the new one.

These actions are available while Basic Auth is enabled. Services with their own basic auth entry keep their own password in previews. Turning Basic Auth on or off applies to previews created afterwards; existing previews keep their current protection until they are deleted.

docs.title: Creating a preview manually
docs.text:
To create a preview for an open pull request yourself, open Apps > [App] > Environments and click New PR preview, or choose it below New environment in the environment menu. Select the pull request and click Create. You need permission to create environments of the app.

The list shows the open pull requests into the base environment's branch. Pull requests that cannot get a preview are shown disabled with the reason, such as a pull request from a fork or one that already has a preview. Draft pull requests can be selected even when Draft pull requests is disabled. The concurrent preview limit still applies.

If previews are not configured for the app yet, the page links to the app's preview environment settings instead.

docs.title: Pull request feedback
docs.text:
Wodby reports each preview deployment to the pull request as a wodby/preview commit status on the commit it built: in progress while the environment is being created, then successful or failed with a link to the preview.

Wodby also keeps one comment on the pull request and edits it as the preview changes: when it is being created, when it is ready (with the preview URL), when a deployment fails, when a preview cannot be created and why, when services start without seed data, and when the preview is deleted. If you delete the comment, Wodby posts a new one on the next change. When a preview is password-protected, the comment links to the preview in the dashboard and never contains the password.

A deployment that did not build the pull request commit, such as a configuration-only redeploy, does not change the status.

When Wodby cannot create a preview for a pull request, it sets the wodby/preview status to failed with the reason, for example that the base environment is not in OK status or that the concurrent preview limit is reached. The next push to the pull request tries again.

When a preview is created but some selected services could not be seeded, Wodby also sets a wodby/preview-data status to failed that names the service and the reason, or the number of affected services. The preview itself works; those services start without data. Fix the cause, such as adding the missing backup preset, then comment /wodby reseed on the pull request to create the preview again with data.

docs.title: Pull request commands
docs.text:
Comment on the pull request with one of these commands on its own line:

Command Result /wodby preview Creates a preview for the pull request, following the same rules as creating a preview manually. /wodby reseed Deletes the preview and creates it again from the base environment, with fresh seed data. The preview's address can change, and the Wodby comment shows the new one. If creating the new preview fails after the old one started deleting, the pull request is left without a preview, and the Wodby comment says how to ask for a new one.

Who can run commands depends on the provider:

Provider Who can run commands GitHub People with write, maintain, or admin access to the repository. GitLab Project members with the Developer role or higher. Bitbucket People with write or admin access to the repository. The integration's Bitbucket account must have the Admin permission on the repository, because Bitbucket shows permissions only to admins. Without it, every command is refused.

On GitHub and GitLab, Wodby reacts with 👍 when it accepts a command and with 😕 when it refuses one. If someone with access gives a command that cannot run, the Wodby comment explains why. Bitbucket has no reactions, so every refusal is explained in the Wodby comment.

/wodby reseed is refused while the preview cannot be deleted, for example while a build is running. Commands are ignored for apps without preview environments.

docs.title: Using previews from AI agents
docs.text: Agents connected through the Wodby MCP server can read and change an app's preview settings, list pull requests that can get a preview, and create one, with the preview tools. Changing settings and creating a preview require your confirmation.

docs.title: Finding previews in the dashboard
docs.text:
Preview environments appear in Apps > [App] > Environments with a PR #<number> tag and can be opened like any other environment. Their creation, deployments, and deletion are listed under the app's Tasks tab, where the creation task is titled with the pull request number.

If a pull request does not get a preview, check the Wodby comment or the wodby/preview status on the pull request for the reason. Also check that previews are enabled for the app, that the pull request targets the branch the base environment follows, and that it is not a draft or from a fork.

docs.title: Application scalability
docs.text:
Before you scale an app, make sure the underlying Kubernetes cluster can scale with it.

Managed Kubernetes clusters give you the most flexibility because they can scale worker nodes dynamically through a cluster autoscaler. With K3s, app scaling is limited by the K3s server and the worker nodes you add to the cluster.

docs.title: Manual scaling
docs.text:
You can scale the replica count of app services manually when the selected service revision supports horizontal scaling. The service overview shows whether horizontal scaling is supported.

Stateless services can usually be scaled up and down directly. Stateful services need service-specific support for scaling, for example through read replicas. A fixed service can be scaled to zero or run as a single replica, but it cannot be configured with multiple replicas.

You can set replica counts:

  • in the stack configuration as the default
  • per app environment as an override

docs.title: Resources management
docs.text:
App services can define resource requests and limits, following the same model as Kubernetes container resources.

Resource limits help contain bursty workloads so they do not affect other workloads on the same cluster. Resource requests help Kubernetes schedule pods correctly and also matter for both pod autoscaling and cluster autoscaling.

CPU requests and limits are specified in millicores, where 1000 millicores equals 1 CPU core. Memory requests and limits are specified in mebibytes, where 1024 MiB is roughly 1 GiB.

You can define resources at:

  • service level, as defaults in the service manifest
  • stack level
  • app-service level

A container uses its service defaults unless its stack service or app service sets resources for it. Each of the four values replaces only that default. If you set only a memory limit, the container keeps the default CPU and memory requests. If you change only the CPU request, the memory request stays as it was. A stack's values apply on top of the service defaults in the same way, and an app service's values on top of the stack's.

A derivative service, such as a cron runner or a queue worker, can have its own defaults for the main container in the service manifest. Each value it sets replaces only that default of the parent service, and stack and app service values still apply on top.

Every container requests at least 10m CPU and 16 MiB of memory, even when nothing sets a request, but never more than its limit. Without a request, Kubernetes would reserve the whole limit for a container that sets only a limit, or reserve nothing at all.

Kubernetes doesn't allow a request above its limit. If a value you set and a default would end up that way, your value wins: a default request is lowered to your limit, and a default limit is raised to your request.

Autoscaling needs a CPU request of at least 100 millicores on the main container, set by the service, the stack, or the app service. The minimum request alone isn't enough. See Autoscaling rules.

App services can also request GPUs with GPU devices: a device name, such as nvidia.com/gpu, and the number of GPUs for each replica. A count of 0 turns off the GPU request of the service's default configuration. App services that request GPUs run on the cluster's GPU node pool.

docs.title: Resource presets
docs.text:
A resource preset is a named set of CPU and memory values. Instead of typing the values, pick a preset from Preset in the resources dialog when you create an app, or on the Resources tab of an app service or a stack service. Picking a preset fills in its values and clears the ones it doesn't set, so those keep their defaults. You can still change any value afterwards. The Preset column shows which preset a container's values match.

Choosing a preset copies its values. Wodby doesn't keep a link to the preset, so changing or deleting a preset later doesn't change any service that used it.

Wodby provides these presets. They set requests only, so containers can use spare CPU and memory on the node:

Preset Requested CPU Requested memory nano 10m 32 MiB micro 20m 64 MiB small 50m 128 MiB medium 100m 256 MiB large 250m 512 MiB xlarge 500m 1024 MiB 2xlarge 1000m 2048 MiB

Wodby's presets never change. A new size gets a new name.

Your organization can add its own presets in Organization > Settings > Resource presets. Every member can view them and use them. Organization owners and admins create, edit and delete them. A custom preset can set any of the four values: requested CPU and memory, and CPU and memory limits. CPU values are multiples of 10 millicores and memory values are multiples of 16 MiB. For example, a preset for Java services can add a memory limit, because the JVM sizes its memory from the limit. A custom preset can't use the name of a Wodby preset.

Service and stack manifests can name a Wodby preset in resources.preset, and override any of its values:

resources:
  preset: medium
  limit:
    memory: 1024

See the service template and the stack template. The API, the CLI and the MCP tools accept the name of a Wodby preset or of a custom preset of your organization.

docs.title: Clearing resources when creating an app
docs.text:
When you create an app, the icons in the TOTAL row of the services table reset all services to the stack's defaults, including their replicas, or clear their resources. You can also clear the values of one service in its resources dialog.

A cleared service reserves nothing and has no limit. It is the first to suffer when a node runs short of memory or CPU. Clearing all services also turns off their autoscaling, because autoscaling needs a CPU request.

docs.title: Cluster capacity
docs.text:
When you create an app or an app environment on an existing cluster, Wodby adds up the resource requests of its enabled services, counting every container and replica, and compares them with what the cluster can offer: the capacity free now, plus any nodes it can still add. When you create an app, the TOTAL row of the services table shows the same requests. A development workspace also counts its workspace container.

  • It can't fit: Wodby refuses to create the environment and shows both amounts. This also applies when one replica of a service is larger than a node. Lower the resources, choose a larger cluster, or scale the cluster.
  • It may not fit: you see a warning and can continue. This happens when the environment fits only if the cluster adds nodes, or when Wodby can't read the cluster's current usage. The deployment fails if there is no room for it.

The same refusal applies when you create an environment through the API, the CLI, or an agent.

A check that passes doesn't guarantee a deployment:

  • Services count only what they request, which can be much less than they use under load. A container that nothing gives a request counts as the minimum of 10m CPU and 16 MiB of memory.
  • Short-lived jobs aren't counted. Post-deploy steps, actions, cron runs and backup creation reserve nothing, so they always fit next to the service they run for, but they can use up to the service's limits. Backup uploads and imports reserve at most 50m CPU and 64 MiB of memory and can use up to 1 GiB of memory.
  • Enough capacity in total can still be split across nodes so that a replica doesn't fit on any one of them.
  • Only creating an environment is checked. Enabling a service or raising its resources later isn't.

docs.title: Autoscaling rules
docs.text:
Autoscaling requires an active paid subscription. Manual replica scaling remains available on all active plans. If your current subscription does not include autoscaling, you cannot enable or increase a rule, but you can turn an existing rule off.

When creating an app, you can define autoscaling rules for supported services. You can change the rule later from Apps > your app > your environment > Stack > App services > your service > Configuration > General.

Turn Autoscaling on to reveal:

  • Requested CPU for the primary container, in millicores
  • Minimum replicas
  • Maximum replicas
  • Avg. CPU utilization, as a percentage of requested CPU

Requested CPU must be at least 100 millicores. Set it to what one replica uses under normal load: autoscaling compares CPU use with this request, so a request near idle use adds replicas at almost any traffic.

When you turn autoscaling on, the field keeps a CPU request of at least 100 millicores that the app service or the stack already sets. Otherwise it suggests 500 millicores, or the service's default if that is higher. Service defaults are sized close to idle use, which is too low for autoscaling. Changing the field updates only the CPU request on the Resources tab before Wodby enables the autoscaling rule; the other resource values stay as they are.

While autoscaling is on, the main container's CPU request can't be removed or lowered below 100 millicores. A rule set up earlier with a smaller request keeps working until you change its autoscaling settings or the main container's resources.

While autoscaling is on, the manual Replicas field is disabled. Wodby controls the replica count between the configured minimum and maximum, using the minimum as the baseline. Turn Autoscaling off to clear the saved rule and manage Replicas manually again.

The dashboard offers new autoscaling configuration only for eligible top-level, non-external services whose service revision supports horizontal scaling. If an existing rule becomes ineligible, its configuration remains visible so you can turn it off, but its settings cannot be increased. The API rejects enabling autoscaling for other services.

The current autoscaling signal is average CPU utilization. The target is expressed as a percentage of the configured CPU request. For example, if a service has a CPU request of 2000 millicores and an autoscaling target of 50%, scaling starts when average CPU usage reaches 1000 millicores.

The replica range works as follows:

  • the minimum replica count is the baseline when CPU usage stays below the target
  • the maximum replica count is the upper limit autoscaling can grow to

The autoscaling controls remain available when the app service is disabled. Disabling an app service preserves its autoscaling rule for a future re-enable; it does not turn autoscaling off or remove the service as a subscription downgrade blocker. To remove the rule, open the disabled service's Configuration > General page, turn Autoscaling off, and select Update.

docs.title: Vertical scaling
docs.text: Wodby does not currently configure automatic vertical pod autoscaling. Adjust CPU and memory requests and limits manually at the stack or app-service level, then deploy the updated configuration. Use metrics to review actual usage before changing requests or limits.

An application service is the per-app environment representation of a stack service.

When you create a new app, Wodby creates one app service for each relevant stack service. The app service starts with stack defaults, then lets you override behavior for that specific app environment.

The app service machine name comes from the stack service name and must follow the Kubernetes service name rules.

This is the main place to customize how one environment behaves without changing the stack for every other environment.

docs.title: App service menu
docs.text:
Inside Apps > [App] > [Environment] > Stack > App services > [Service], the dashboard groups related pages under primary tabs:

  • Overview
  • Configuration: General, Deployment, Variables, Helm, Settings, Configs, Tokens, and Annotations
  • Connections: Integrations, Links, and Database
  • Runtime: Resources and Volumes
  • Actions
  • Metrics

Selecting Configuration, Connections, or Runtime opens its subtabs in a second navigation row. Actions and Metrics remain direct tabs. Not every app service gets every tab or subtab; the menu depends on the service type and whether it is external or derivative.

When an app service needs required configuration, the dashboard marks the affected subtab and its parent group.

In general:

  • Metrics appears only when cluster monitoring is enabled and the app service is not external or disabled
  • Actions appears only when the service defines user-runnable actions
  • Database appears only for services with database support
  • Deployment, Variables, Helm, and Resources appear only for non-external services
  • Links, Volumes, Settings, and Configs appear only when the service supports them
  • Tokens appear only for non-external top-level services
  • Annotations appear only for non-external services

docs.title: Overview tab
docs.text:
The Overview tab shows the current state of the app service, including:

  • status
  • machine name
  • title
  • version
  • linked service revision
  • container images
  • build image, if the service is built
  • last build
  • last deploy

The same screen also exposes Connect via web terminal.

The web terminal button is available only when both the app environment and the app service are in a healthy OK state. It opens an interactive shell session in a separate window. If the service has multiple workloads or containers, you can target a specific one. Otherwise Wodby uses the primary workload and its first container automatically.

See Web terminal for the full behavior and requirements.

docs.title: Metrics tab
docs.text:
When cluster monitoring is enabled, non-external enabled app services expose a Metrics tab.

It shows aggregate runtime metrics for the service and detailed per-pod and per-container metrics, including:

  • CPU and memory usage, with the service's share of its limit, or of its request when only a request is set
  • CPU and memory requests and limits
  • persistent volume storage usage and capacity for volumes associated with the service
  • pod and container readiness
  • restart counts
  • node placement
  • container start, finish, and exit data

Storage usage is shown at the app service level. Per-pod and per-container storage usage is not reported separately, because Kubernetes exposes PVC usage for volumes rather than individual containers.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Some app services expose an Actions tab. It lists the user-runnable service actions available for that specific app service. User-runnable actions are button and output actions.

Running an action creates a background task for the app service. Use the task details and logs to follow progress and inspect command output. output actions do not return output directly in the run request.

Actions can appear disabled when the app environment or app service is not in a healthy OK state. They are not available for external services or derivative app services.

docs.title: General configuration
docs.text:
The Configuration > General subtab is the main operational form for the service.

Depending on the service, you can:

  • enable or disable the service
  • mark it as the main service when its main endpoint exposes a public HTTP port
  • change the service version
  • change the number of replicas for non-external services when autoscaling is off; fixed services are limited to zero or one replica
  • configure CPU-based autoscaling for supported services, including requested CPU, the minimum and maximum replica counts, and the average CPU utilization target
  • change build source settings for services that support a build source

The main app service owns the app environment's root Wodby technical hostname. Selecting a different main app service retargets that technical route to the new service's primary public HTTP endpoint. It does not replace the app environment's canonical Main route, which may be a customer-added custom route.

Disabled, external, and derivative app services cannot be main. You can disable the current main app service: Wodby selects another eligible enabled service for the root technical hostname, or removes that technical route when no replacement exists. Disabling a service also disables all domains and redirects associated with it; it does not move those customer routes to another service. Re-enabling the service re-enables domains and redirects that were disabled with the service, but leaves items you had disabled individually disabled.

For an app environment with an established runtime, re-enabling a service automatically starts a partial deployment of that service and any required dependencies. If the app remains awaiting—including after an explicit partial deployment initialized only some services—Wodby saves the enabled state and marks the environment needs redeploy instead. Finish configuring the environment, then start a deployment that includes the remaining services. See deferred initial deployment.

An EOL flag next to a service version means that the app service currently uses a version whose end-of-life date has passed. If newer supported versions are not available in the selector, update the app environment to a stack revision that uses the latest service revision first, then choose a non-EOL service version.

Scaling and resource changes, including replicas, autoscaling rules, and requested CPU, mark the app environment as needing redeploy. Changes that affect a built image, such as changing the version of a service with a build source, mark it as needing rebuild instead.

docs.title: Build source
docs.text:
If a service supports a build source, the General page shows a separate Build source card with its own update action.

The build source shows its effective CI. A connected source inherits the app environment's Default CI. Public and cloned boilerplate sources use Wodby CI.

For Wodby CI, point a connected or cloned service to a Git repository and a reference such as:

  • branch
  • tag
  • commit SHA

When a connected source inherits third-party CI, linking a Git repository is optional. You can leave the repository unlinked and run the pipeline with wodby ci init $WODBY_APP_SERVICE_ID; Wodby CLI uses the app service ID and metadata from the CI checkout to create the build.

To start builds from the dashboard, meet the provider-specific requirements:

  • GitHub Actions requires a linked repository and a previously recorded workflow that supports workflow_dispatch.
  • GitLab CI requires a linked repository and branch or tag.
  • CircleCI requires a linked repository and a previously recorded workflow.
  • Custom CI builds always start in the external pipeline.

The available options depend on your CI mode and Git integrations. Build source is chosen during app creation, but can also be changed later from the app service.

docs.title: Database tab
docs.text:
The Connections > Database subtab appears for services that can attach to a database resource.

From there you can choose:

  • database user
  • DB

The available choices are filtered by databases visible in the current project context and by actual user-to-DB access inside the selected database resource.

docs.title: Integrations tab
docs.text:
If a service supports integrations, the Connections > Integrations subtab lets you attach compatible integrations of the required type. When the service requirement also specifies provider labels, Wodby lists only integrations with a selected provider kind that has the required type and every label. The matching kind is shown with the integration so you can see which capability the service will use.

This is commonly used for storage, mail, monitoring, or other provider-backed features exposed by the service.

Variable integrations inject provider-wide fields and fields from the matching selected kind into runtime containers only. Fields owned by other provider kinds are not injected through that service requirement. Variable integration values are not passed to image builds.

docs.title: Deployment tab
docs.text:
The Configuration > Deployment subtab controls rollout strategy, readiness timing, and graceful shutdown for this app service. For a service with multiple workloads, select All workloads in the Workload selector for service-wide settings, or select a workload to override settings only for it.

Each unset field inherits independently from the stack service or service manifest. If no inherited value exists, the Helm chart keeps its default. Saving a deployment override marks the app environment as needing redeploy. See Deployment configuration for supported settings, workload-kind restrictions, and the full precedence order.

docs.title: Variables tab
docs.text:
The Configuration > Variables subtab lets you add, remove, or override environment variables for the app service.

Some values are inherited and cannot be deleted directly, but they can usually be overridden. See Environment variables for sources, precedence, runtime and build scope, secrets, environment-type targeting, reserved names, and the platform-provided WODBY_* variables.

docs.title: Helm tab
docs.text:
The Configuration > Helm subtab lets you add or override Helm values for the app service.

Use this when a specific environment needs a chart-level override without changing the stack for every other environment.

App-level Helm values override values coming from the service and stack. Helm values can also be stored as secrets.

docs.title: Resources tab
docs.text:
The Runtime > Resources subtab lets you configure CPU and memory requests and limits per workload and container.

CPU values are set in millicores, where 1000 means 1 CPU core. Memory values are set in megabytes in the dashboard UI.

Values the app service sets appear in regular text. Values it doesn't set appear in grey italics: these are the stack's or the service's defaults, or the minimum request. While you edit a container, a field left empty keeps its default, which the field shows as a placeholder, and Preset fills in the values of a resource preset. See Resources management for how set values and defaults combine.

Resource requests directly affect whether the service can be scheduled. If the cluster does not have enough available CPU or memory for the requested pod size, the pod stays pending until enough capacity becomes available. If cluster autoscaling is enabled, the cluster may add nodes to satisfy that demand.

Apps running on a demo cluster cannot change service resources.

docs.title: Replicas
docs.text:
Replicas are configured from Configuration > General, but they directly affect service scaling.

Service revisions explicitly declare whether they support horizontal scaling. The service overview displays this capability. Scalable services can run multiple replicas for higher throughput and high availability, and their replicas can be adjusted automatically with autoscaling. Fixed services are limited to zero or one replica. Stateful replication that requires service-specific topology, quorum, or failover is not represented as ordinary app-service scaling.

docs.title: Links tab
docs.text:
The Connections > Links subtab lets you change links between app services.

Links are usually defined in the stack, but app services can override them per app environment.

Those overrides also affect deployment ordering for that app environment. If linked services are deployed together, Wodby deploys the linked target first.

For each link, choose its target from the list:

  • a service of this app environment;
  • a service of another app, for links that allow it. The list shows the apps and environments you can link to. See Links to other apps;
  • Custom, for links that allow it: enter the values the link asks for. Secret fields start empty. Saving replaces all values, so enter a stored secret again before saving.

Choose - none - to remove a target. Required links cannot be removed. When the service needs at least one of several links, the tab shows each such group and whether it is satisfied.

After changing a link, deploy the app service so it picks up the new values.

docs.title: Volumes tab
docs.text:
The Runtime > Volumes subtab lists the volumes declared by the current service revision. Configured volumes show their app-level values and the effective storage class observed on the live Kubernetes claim. A healthy volume shows its effective class once. When the selected and effective classes differ or cannot be verified, the dashboard expands the value to show both and adds a Mismatch, Mixed, Unknown, or Unavailable status.

An optional volume omitted during app creation remains in the table with an Optional label, empty size and storage class values, and an Add volume action. This is a valid configuration, not a warning or configuration issue. Adding the volume asks for a positive size and, when supported, a storage class. Shared volumes and volumes that reuse a linked claim inherit their storage configuration. Saving the volume marks the app service and environment for redeploy; the claim is created by the subsequent deployment.

After a volume has been added, it cannot be resized or removed from app-service settings, and its storage class cannot be changed. See Current storage class for the status definitions and Choose a storage class for storage-class selection.

docs.title: Settings tab
docs.text:
The Configuration > Settings subtab lets you change values of settings exposed by the service.

These settings often flow into environment variables or runtime configuration generated by the service templates. The service template decides whether each setting is runtime-scoped, build-scoped, or both. Changing a build-scoped setting marks the app service for rebuild; changing a runtime-only setting marks it for redeploy.

docs.title: Configs tab
docs.text:
The Configuration > Configs subtab lets you view default configs and override them for this app service. The dashboard identifies whether a default comes from the service repository or from the selected service image and shows image source details when available.

An app override takes precedence over the displayed default. Use Reset override to delete it. For an image-backed config, resetting means the next deployment stops mounting the override and the container uses the file supplied by its image; Wodby does not save a copy of the image default as another override.

A changed or reset config takes effect when you deploy the app service. If Wodby mounts the config as a file in the container, that deployment restarts the service's pods so the application reads the new file. A config that Wodby passes to the service's Helm chart takes effect the way that chart applies it.

docs.title: Tokens tab
docs.text:
The Configuration > Tokens subtab lets you add or remove tokens that can be used in environment variables and other generated configuration.

Tokens can be plain or secret-backed. Secret-backed token values are revealed only on demand in the dashboard. You need runtime secret reveal permission and recent secret reveal confirmation to display a secret-backed value.

docs.title: Annotations tab
docs.text:
The Configuration > Annotations subtab lets you add custom annotations to the app service.

Like env vars, annotations can come from several sources:

  • the service
  • the stack
  • Wodby system defaults

Inherited annotations are shown in the list, and app-level annotations can override them.
