Name of the main stack this stack is a variant of. Use it for stacks that run the same application in a different way, for example a stack that builds Matomo from your repository next to a stack that runs the prebuilt Matomo image. The stack page in the dashboard lists the other variants under Other variants of this stack, so people can find the one that fits.

  • The main stack must belong to the same organization.
  • The main stack can't be a variant itself, and a stack that has variants can't become one.
  • The main stack can be imported later. The variants appear once both stacks exist.
  • A copy of the stack, for example one added from the catalog, is not a variant.
name: matomo-buildable
title: Matomo (buildable)
variantOf: matomo

docs.title: variant
docs.text:
Type: string. Optional. Requires variantOf.

Short label that tells this variant apart, such as Buildable. Up to 64 characters.

docs.title: variantDescription
docs.text:
Type: string. Optional.

When to choose this stack over its other variants. The stack page shows it under the link to this stack on the other variants' pages. Up to 500 characters. The main stack can have one too, without variantOf.

variantDescription: >-
  Choose this when you want to customize Matomo: pin the Matomo version and add
  your own plugins in a Git repository, and Wodby builds Matomo from it.

docs.title: access
docs.text:
Type: object.

Optional Private App Access requirement for app environments created from the stack. This policy describes the access outcome the stack needs. The app environment still stores the actual access configuration and the user selects an eligible Private App Access integration.

  • required: required boolean. When true, Private App Access must be configured during app creation and cannot be removed while the app environment uses this stack revision.
  • provider: optional provider machine name, such as tailscale or cloudflare. Omit it to accept any provider that supports the required mode and scope. Set it only when the stack depends on provider-specific behavior.
  • mode: required access type. Allowed values are protected and private_network.
  • scope: required access scope. Allowed values are entire_app and selected_endpoints.

For example, a stack that must be private but works with either Tailscale or Cloudflare can use a provider-neutral policy:

access:
  required: true
  mode: private_network
  scope: entire_app

Existing stack revisions that specify provider remain provider-specific.

docs.title: services
docs.text:
Type: array. Required. Must contain at least one item.

List of stack services. Each item references an existing service and can apply stack-level overrides to it.

docs.title: env
docs.text:
Type: array.

Stack-wide environment variables. They are applied to app services created from this stack.

Stack environment variables are runtime-only. They are not passed to Docker image builds. See the environment-variable naming and reserved-name rules.

docs.title: tokens
docs.text:
Type: array.

Stack-wide tokens. Tokens can either store a fixed value or generate one from a regular expression. A stack-wide token overrides a service-defined token with the same name and environment type.

docs.title: annotations
docs.text:
Type: array.

Stack-wide annotations applied to deployed app services where the service template maps annotations into Kubernetes resources. Use app endpoint route settings for HTTP routing behavior.

docs.title: helm
docs.text:
Type: array.

Stack-wide Helm values. Use this to override values required by the service Helm integration.

docs.title: env[]
docs.text:
Used by top-level env, services[].env, and services[].workloads[].containers[].env.

  • name: required environment variable name.
  • value: required string value. Use quoted strings in YAML.
  • secret: optional boolean. When true, the value is stored as a secret.
  • envType: optional environment type filter. Allowed values: prod, dev, staging, test, feature.

The environment-variable naming and reserved-name rules apply to top-level stack variables, stack-service variables, and container-scoped stack variables.

Stack env vars do not support build scope. Use a build-scoped service setting, service env var, or app-service env var when a Dockerfile needs a build argument.

docs.title: tokens[]
docs.text:
Used by top-level tokens and services[].tokens.

  • name: required token name. Names that start with wodby_ are reserved; see token names.
  • value: fixed token value.
  • generate.regex: regex used to generate the token value.
  • secret: optional boolean for fixed-value tokens.
  • envType: optional environment type filter.

Exactly one of value or generate.regex must be specified. Regex tokens are always secret regardless of the secret setting.

Within one token scope, each name and envType pair must be unique. You can define the same token name more than once only when each definition has a different envType.

docs.title: annotations[]
docs.text:
Used by top-level annotations.

  • name: required annotation name.
  • value: required annotation value.
  • envType: optional environment type filter.

Annotations are Kubernetes resource annotations. They are separate from app endpoint route settings.

docs.title: helm[]
docs.text:
Used by top-level helm, services[].helm, and services[].derivatives[].helm.

  • name: required Helm values path.
  • value: required value. Can be a scalar, array, or object.
  • secret: optional boolean. When true, the value is stored as a secret.
  • envType: optional environment type filter.

docs.title: services[].name
docs.text:
Type: string. Required.

Stack service machine name. It must be unique within the stack, including derivative stack services.

It must follow the Kubernetes service name rules: lowercase letters, numbers, and dashes only; start with a letter; end with a letter or number; 63 characters or shorter.

docs.title: services[].title
docs.text:
Type: string. Required.

Human-readable service title shown in the stack and app UI.

docs.title: services[].service
docs.text:
Type: string. Required.

Reference to an existing service. You can use either a plain service name such as php or a versioned reference such as php:8.3.

The referenced service must exist and be available to your organization.

Versioned references pin the stack service to the service revision that matches the requested service version. Stack service revision updates skip pinned services. Use an unversioned reference when the stack service should move to newer service revisions through manual or automatic stack service revision updates.

docs.title: services[].serviceRevPinned
docs.text:
Type: boolean. Default: false.

Pins the stack service to the service revision selected during import. This is useful when the service reference is unversioned but the stack should still keep the current service revision until you update the stack template or unpin the service in the dashboard.

Derivative stack services inherit the pin state from their parent stack service.

docs.title: services[].required
docs.text:
Type: boolean. Default: false.

Marks the service as mandatory when a new app is created from the stack.

A required stack service cannot be disabled.

docs.title: services[].disabled
docs.text:
Type: boolean. Default: false.

Disables the stack service by default.

docs.title: services[].replicas
docs.text:
Type: integer. Default: 1.

Default number of replicas for the stack service. Fixed service revisions accept 0 or 1; service revisions that support horizontal scaling can use higher values.

docs.title: services[].deployment
docs.text:
Type: object.

Service-wide deployment overrides for every app created from this stack revision. Each property overrides the matching service-manifest default independently.

The object supports:

  • strategy
  • maxUnavailable
  • maxSurge
  • minReady
  • progressDeadline
  • shutdownGracePeriod

For field formats, workload-kind restrictions, and precedence, see Deployment configuration.

docs.title: services[].main
docs.text:
Type: boolean.

Marks the main service in the stack. Only one stack service can be main, and its main endpoint must expose a public HTTP port. A port the stack makes private with services[].endpoints doesn't count. The corresponding app service owns the app environment's root technical route. This is independent of the app app environment's canonical Main route.

If no service is marked as main, Wodby will automatically pick the first eligible service. The same fallback applies when a stack without a main service later gains an eligible service through the dashboard or Git sync. If the stack has no eligible services, no main service is required.

docs.title: services[].depends
docs.text:
Type: array[string].

List of stack service names that this service depends on. Every referenced name must exist in the same stack.

This affects deployment order: a service is deployed after its dependencies and deleted before them.

Wodby also derives deploy-time ordering from the current service links in an app environment. Use depends when you need explicit ordering even when no link exists between the services.

The combined graph formed by depends entries and service links must be acyclic. This also applies to disabled services, so enabling a service cannot expose a dependency cycle later.

docs.title: services[].options
docs.text:
Type: array.

Limits which options from the referenced service can be used in this stack and sets the default option.

Each item supports:

  • version: required option version from the referenced service.
  • default: optional boolean.

If no option is marked as default, the first listed option becomes the default automatically.

docs.title: services[].env
docs.text:
Type: array.

Service-specific environment variables.

See the environment-variable naming and reserved-name rules.

docs.title: services[].helm
docs.text:
Type: array.

Service-specific Helm values.

docs.title: services[].workloads
docs.text:
Type: array.

Per-workload overrides for workloads defined by the referenced service.

Each item supports:

  • name: required workload name from the referenced service manifest. It must follow the general Kubernetes name rules.
  • deployment: optional deployment override for this workload. It supports the same fields as services[].deployment.
  • containers: optional list of container overrides for that workload.

Each workload override must contain deployment, containers, or both.

Each services[].workloads[].containers[] item supports:

  • name: required container name from the referenced service manifest. It must follow the general Kubernetes name rules.
  • env: optional container-specific environment variables.
  • resources: optional resource overrides. Each value overrides only the service's default for that value; the values you leave out keep the service's defaults.

resources supports:

  • preset: name of a Wodby resource preset, such as small or large. Its values fill in the four values below that you leave out, and the values you write override it. Custom presets of an organization can't be used in manifests.
  • request.cpu
  • request.memory
  • limit.cpu
  • limit.memory

CPU values are in millicores (1000 is one core) and must be multiples of 10. Memory values are in MiB and must be multiples of 16.

Use the same workload names and container names declared by the referenced service. You only need to list the workloads and containers you want to override. Stack import validates these targets against the referenced service manifest.

docs.title: services[].volumes
docs.text:
Type: array.

Overrides sizes for volumes defined by the referenced service.

Each item supports:

  • name: required service volume name. It must follow the general Kubernetes name rules.
  • size: required size in GB, minimum 1.

docs.title: services[].endpoints
docs.text:
Type: array.

Keeps ports of the referenced service private in this stack's app environments. A private port gets no domain, no certificate, and no public port. Services in the same app environment still reach it by service name and port.

Use it when a service is public by default but this stack only needs it on the app environment's private network, for example an OpenTelemetry Collector that only the stack's own services send to.

Each item supports:

  • name: required name of an endpoint of the referenced service.
  • ports: required list of ports, each with:
  • name: required name of a port of that endpoint.
  • private: required, must be true.
services:
  - name: otel-collector
    title: OpenTelemetry Collector
    service: opentelemetry-collector
    endpoints:
      - name: otlp
        ports:
          - name: otlp-http
            private: true

A stack can only make a public port private. It can't publish a port that the service keeps private. Validation fails when the endpoint or port doesn't exist in the service's endpoints, or when the port uses routeToPublicPort. The main service's public HTTP port on its main endpoint can't be made private, because it serves the app environment's root technical route. Derivatives keep the ports their service defines.

When an app environment is upgraded to a stack revision that makes a port private, Wodby removes the port's technical routes and closes its public port. A custom domain on that port stops the upgrade; remove the domain first.

docs.title: services[].links
docs.text:
Type: array.

Links a stack service to another stack service to satisfy links defined by the referenced service.

Each item supports:

  • name: required service-defined link name.
  • service: required target stack service name.

Required service links must be satisfied in the stack definition.

The link mapping remains part of the stack configuration when the source service is disabled. An enabled source service cannot have a disabled target for a required link; both source and target may be disabled. Stack drafts can temporarily omit required mappings while being edited, but they cannot be published or used to create or upgrade an app until all required links are valid.

When both linked services are part of the same app deployment, Wodby deploys the linked target service first. App-level link overrides can change that order for a specific app environment. A link override cannot introduce a dependency cycle.

docs.title: services[].cron
docs.text:
Type: array.

Additional cron schedules for the stack service.

Each item supports:

  • name: required schedule name.
  • title: required human-readable title.
  • command: required command to run.
  • schedule: required cron schedule.

Use standard five-field crontab syntax such as 0 * * * *. Cron schedules cannot run more often than once per hour.

docs.title: services[].configs
docs.text:
Type: array.

Provides stack-specific file contents for configs defined by the referenced service.

Each item supports:

  • name: required config name from the referenced service. It must follow the general Kubernetes name rules.
  • config: required file path relative to the stack directory.
  • disabled: optional boolean.

The stack override only replaces the config content or disables the config. The delivery target (helm, filepath, or filename) is still defined by the referenced service template.

docs.title: services[].tokens
docs.text:
Type: array.

Service-specific tokens. The object shape is the same as top-level tokens. A service-specific token overrides both service-defined and stack-wide tokens with the same name and environment type.

docs.title: services[].derivatives
docs.text:
Type: array.

Overrides derivative services declared by the referenced service.

Each item supports:

  • name: required stack service name for the derivative service.
  • service: required derivative name from the referenced service.
  • required: optional boolean.
  • env: optional environment variables.
  • helm: optional Helm values.
  • deployment: optional service-wide deployment overrides.
  • workloads: optional workload-specific deployment and container overrides, with the same shape as services[].workloads.

Only derivatives declared by the referenced service can be used here. Derivative stack service names follow the same Kubernetes service name rules as services[].name.

If the referenced service inherits derivatives from another service, use the rewritten derivative name in service. For example, if drupal11-php inherits php-sshd from php, the stack derivative should reference service: drupal11-php-sshd. The name can still be a stack-local alias such as sshd.

docs.title: Stack updates
docs.text:
Stacks are versioned. Dashboard-managed stack configuration edits create or update an unpublished draft revision first. The currently published revision remains active for running app environments until you publish the draft. Manual stack service revision updates also create or update an unpublished draft. Git updates, sync with origin, and automatic stack updates create a new published stack revision directly after the update task succeeds.

When a new revision is published, from a draft or by a stack update, app environments with auto-upgrade enabled move to it during their upgrade time window. Other app environments keep their current revision until you upgrade them.

There are several common update paths.

docs.title: Update stack service revisions
docs.text:
Use this when the stack should keep the same stack definition but move included services to newer service revisions.

Open Stacks, select the stack, and go to Operations. Owned stacks show a Service update card with the available updates and actions to update all eligible services.

When updates are available, the card lists the affected services and shows the current and latest service revision versions. When every unpinned service already uses the latest available service revision, the card shows an Up to date tag and the update button is disabled.

Select Ignore this version on an update row when that exact target revision should not be used by this stack. Confirming the action removes it from the update suggestions and prevents service revision auto-update from selecting it. Ignoring does not create a stack draft or change running app environments. If the service later publishes another revision, that new revision is suggested again even when it has the same visible version label.

An ignore applies to the named root stack service and its derivatives. If a stack includes the same underlying service under another root name, that other inclusion keeps its own update choice. Ignore choices are not copied when you create a new stack from an existing one.

Select Show changelog to review published release notes before updating. For semantic-version updates, the changelog includes stable release tags after the current version through the target version and groups them by service. For other version formats, Wodby can show the target tag's notes when the service is tag-backed. Release notes come from the Git provider, so services without published tag or release descriptions show that no release notes were found.

When a service used by the stack has a newer service revision, Wodby can update the stack services in a new or existing draft. Review the task warnings and publish the draft when it is ready.

This is also the path to refresh service option metadata used for EOL review. If a stack shows an EOL flag, update the stack services to the latest service revisions before checking exact EOL dates or selecting newly available non-EOL versions.

This update keeps stack service names and valid stack-level configuration. It is intended for service-template changes inside services that are already part of the stack, such as newer images, Helm changes, added settings, added configs, added links, new resource defaults, or new cron definitions.

If a stack-level override no longer matches the new service revision, Wodby may remove the invalid override while keeping the rest of the stack configuration. For example, a config override can be removed if the service no longer defines that config, a cron override can be removed if it targets a workload that no longer exists, or an integration can be removed if the linked integration no longer satisfies the service requirements.

When Wodby chooses a safe fallback during the update, the update task can finish with warnings. Open the task logs to review what changed. Warnings can include removed invalid overrides or derivative stack services created with a fallback name because the expected name was already taken.

If a new service revision introduces a required link, Wodby preserves any existing compatible target but does not guess a new one. A missing or incompatible target remains an unresolved draft issue and blocks publication. Configure the link target on the affected stack service, then publish the draft. If a required link already selects a compatible disabled stack service, Wodby enables that target and its required dependencies automatically.

This workflow can be used for dashboard-managed and Git-backed stacks. For Git-backed stacks, it does not fetch the stack repository or apply stack.yml changes. Use Update from Git when the stack manifest itself changed, or when you want to change a pinned/versioned service reference from Git.

docs.title: Auto-update stack service revisions
docs.text:
Use this for stacks that should follow newer service revisions without a manual stack update step.

When auto-update is enabled for stack service revisions, Wodby can create a new stack revision after a service used by the stack gets a newer revision. Before creating the revision, Wodby checks the eligible service updates against the stack's complete link graph. A service revision that would introduce an unresolved required link is skipped and the update outcome reports why. Other safe service revision updates can continue in the same run.

Automatic reconciliation preserves compatible mappings and removes invalid optional mappings. When an existing compatible mapping becomes required, its target and required dependencies are enabled automatically. Wodby never chooses a target for a missing required mapping.

For custom stacks, auto-update is disabled by default. Git-backed stacks can use this setting for service revision updates; Wodby updates stack service rows in a new stack revision without fetching the stack repository.

In the dashboard, open Stacks, select the stack, and go to Operations. Service revision automation is configured in the Services auto update card. For Git-backed stacks, this card is shown separately from Auto update from git, which controls Git imports.

Wodby catalog stacks added from the catalog enable this setting by default unless you turn off Services auto update in the Add stack form. Their default policy updates stateless services only, uses semantic-version mode, allows patch and minor updates, and disables major updates.

Pinned stack services are skipped by manual and automatic service revision updates. They do not make the stack Outdated. Pin a stack service when it should stay on its current service revision until you explicitly unpin it or update the stack from Git with a different service reference.

A stack service that stack.yml pins with serviceRevPinned and an unversioned service reference keeps its current service revision when the stack is updated from Git or from a stack template. Remove the pin, or use a versioned reference such as php:8.3, to change it.

Disabled stack services are still considered by manual and automatic service revision updates. If a disabled service should stay on its current service revision, pin it. To skip only the update currently being offered, use Ignore this version in the Service update card instead.

The stack auto-update policy controls which service revision changes are allowed. Choose the service update scope and one version mode: semantic-version updates, non-semver updates, or revision updates.

Option Effect Update stateless only Update only services whose target manifests have no database, StatefulSet workloads, or owned persistent volumes. Update all services Allow stateful and stateless services. Use this only when the stack can accept automatic stateful-service changes. Semantic-version updates Update only when the target service version is a stable semantic version. If the current service version is also semantic-version compatible, the target must be newer. If the current version is not semantic-version compatible, Wodby allows the first move to a stable semantic-version target. Non-semver updates Update only when the target service version is non-empty, non-semver, and different from the current service version. Revision updates Update whenever the target service revision changed, even when the service version string stayed the same. Allow patch, minor, or major versions In semantic-version mode, limit updates by version segment.

By default, the saved policy allows patch and minor semantic-version updates for stateless services. It does not allow major version updates or non-semver version changes unless you enable those options. When you enable service revision auto-update for a Git-backed stack in the dashboard, Update stateless only is selected by default; review the scope before saving if the stack can accept automatic stateful-service changes.

For the Update stateless only scope, a service that mounts storage from another service is not treated as the storage owner. Volumes that borrow storage with from or delegate storage to a linked storage service with shared and link can still be updated under the stateless-only policy.

Use revision mode for services imported from a branch, such as main, when each service revision may keep the same service version string.

docs.title: Update from Git
docs.text:
Use this for stacks imported from a Git repository.

Open Stacks, select the stack, and go to Operations. Git-backed stacks show an Update from Git card with the current repository, ref type, and Git ref. Select the Git tag or branch to import and click Update.

Wodby imports the stack definition from the selected Git ref, finds the same stack by name, and creates a new stack revision from the updated stack.yml.

If an updated service revision adds a required link, stack.yml must include a compatible target for that link. Git updates fail instead of selecting a target or publishing an unresolved revision.

Use this workflow when the stack manifest itself changed in Git, for example when services were added or removed, stack-level defaults changed, or stack service configuration changed.

The update form is available only on the latest stack revision. Older stack revisions can be viewed, but they cannot be updated from Git.

docs.title: Service versions on updates from Git
docs.text:
An update from Git decides what happens to existing stack services that stack.yml names without a version, such as service: mariadb:

  • Automatic updates, which run when the repository gets new commits or tags, follow Service versions in the Git auto update settings card on Operations. The default is Use service auto update settings.
  • Manual updates move these stack services to the service's latest version, including major versions. This covers the Update from Git form, the API, and updating every stack and service that uses the same repository. The Update from Git form has its own Service versions choice for that one update.
Option What the update does with existing stack services Always update to latest Moves them to the service's latest version, including major versions. Use service auto update settings Moves them only when Services auto update is enabled and its policy allows the update, for example Update stateless only or no major updates. Otherwise they keep their version. Do not update services Keeps their current versions.

In every mode:

  • a versioned reference such as php:8.3 selects that version;
  • a stack service pinned with serviceRevPinned keeps its version;
  • a stack service that is new in stack.yml uses the latest version;
  • a stack service whose stack.yml configuration needs a newer version, for example an option, volume, or link that only the newer version has, moves to that version.

The update task log lists the stack services it kept and the ones it moved anyway, with the reason.

docs.title: Delete a Git-backed stack
docs.text: Open Stacks, select the stack, and go to Edit. Git-backed stacks show the delete action on the Edit tab, not on the Operations tab. The delete action is available only on the latest stack revision.

docs.title: Auto-update from Git
docs.text:
Git-backed stacks can be updated automatically when a supported Git provider sends a push event for the stack source. Auto-update uses the same import logic as manual Update from Git, but it is started by the webhook instead of a dashboard action.

In the dashboard, Git auto-update settings for stacks are shown in Operations > Auto update from git. Keep them separate from Services auto update: Git auto-update imports the stack manifest from Git, while service revision auto-update keeps the current stack revision definition and updates eligible stack service revision references.

The auto-update settings decide which push events are allowed:

  • Branch updates run only when the pushed branch matches the stack's tracked Git ref.
  • Tag updates run only when the stack currently tracks a valid semantic-version tag and the pushed tag is a newer semantic version.
  • Tag updates can be limited to patch, minor, or major version changes.
  • Commit-pinned stacks are not auto-updated.

When auto-update is enabled, choose either branch updates or semantic-version tag updates. Semantic-version tag updates can be enabled only when the stack currently tracks a valid semantic-version Git tag.

New Git-backed catalog stacks default to auto-update enabled. Branch-based stacks follow the tracked branch. Tag-based stacks follow newer semantic-version tags, with patch and minor updates allowed by default and major updates disabled. Custom Git-backed stacks can use the same settings when they should follow their source repository automatically.

Auto-update is skipped while a stack is already updating, while another stack update task is active, or while the stack has an unpublished draft. Resolve the draft first, then run the update again or wait for the next matching push event.

docs.title: Sync with origin
docs.text:
A copied catalog stack keeps a reference to the origin stack revision it was copied from or last synced to. Syncing with origin creates a new stack revision that brings in what changed in the origin since then.

Open Stacks, select the copied stack, and go to Operations. If the stack has an origin, the Sync with origin stack card appears with a Sync with origin button.

docs.title: How sync merges changes
docs.text:
Sync compares three versions of each item: your stack, the origin revision your stack last synced to, and the latest origin revision. Items include stack services, their settings, options, volumes, tokens, environment variables, Helm values, configs, cron schedules, annotations, links, resources, and fields such as the title or replicas.

  • What you left unchanged follows the origin: new items are added, changed values are updated, and items the origin removed are removed.
  • What you changed in your stack keeps your value. When the origin changed the same item, the sync task log lists it under Kept this stack's own changes.
  • What you removed from your stack stays removed.
  • A stack service that the origin removed is deleted only when you didn't change it in your stack and none of your app environments turned it on. Otherwise it is kept, and the task log says why.
  • If the stack ends up without a main HTTP service, Wodby picks the first stack service whose main endpoint exposes a public HTTP port.

Each stack service keeps its own service version. The service revision, pin, build source, update schedule, integrations, and SSH keys of a stack service are never taken from the origin.

docs.title: Service updates during sync
docs.text:
When the origin moved a stack service to a newer service version and configured something only that version has, such as a new option, volume, or link, your stack service has to move to the same version to take the change. Sync updates only the stack services that need it, to the service version the origin uses, and lists them before it runs.

Sync never updates a pinned stack service or a service version your stack ignores, and never moves a stack service to an older version. If such a stack service blocks the sync, the sync stops and names it. Update it yourself, or unpin it, and then sync again.

docs.title: Preview and confirm
docs.text:
Selecting Sync with origin first shows a preview of what the sync would do with the chosen options:

  • the stack services it has to update, with the current and target service versions and what needs the newer version;
  • the changes it would make, as its task log will list them;
  • the reason the sync can't run, if it can't.

Nothing changes until you confirm. When the preview lists stack services to update, confirm with Update services and sync. When your stack already follows the latest origin revision, the sync runs without a preview.

docs.title: Delete what the origin doesn't have
docs.text:
The sync form also has options for cases where you want your stack to become closer to the origin. Each option deletes items that the origin doesn't have, including items you added or changed yourself:

Dashboard option Effect Origin Helm values only Delete stack-level Helm values that do not exist in the origin. Origin env vars only Delete stack-level environment variables that do not exist in the origin. Origin tokens only Delete stack-level tokens that do not exist in the origin. Origin annotations only Delete stack-level annotations that do not exist in the origin. Origin services only Delete stack services that do not exist in the origin. Origin service config only For services that exist in both stacks, delete service-level configuration entries that do not exist in the origin.

Use the deletion options only when you are comfortable removing local stack customizations that are no longer present in the origin.

After merging, Wodby enables explicitly configured required-link targets and validates the complete link graph. Sync does not publish a revision with a missing or incompatible required link.

docs.title: Auto-sync with origin
docs.text:
Use this for copied catalog stacks that should follow their origin stack automatically.

When origin auto-sync is enabled, Wodby can create a new stack revision after the origin stack publishes a new revision. The first check is revision-based: if your stack still points to an older origin revision, it becomes a candidate for sync.

When you add a Wodby catalog stack, the Add stack form shows Auto sync with origin enabled by default. Turning that switch off creates the stack with origin auto-sync disabled. When enabled by default, origin auto-sync uses semantic-version mode with patch and minor updates allowed, major updates disabled, and no deletion options. Origin auto-sync is available only for stacks that have an origin stack revision and are not Git-backed.

In the dashboard, origin auto-sync settings are shown in the Auto sync with origin stack card next to Services auto update.

The origin version policy controls which origin revisions are allowed:

Option Effect Semantic-version updates Sync only when the target origin version is a stable semantic version. If the previously tracked origin version is also semantic-version compatible, the target must be newer. If the previously tracked version is not semantic-version compatible, Wodby allows the first move to a stable semantic-version target. Non-semver updates Sync only when the target origin version is non-empty, non-semver, and different from the previously tracked origin version. Allow patch, minor, or major versions In semantic-version mode, limit updates by version segment.

The default origin auto-sync version policy uses semantic-version mode with patch and minor updates allowed and major updates disabled. EOL status does not control origin auto-sync.

If the previously tracked origin version is not semantic-version compatible and the target origin version is semantic version compatible, semantic-version mode allows the sync as the first move to a stable semantic-version target. Non-semver mode still skips that change because it accepts only non-semver target versions.

Automatic sync merges changes the same way as a manual sync. When the origin's changes need a newer service version for some stack services, automatic sync updates them only if Services auto update is enabled for your stack and its policy allows each update, for example Update stateless only or the allowed version changes. Otherwise your stack keeps its current origin revision until you update those stack services or sync manually.

You can also configure origin auto-sync to delete items that no longer exist in the origin, including items you added or changed yourself. The available auto-sync deletion options match manual sync:

Auto-sync option Effect Keep only origin stack env vars Delete stack-level environment variables that do not exist in the origin. Keep only origin stack Helm values Delete stack-level Helm values that do not exist in the origin. Keep only origin stack tokens Delete stack-level tokens that do not exist in the origin. Keep only origin stack-level annotations Delete stack-level annotations that do not exist in the origin. Keep only origin stack services Delete stack services that do not exist in the origin. Keep only origin stack services configuration For services that exist in both stacks, delete service-level configuration entries that do not exist in the origin.

Use deletion options only when the copied stack should closely mirror the catalog origin. Leave them disabled when the stack has local customizations that should survive catalog changes.

docs.title: Publish or discard a draft
docs.text:
After any stack configuration edit creates a draft, the stack shows an unpublished draft notice.

Use Publish draft when you are ready to release the draft as a real stack revision. Publishing is the point where app environments using older stack revisions can become outdated.

Every required service link must have a compatible target before publication. A configured target is enabled automatically when an enabled source requires it, but Wodby does not select missing targets. Resolve every required-link issue on the affected stack service before retrying publication.

Use Discard to delete the draft and abandon the unpublished changes. After discard, the stack returns to its current published revision and app environments are unaffected.

docs.title: App environment upgrades
docs.text:
After a draft is published as a new stack revision, app environments still run their current stack revision until you upgrade them.

Open Apps, select the app, select an app environment, and go to Stack > Operations. See Application stack for the app environment upgrade workflow, available upgrade settings, selective deployment behavior, and the rules for repository post-deployment scripts.

docs.title: Catalog stack guides
docs.text:
Every stack in the catalog has a guide here. Guides explain what to set when creating an environment, how to sign in or connect, and what to back up. Use them together with the stack and service configuration shown in the dashboard.

A buildable stack runs the same application built from your Git repository, with your own modules, plugins, themes or code. Its guide covers what differs from the stack it is a variant of.

The source repository for each stack remains the authoritative reference for its current services, versions, links, storage, and defaults. Browse all available stacks in the Wodby stack catalog or the wodby/stacks repository.

docs.title: Application stacks
docs.text: Drupal (connect to Solr), WordPress, Ghost, Matomo (buildable), Mautic (buildable), Moodle (buildable), Discourse (buildable), Chatwoot, Mattermost, Nextcloud, Odoo (buildable), GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo, Dagster, Zammad, n8n, Metabase, Slack Inviter

docs.title: Kubernetes system stacks
docs.text: Kubernetes system stacks are deployed by Wodby to operate a cluster.

docs.title: Shared operations
docs.text:
Common application operations are documented once in the shared product documentation:

  • use database details for MariaDB and PostgreSQL connection metadata
  • use published ports for external database, Redis, and other non-HTTP access
  • use the web terminal for interactive access to running containers
  • use imports, backups, and cron schedules for application operations
  • use SMTP providers for reusable outbound mail credentials

Version histories are not duplicated here. See releases and tags in the corresponding stack and service source repositories.

docs.title: 3X UI stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby 3X UI catalog stack runs the 3X UI panel. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-3xui.

docs.title: Open the panel
docs.text:
The panel listens on port 2053, the only endpoint of the service. Wodby protects the service's public domains with basic auth by default. Each app service gets its own generated password. Reveal it under Endpoints > Auths for the app environment. See Auths. You can turn the protection off when you create the app, or later by deleting the auth entry.

On the first start with an empty database, the panel creates its default administrator account. Wodby generates no credentials. Change the account in the panel.

docs.title: Panel settings
docs.text:
The panel keeps its settings, including the panel port and path, in its database. Change them in the panel, not through environment variables. Keep the panel port at 2053, because the endpoint and the health checks use it.

Wodby does not expose the ports of inbounds that you create in the panel.

Add other variables as environment variables on the app service and deploy.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
The stack creates two volumes, each 1 GB:

Volume Path Contents Data /etc/x-ui The panel database with users, panel settings, and inbounds Certs /root/cert Files kept in the /root/cert directory

Wodby defines no links, backups, or imports for this service.

docs.title: Apache Airflow stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Apache Airflow stack runs Apache Airflow built from your Git repository: the repository holds your DAGs, plugins and the Python packages they need, and every Airflow component runs the build. PostgreSQL holds Airflow's metadata. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-airflow.

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
Start the repository from the Airflow boilerplate and connect it when you create the app.

Path Purpose dags/ Your DAGs plugins/ Your Airflow plugins requirements.txt Python packages your DAGs need, such as providers

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Choose the Airflow version when you create the app. The build starts from the official Airflow image of that version, adds your DAGs and plugins, and installs requirements.txt with Airflow pinned to that version: a package that needs another Airflow version fails the build. Don't list apache-airflow itself.

Changes to DAGs, plugins or packages reach Airflow with the next deployment. Airflow reads DAGs and plugins from the build, not from the dags and plugins directories on the data volume, so keep them in the repository.

docs.title: What the stack runs
docs.text:
Both services are required. One Airflow app service runs four containers on the same volume: the API server and web interface (port 8080), the scheduler, the DAG processor, and the triggerer. All four, and the setup step that runs before them, use the build. Tasks run inside the scheduler container (LocalExecutor). The service is not scalable.

PostgreSQL is Airflow's metadata database. Wodby sets the connection in AIRFLOW__DATABASE__SQL_ALCHEMY_CONN, so do not set it elsewhere. The stack creates a 20 GB PostgreSQL volume. See Databases.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
Open the Airflow domain listed under Endpoints for the app environment. Before the containers start, Wodby migrates the metadata database and creates an administrator account. Open the Airflow app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal admin_username (admin) and admin_password. If the user already exists, Wodby leaves it as it is. See Tokens.

The stack also generates fernet_key, api_secret_key, and api_auth_jwt_secret. Airflow uses the Fernet key to encrypt connection passwords stored in the database. The other two secure API server sessions and tokens between Airflow components.

Users are managed by Airflow's FAB auth manager. Example DAGs are off.

docs.title: Data volume
docs.text: The Airflow data, DAGs, and logs volume is mounted at /opt/airflow in every container and holds Airflow's logs. The stack creates it with a size of 10 GB. Wodby defines no backups or imports for this service; your code lives in Git and the metadata in PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text: Add or change AIRFLOW__* environment variables on the Airflow app service and deploy it. The scheduler, DAG processor, and triggerer are separate containers with their own variables. After a change, check that it reached the container that uses it.

docs.title: Check that Airflow is healthy
docs.text: /api/v2/monitor/health on port 8080 reports the state of the metadata database, scheduler, DAG processor, and triggerer.

docs.title: Angular stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Angular catalog stack serves a built Angular application with Nginx. The current service and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-angular.

docs.title: Build and deployment
docs.text:
Start from the Angular boilerplate or connect your own repository. The deployed app service runs no Node.js process. The pipeline installs dependencies, runs the production build, and builds the image from the output directory only (dist/<project>/browser in the boilerplate). Source files and node_modules are not in the image.

If you change the name or location of the build output, change the pipeline's wodby ci build --from step too. Otherwise the image is built from the wrong directory. See Application Builds.

Nginx answers requests for paths that are not files with index.html, so client-side routes work without extra configuration. /.healthz returns status 204.

docs.title: Configuration reaches the build, not the browser
docs.text: The application runs in the browser. Environment variables of the app service, including WODBY_*, do not reach it at run time. Put the values it needs into the build, or have the application fetch them from an API.

docs.title: Web server settings
docs.text: Set NGINX_* environment variables on the app service to change Nginx, such as NGINX_HEADERS_CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY or NGINX_STATIC_EXPIRES. Do not add an nginx.conf to the repository. Changes apply with the next deployment.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace, the app service runs the Angular CLI development server in a Node.js image instead of Nginx. Expect these differences:

  • Setup installs dependencies from the lockfile. Run setup again after you change dependencies.
  • The server starts with ng serve, not with the start script in package.json. Options in that script do not apply. Options in angular.json do.
  • The server listens on port 8080 and the container's health checks probe that port. Do not change the port.
  • If the server rejects the preview host name, allow the environment's hosts with allowedHosts in the serve options of angular.json.
  • To start the server another way, set WORKSPACE_NODE_COMMAND on the app service. The command must listen on $HOST:$PORT and poll for file changes itself.

docs.title: ASP.NET Core stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby ASP.NET Core catalog stack runs an ASP.NET Core app service on .NET 10 with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and Cloud PostgreSQL services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-aspnetcore.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the ASP.NET Core boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

To use a managed database instead of the PostgreSQL container, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service's Dockerfile publishes your project with the .NET SDK and runs the result on an image that has the ASP.NET Core runtime but no SDK. It publishes the only project file (*.csproj, *.fsproj or *.vbproj) at the repository root, or else the only one in a src/<name>/ directory. When there are several, it takes the only web, worker, or executable project. Otherwise the build fails: add a build variable DOTNET_PROJECT with the project's path, such as src/Api/Api.csproj, to the app service.
  • When the repository has a packages.lock.json, the build restores exactly the locked package versions and fails if a lock file is out of date.
  • A Dockerfile from your repository replaces the service's. Its last stage must start from the service image, as in the boilerplate. See Application builds.
  • The project's target framework (TargetFramework in the project file) must match the .NET version you choose for the service.
  • The application must listen on port 8080. ASP.NET Core does that by default in this image; don't set other URLs in code. launchSettings.json is not used by a deployed application.
  • The image includes ICU and the full culture data, so cultures, number and date formats, and collation work.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Environments and requests
docs.text:
• Development environments run the application as Development. Other environment types run it as Production, so appsettings.Production.json applies and the developer exception page is off.
  • Wodby's gateway terminates HTTPS. ASP.NET Core is configured to use the forwarded headers, so request schemes, generated links, redirects, and client addresses are those of the visitor. Don't add HTTPS redirection in the application: checks inside the environment use plain HTTP.
  • WODBY_HOSTS holds the environment's domains as a JSON array. The boilerplate answers only for those domains, the app service's name, and localhost, and returns 400 Bad Request for others. Add more names to AllowedHosts in appsettings.json, separated by ;.
  • Settings from environment variables use __ for nesting. A variable named ConnectionStrings__Default on the app service is read as the Default connection string.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
The application reads these variables itself. Build connection strings from them with your client's connection string builder, such as NpgsqlConnectionStringBuilder, which quotes values correctly. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Data Protection keys
docs.text: ASP.NET Core protects authentication cookies and antiforgery tokens with Data Protection keys. By default the keys live inside the container, so they change with every deployment and differ between replicas: users are signed out and forms fail. If your application uses cookies or antiforgery, persist the keys to Valkey or to the database.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail client without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 20 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • Wodby runs the project with dotnet watch. Code changes are applied to the running application, usually within a few seconds, or the application is rebuilt and restarted when a change can't be applied. A failed build leaves the running application up; read the compiler errors in the service's logs. Reload the browser page yourself.
  • The workspace runs the application as Development unless you set DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT or ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT on the app service.
  • Setup restores the solution's packages when there is exactly one *.sln or *.slnx file at the repository root, otherwise the project's, and restores local tools from .config/dotnet-tools.json. With a packages.lock.json, restores fail instead of changing the lock file.
  • The project is chosen as in the build. Set WORKSPACE_DOTNET_PROJECT on the app service to run another one, such as src/Api/Api.csproj, or WORKSPACE_DOTNET_COMMAND to replace the start command.
  • bin/ and obj/ directories and the package cache stay out of Git status without changes to .gitignore.

docs.title: Astro stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Astro catalog stack runs a Node.js (Astro) app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and OpenTelemetry Collector services. The app runs Astro's Node.js server, which renders pages on demand and serves prerendered pages and assets. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-astro.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the Astro Boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, Mailpit for mail, and the OpenTelemetry Collector for telemetry. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

The app service's version is the Node.js version.

The boilerplate includes a health endpoint at /healthz and checks it after each deployment.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service's Dockerfile copies your build context, runs npm run build while the image is built, and starts the container with npm run start. package.json must define both scripts.
  • Use the standalone server of Astro's Node.js adapter: adapter: node({ mode: 'standalone' }) in astro.config.mjs, astro build as the build script, and node ./dist/server/entry.mjs as the start script. The boilerplate is set up this way. A static site without an adapter has no server to start, and the adapter's middleware mode needs a server of your own.
  • The Dockerfile does not install dependencies. Install them in your pipeline before the image is built, for example with wodby ci run -- npm ci, so that node_modules is part of the image. See CI/CD.
  • The service sets HOST to 0.0.0.0 and PORT to 3000. The standalone server reads both when it starts, and PORT takes precedence over server.port in your configuration. Do not change them.
  • NODE_ENV is production in every environment type, including dev, because the container runs a production build. Do not set it to development for a deployed environment.
  • The image build leaves out dist and .astro from your repository and builds them again.
  • When a container is stopped, for example during a deployment, the server ends at once. Requests in progress are cut off.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Prerendered and on-demand pages
docs.text:
Astro prerenders pages while the image is built, unless a page sets export const prerender = false or the configuration sets output: 'server'. The same server serves prerendered pages, files in public/, and pages rendered on demand.

Runtime variables are not available to npm run build. That includes link variables and secrets, so prerendered pages are built without them. Render on demand every page, endpoint, and Action that reads request data, cookies, or runtime variables, as the boilerplate's home page and /api/server-info endpoint do.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Read runtime variables on the server when a request is handled, in one of two ways:

  • process.env.
  • astro:env fields declared with context: 'server' and access: 'secret', imported from astro:env/server. Astro checks them when the server first uses them, not during the build, unless you set env.validateSecrets to true.

import.meta.env and astro:env fields with access: 'public' are replaced with their values at build time, so they cannot hold runtime variables or secrets. Only PUBLIC_ variables and context: 'client' fields reach the browser. astro.config.mjs runs during the build and reads process.env, not astro:env.

See Environment variables.

docs.title: Domains and form submissions
docs.text:
Wodby's gateway terminates TLS and passes the original Host header with X-Forwarded-Proto: https. Astro uses these headers only for the domains listed in security.allowedDomains. Without a match, Astro.url is http://localhost:3000/....

The environment's domains are in WODBY_HOSTS at runtime, but not while the image is built, where allowedDomains is fixed. The boilerplate handles this in two files. Keep both if you change them:

  • astro.config.mjs sets allowedDomains: [{}], which accepts every domain.
  • src/middleware.ts rejects, with 400, any request whose X-Forwarded-Host is not one of the domains in WODBY_HOSTS. Without it, a client could choose the host of Astro.url itself.

With this setup, Astro.url is https://<your domain>/.... Astro.clientAddress is the first X-Forwarded-For value, which a client can set, so do not use it for access control.

Astro rejects form-encoded POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE requests from another origin to on-demand pages and Actions with 403 (security.checkOrigin, on by default). When the browser sends no Sec-Fetch-Site header, Astro compares the Origin header with the origin of Astro.url, which is why the domain setup above matters.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, mail, and telemetry
docs.text:
On-demand pages, endpoints, Actions, and middleware read these variables when a request is handled. They are not exposed to the browser. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT OpenTelemetry Collector OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

The Node.js adapter stores sessions in the container's file system by default. They are lost on every deployment and are not shared between replicas. Configure a Redis session driver with the Valkey link before you use Astro.session.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
The OpenTelemetry variables are the standard SDK settings, so an OpenTelemetry SDK in your application exports to the Collector without further configuration. The boilerplate does not include one. Set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME to name the application in traces.

The Collector accepts data only from inside the environment. It forwards traces, metrics, and logs to the OTLP/HTTP endpoint in its Upstream OTLP endpoint setting, with the Upstream Authorization header setting if your backend needs one.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail transport without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 10 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

The app service has no volume, and no backup or import operation in Wodby.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • Setup installs dependencies from the lockfile. Run setup again after you change dependencies.
  • The app service runs astro dev from node_modules with your Astro configuration, not the dev script in package.json. Options in that script do not apply. astro must be a dependency of the project.
  • The development server listens on 0.0.0.0:3000. server.host and server.port in your configuration do not apply.
  • The development server rejects host names it does not know. Add the environment's hosts to server.allowedHosts in astro.config.mjs. WODBY_HOSTS holds them as a JSON array; the boilerplate's astro.config.mjs reads it.
  • NODE_ENV is development. Saved files are picked up within seconds, without a restart. New files can take longer. The npm run build step does not run.
  • dist/ and .astro/ are kept out of Git status.
  • To start the server another way, set WORKSPACE_NODE_COMMAND on the app service. The command must listen on $HOST:$PORT and poll for file changes itself.
  • A change to variables or linked services still needs a deployment of the environment.

docs.title: authentik stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby authentik catalog stack runs authentik, the open source identity provider for single sign-on with OAuth2, OpenID Connect, SAML, LDAP and more. It runs the official authentik image as a server and a worker, with PostgreSQL, shared file storage, and an optional OpenSMTPD service for mail. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-authentik.

Service What it does authentik Serves the user and admin interfaces, the API, and the sign-in flows Worker Runs authentik's background tasks, such as blueprints, email, and directory synchronization. Required PostgreSQL Stores users, applications, providers, flows, sessions, authentik's cache, and its task queue Shared file storage Holds uploaded icons, logos, backgrounds, and reports for the server and the worker OpenSMTPD Sends authentik's email. Disabled by default

docs.title: Administrator account
docs.text:
Set the first administrator in the authentik service's settings when you create the app. Both settings are required:

Setting What it sets Admin email The email address of the akadmin administrator Admin password The administrator's password

The first deployment creates the akadmin user in the authentik Admins group. Because this account has a password, authentik's initial setup page is closed, so nobody else can claim a new installation.

Open the app's main route and sign in with akadmin or the admin email, and the admin password. The admin interface is at /if/admin/.

The settings are only used when the administrator is created. Changing them later does not change the account. Change the password, and add other people, in authentik.

docs.title: Connect your applications
docs.text:
In the admin interface, create a provider, for example OAuth2/OpenID Provider or SAML Provider, and an application that uses it, under Applications > Applications. For OpenID Connect, the issuer of an application with the slug my-app is https://<your-domain>/application/o/my-app/, and the discovery document is at /application/o/my-app/.well-known/openid-configuration.

To protect an app that has no sign-in of its own, use a Proxy Provider with authentik's embedded outpost, which runs in the authentik service.

docs.title: Domain and base URL
docs.text:
authentik uses the environment's primary URL as its base URL, which it uses for links in emails and other places outside a request. authentik stores it the first time it starts. After you add a domain or change the primary domain, update the base URL under System > Settings in authentik. See Domains.

TLS ends at Wodby's router, and authentik builds https:// addresses from the request's domain.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
authentik sends password recovery, email verification, and notification emails. The OpenSMTPD service is disabled by default. Either enable it, or set your own SMTP server with AUTHENTIK_EMAIL__* environment variables on the authentik service. See Environment variables.

While authentik is linked to OpenSMTPD, it sends from noreply@ and the primary domain. Attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD for production delivery, and make sure your provider accepts that sender. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
Add or change AUTHENTIK_* environment variables on the authentik service and deploy it. The worker gets the same variables. Manage applications, providers, flows, policies, and users in the admin interface or the API.

The secret_key token in Configuration > Tokens signs cookies and sessions. Changing it signs everyone out. See Tokens.

docs.title: Resources and replicas
docs.text:
The authentik server requests 0.2 CPU and 768 MB of memory, with a 1.5 GB memory limit. The worker requests 0.1 CPU and 384 MB of memory, with a 1 GB memory limit. Change them in Runtime > Resources. See Resources tab.

You can run several replicas of the server and the worker. They share the database and the file storage. See Replicas.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL (10 GB by default) holds authentik's data. The shared file storage (5 GB volume) holds uploaded files. Back up the PostgreSQL database and the shared file storage to keep a complete installation. See Backups and Imports.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text: authentik migrates its database when a newer version starts and refuses to skip a version. Back up the PostgreSQL database, then choose the next version on the General configuration tab or upgrade the stack. Moving back to an older version is not supported: restore the backup instead.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• authentik can't deploy outposts to the cluster. The embedded outpost serves proxy providers. Run other outposts, such as LDAP or RADIUS, yourself and connect them to authentik.
  • Wodby delivers new authentik releases as new versions of the service, so authentik's own update check is off.

docs.title: Chatwoot stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Chatwoot catalog stack runs Chatwoot with a Sidekiq worker, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Redis, shared attachment storage, and an optional OpenSMTPD service. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-chatwoot.

docs.title: Sign in as the first administrator
docs.text:
Set Admin email on the Chatwoot app service when you create the app. Replace the admin@example.com placeholder with your own address, because Chatwoot sends password resets to it.

Before the web server starts, Wodby creates a super admin and a first Chatwoot account named Chatwoot, so Chatwoot's onboarding page is never offered. No mail is needed.

  1. Open the Chatwoot app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal admin_password. See Tokens.
  2. Open the app's main domain and sign in with Admin email and that password.
  3. Change the password in your profile settings, and rename the account under Settings > Account Settings.

The token and Admin email are used only while no super admin exists. Changing them later does not change an existing administrator, and neither does a later deployment. To change the administrator's address, edit the user in the Super Admin console at /super_admin. This is also how you replace the placeholder if you kept it.

If Admin email is not a valid address, the Chatwoot service does not start and the deployment fails. The reason is in the service's logs. Correct the setting and deploy again.

docs.title: Upgrade an existing environment
docs.text:
When you upgrade the stack, Admin email is added with the admin@example.com placeholder and admin_password is generated.

  • If the environment already has a super admin, nothing changes. Keep signing in with your existing account.
  • If nobody finished the onboarding page, the deployment after the upgrade creates the administrator and closes the page. The page stays open until that deployment starts the new version, so upgrade soon. Sign in as described above, then replace the placeholder address in the Super Admin console.

docs.title: Settings to review when creating the app
docs.text:
Set these on the Chatwoot app service:

  • Admin email: the first administrator's sign-in address. Required.
  • Account signup: false by default, which disables public signup. api_only allows signup through the API only. The first administrator does not depend on this setting.
  • Mailer sender: the address Chatwoot uses for outbound email. Use an address your mail relay accepts.
  • Force SSL, Default locale, Log level, Rails threads, and Sidekiq concurrency.

Wodby generates the first administrator's password, the application secret, and the three Active Record encryption keys when the app is created. They are tokens on the app service's Configuration > Tokens tab.

On start, the web container prepares the database. Later deployments apply new migrations the same way.

docs.title: Mail delivery
docs.text: OpenSMTPD is optional, but SMTP is recommended for password resets and notifications. If you keep it, attach an SMTP provider integration for production delivery. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Attachments and object storage
docs.text:
Attachments are stored on the shared /app/storage volume, which the Shared attachment storage service provides.

To use S3, S3-compatible storage, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Storage instead, attach the Additional Chatwoot environment variables integration. Add the variables that Chatwoot requires for the storage provider, and override ACTIVE_STORAGE_SERVICE.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL stores Chatwoot's relational data.
  • Redis stores queue data with persistence on and eviction off.
  • The shared attachment storage service stores local attachments.

Back up both the PostgreSQL database and the shared attachment storage service to keep a complete installation. See Backups and Imports.

docs.title: ClickHouse stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby ClickHouse catalog stack runs a single ClickHouse server. The current service and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-clickhouse.

docs.title: Connect an application
docs.text:
Link your application's app service to the ClickHouse app service. See Links. The app service receives the host, port and the tokens below in variables named by the linking service. Read them in code. Do not copy the password into your repository.

Port Use 8123 HTTP interface 9000 Native protocol, private

Applications in the same app environment use both ports directly, without TLS.

The tokens are on the ClickHouse app service's Configuration > Tokens tab:

  • database: default
  • username: wodby
  • password: generated by Wodby

The account can create other users, roles and databases with SQL. Create further databases, users and grants with SQL instead of adding environment variables. Server settings are not exposed as settings or config files.

docs.title: Public address
docs.text:
Port 8123 is the main HTTP endpoint, so it gets a public HTTPS address. Port 9000 has no route.

The address answers Ok. at its root. Open /play to run queries and /dashboard for the built-in charts. Sign in with the account above.

Anyone with the password can run SQL from anywhere

The public address accepts any SQL the account allows, including statements that change or delete data. Requests without the password are refused. /play and /dashboard send the password in the URL of every query, so it can appear in ingress logs. A link such as /play?password=... also carries it.

To protect the address:

  • Keep the generated password, or replace it with one as long and random.
  • Do not share /play or /dashboard URLs or copy them into tickets or chat. Do not add the password to a URL.
  • Restrict who can reach the address with Private App Access, or disable the route. Services in the same app environment keep connecting directly. Private App Access needs an active paid subscription.
  • Do not turn on Wodby Basic Auth for this service. ClickHouse uses the Authorization header for its own login, so /play, /dashboard and HTTP clients stop working behind Basic Auth.

docs.title: Resources, data and backups
docs.text:
ClickHouse runs as a single node and does not scale. The stack requests 0.5 CPU and 1024 MiB and limits it to 2 CPU and 4096 MiB. Change resources under Runtime > Resources.

The stack adds a 20 GiB ClickHouse data volume. The service has no backup or import support.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
From any service in the app environment, GET http://<app service name>:8123/ping answers Ok. In a web terminal on the ClickHouse app service, run:

clickhouse-client --user "$CLICKHOUSE_USER" --password "$CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD" --query "SHOW DATABASES"

docs.title: Cloud MariaDB stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Cloud MariaDB catalog stack declares a MariaDB database server that runs at a cloud provider, outside the cluster. It has no containers, volumes, or configuration of its own. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-cloud-mariadb. To run MariaDB inside the app environment instead, use the MariaDB guide.

docs.title: Create an environment
docs.text:
1. Create the managed database first, from Databases, with the required cloud integration. See Managed databases and Database providers.
  2. Create the app from the Cloud MariaDB stack. When Wodby asks you to choose a database server for the service, select the managed database.

Managed database names must use lowercase letters, numbers, and dashes, start with a letter, end with a letter or number, and be 3 to 32 characters long.

docs.title: Database, user, and password
docs.text: Wodby declares one database and one user for the environment. Both are named after the app and the app environment. The application does not create them. Wodby generates the user's password once per environment. Open the app service's Configuration > Tokens tab to reveal the password token. See Tokens.

docs.title: Connect to the database
docs.text:
The host and port are those of the managed database server, not an app service name inside the environment. An app service linked to this service receives the host, port, database name, user name, and password as environment variables defined by its own link, for example DB_HOST and DB_PASSWORD on a PHP service. Read them in the application instead of hardcoding the provider's address.

For a managed database on Amazon RDS, DigitalOcean, or Azure, Wodby gives the app the server's CA certificate. Some servers accept only TLS connections. See Encrypted connections.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• There is no database container, so the web terminal has nothing to open for this service.
  • This service has no server settings. Server parameters, storage, and versions are managed on the managed database itself.
  • The service defines no backups, imports, or actions.

docs.text: The Wodby Cloud MySQL catalog stack declares a MySQL database server that runs at a cloud provider, outside the cluster. It has no containers, volumes, or configuration of its own. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-cloud-mysql. To run MySQL inside the app environment instead, use the MySQL guide.

docs.text:
1. Create the managed database first, from Databases, with the required cloud integration. See Managed databases and Database providers.
  2. Create the app from the Cloud MySQL stack. When Wodby asks you to choose a database server for the service, select the managed database.

docs.text: The Wodby Cloud PostgreSQL catalog stack declares a PostgreSQL database server that runs at a cloud provider, outside the cluster. It has no containers, volumes, or configuration of its own. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-cloud-postgres. To run PostgreSQL inside the app environment instead, use the PostgreSQL guide.

docs.title: Create an environment
docs.text:
1. Create the managed database first, from Databases, with the required cloud integration. See Managed databases and Database providers.
  2. Create the app from the Cloud PostgreSQL stack. When Wodby asks you to choose a database server for the service, select the managed database.

Managed database names must use lowercase letters, numbers, and dashes, start with a letter, end with a letter or number, and be 3 to 32 characters long.

Wodby generates the user's password once per environment. Open the app service's Configuration > Tokens tab to reveal the password token. See Tokens.

docs.title: Dagster stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Dagster stack runs Dagster with your own code: your Git repository holds a Dagster project, and Wodby builds it as a code location that Dagster's webserver and daemon load. The stack runs the Dagster webserver and daemon, the code location and a PostgreSQL database, and all three are required. Its composition is documented in wodby/stack-dagster.

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
Start the repository from the Dagster boilerplate and connect it to the code service when you create the app.

Path Purpose app/definitions.py The code location's Definitions: your assets, jobs, schedules and sensors requirements.txt Python packages your code needs

The code server loads the app.definitions module. To load another module, change the code service's Python module setting.

docs.title: Build
docs.text: The build starts from the Dagster image of the Dagster service's version, so the code location runs the same Dagster as the webserver and daemon.
