It installs requirements.txt and fails when the packages change Dagster's version: don't list dagster itself, and use Dagster libraries that match its version.

docs.title: Open the Dagster interface
docs.text: Wodby protects the Dagster app service's public domains with HTTP basic authentication. Find the generated password in Apps > [App] > [Environment] > Endpoints > Auths. Other services in the same app environment reach Dagster without the password. You can turn the protection off when you create the app, or later by deleting the entry. See Auths.

docs.title: Code locations
docs.text:
The stack sets the Dagster service's Workspace config (workspace.yaml) to load the app code location from the code service. Every deployment builds a new image and restarts the code server, and Dagster reloads the code location.

To load more code locations, such as gRPC servers that run elsewhere, open the Dagster app service's Configuration > Configs tab, override the Workspace config, add them next to app, and deploy the app service.

docs.title: Runs
docs.text:
Runs execute inside the code server, which has your code and packages, and their events are stored in PostgreSQL. Give the code service enough memory and CPU for your runs. Outputs that Dagster's default IO manager writes to the code server's disk don't survive a restart: configure an IO manager that writes to external storage for outputs that later runs read.

The Wipe all run history action deletes all run history and event logs. It cannot be undone.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: Dagster has no volume. Runs, events, and schedules are stored in the linked PostgreSQL database, so back up that database. See Backups and Database details.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The Dagster and code location services are not scalable.

docs.title: Discourse stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Discourse catalog stack runs Discourse with PostgreSQL, Redis, and OpenSMTPD. All four services are required. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-discourse.

The stack runs Wodby's prebuilt Discourse image, so there's nothing to build and no repository to connect.

docs.title: Your own plugins
docs.text: To add plugins that don't ship with Discourse, use the buildable Discourse stack instead. You list plugins by Git URL, or commit your own, in a repository started from the Discourse boilerplate, and Wodby builds Discourse with them on every push.

docs.title: Before you create the app
docs.text:
• Choose a Discourse release line as the Discourse service's version: the monthly release, the default, or the extended support release (ESR), which changes less often.
  • Set Administrator email addresses on the Discourse app service. It is required. Whoever registers an account with one of these addresses becomes an administrator. Wodby creates no administrator account.
  • Optionally set Notification email address. Without it, Discourse derives a sender from the primary hostname. The domain of this address should have valid SPF, DKIM, and reverse DNS records.

docs.title: Plugins and themes
docs.text: The plugins bundled with Discourse, such as chat, AI, solved, assign, reactions and voting, are available. Install themes and theme components from the Discourse administration interface. Other plugins need the buildable Discourse stack.

docs.title: Mail delivery
docs.text: Discourse sends mail through the stack's OpenSMTPD service, and account and administration workflows depend on it. Attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD for reliable delivery. Without a relay, mail leaves directly from the cluster address, and recipient providers often reject it. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
The two settings above and the links supply the database, Redis, and mail values. Do not set those values elsewhere.

Add other upstream DISCOURSE_* settings through the Additional environment variables integration. A change applies with the next deployment of the app service. A site setting that has a variable of the same name takes its value from the variable and cannot be changed in the Discourse administration interface.

On every start, Discourse applies database migrations and rebuilds theme and CSS assets. The health endpoint is /srv/status.

docs.title: Updates and upgrades
docs.text:
Discourse patch releases arrive as updates of the Discourse service; see stack upgrades. To move to another release line, choose its version on the General configuration tab and deploy. Back up the app first: Discourse migrates its database when the new release starts.

Do not update Discourse from its administration interface or install docker_manager.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• The Discourse volume (20 GB by default) holds uploads, backups, and logs.
  • PostgreSQL has a 20 GB volume. Redis has a 5 GB volume with persistence on and eviction off. OpenSMTPD has a 1 GB queue volume.

Use the Discourse app service backup, Discourse database and uploads, for one archive that contains the database and local uploads. It is Discourse's own backup format. Restore an archive into a disposable app from time to time to verify recovery. See Backups.

docs.title: Apps created before the prebuilt image
docs.text: Earlier versions of the Discourse stack built Discourse from a repository. Apps created from them keep building from their repository, because a new major version of a service is never applied automatically. To move to the prebuilt image, create a new app from the Discourse stack, with the same or a newer Discourse release, and restore a Discourse backup of the old app into it from Admin > Backups in Discourse.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Discourse runs as one replica. It is not scalable.
  • The Discourse container requests 0.5 CPU and 2 GiB of memory, with limits of 2 CPU and 4 GiB.

docs.title: Discourse (buildable) stack guide
docs.text:
The buildable Discourse stack runs Discourse with plugins that don't ship with it: your Git repository lists them or holds them, and Wodby builds Discourse with them. The stack has the same services as the Discourse stack: PostgreSQL, Redis and OpenSMTPD. Its composition is documented in wodby/stack-discourse-buildable.

Everything in the Discourse guide applies, from the administrator emails to mail, data and upgrades. This page covers what differs.

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
Start the repository from the Discourse boilerplate and connect it when you create the app.

Path Purpose plugins.txt Plugins to clone, one Git repository URL per line, optionally followed by a branch or tag plugins/ Plugins committed to the repository, one directory per plugin with its plugin.rb

For example:

https://github.com/discourse/discourse-bbcode.git
https://github.com/example/discourse-my-plugin.git v1.2.0

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Choose the Discourse release line when you create the app. The build starts from Wodby's Discourse image of that line, adds your plugins, installs their gems and compiles only their JavaScript: Discourse's own is reused from the image.

The build fails when a plugin has the name of a plugin that ships with Discourse, such as chat, solved or data explorer, when a directory has no plugin.rb, or when a repository can't be cloned. Turn the plugins that ship with Discourse on in its settings instead.

A plugin must support the release line you run. Pin a plugin to a branch or tag that does, for example the branch a plugin keeps for the extended support release.

docs.title: Plugins and updates
docs.text:
Discourse migrates its database when it starts, plugins' migrations included. A plugin removed from the repository disappears from Discourse on the next deployment; its data stays in the database.

Discourse's version comes from the service version and its image, not from the repository. It moves forward with service updates, and the app's next build uses it.

To run Discourse with only the plugins it ships with, use the Discourse stack.

docs.title: Distribution Registry stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Distribution Registry catalog stack runs a private CNCF Distribution Registry v3 with an optional Valkey metadata cache. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-distribution.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
Basic authentication is on by default. The account is admin. Its password is the password token on the registry app service's Configuration > Tokens tab. The registry listens on port 5000 over HTTP, so Wodby generates a technical route for it. See Endpoints.

To use the registry for your Wodby builds, create a Distribution Registry integration with the registry's hostname and this account. See Distribution Registry. The host must be reachable from the public internet.

Delegated token authentication is optional. It needs a compatible distribution-auth service linked to the registry in a custom version of the stack.

docs.title: Choose storage
docs.text:
By default the registry stores images on its persistent volume. The stack adds a 20 GiB Registry data volume.

For object storage, attach one integration to the registry app service under Connections > Integrations:

  • Google Cloud Storage: asks for a bucket and a service-account key.
  • Amazon S3: asks for a bucket, an access key, a secret key and a region.

Attach at most one storage integration. See Integrations tab.

docs.title: Replicas and zero-downtime releases
docs.text:
The registry can run several replicas. Releases start a new replica before stopping the old one. Both need the same registry storage:

  • Google Cloud Storage and Amazon S3 give every replica the same storage.
  • A filesystem volume works only if the storage class can mount the same volume in the old and the new pod. A ReadWriteOnce volume may stall the rollout. Use object storage when releases must not cause downtime.

docs.title: Metadata cache
docs.text: The Registry metadata cache is a Valkey service linked to the registry through its redis link. It is optional and enabled by default. It is a disposable cache: it writes nothing to disk, holds up to 256 MB and evicts the least recently used keys. You can exclude it when you create the app. The link also accepts a Redis service.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: The registry service has no backup or import support.

docs.title: Django stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Django catalog stack runs a Django application with Gunicorn, PostgreSQL and Valkey. A Celery worker, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg and Cloud PostgreSQL are optional. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-django.

docs.title: Build and deployment
docs.text:
Start from the Django boilerplate or connect your own repository. The boilerplate is offered only for the Python versions it supports. See Application Builds.

The container runs Gunicorn on port 8080. The defaults assume the project package is named myapp. When it is not, set both GUNICORN_APP (default myapp.wsgi:application) and CELERY_APP (default myapp) on the app service. Gunicorn must be one of your application's dependencies.

After every deployment Wodby runs these commands, in this order:

  1. python manage.py migrate
  2. python manage.py collectstatic --no-input

manage.py must be in /usr/src/app, and STATIC_ROOT must be set. Do not add these commands to the start command or the pipeline. Nothing in the stack serves the collected files, so your application serves its static files itself.

docs.title: Settings your project must read
docs.text:
The stack sets variables, but Django reads none of them by itself. Make settings.py read them:

Variable Use it for DJANGO_SECRET_KEY SECRET_KEY. Wodby generates it once, and it stays the same across deployments. DJANGO_DEBUG DEBUG. It is true in environments of type dev and absent in every other type. DATABASE_URL DATABASES. The whole connection as one URL, with credentials. CELERY_BROKER_URL The Celery broker. A redis:// URL with the password, database 0. SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT Mail settings, when Mailpit or OpenSMTPD is enabled.

You can build DATABASES from the DB_* variables instead. Do not generate or commit another secret key. Never print or commit the values of DATABASE_URL and CELERY_BROKER_URL: both contain a password.

A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled, so the settings must work without it. The mail link carries no credentials.

Set ALLOWED_HOSTS yourself. The environment's hosts are in WODBY_HOSTS, a JSON array. The internal host name is in WODBY_APP_SERVICE_NAME. See Environment variables.

docs.title: Background jobs with Celery
docs.text:
The optional Celery service runs celery worker --loglevel=INFO instead of Gunicorn. Your project needs celery among its dependencies and a Celery application in the package named by CELERY_APP. The boilerplate configures it through CELERY_BROKER_URL.

Valkey is required because it stores queued and unacknowledged work. The stack gives it a 5 GB data volume, persistence, and the noeviction policy, so broker messages are not treated as disposable cache entries. Do not use this Valkey instance for Django's cache. Add a separate cache service with an LRU policy so cache pressure cannot block broker writes.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text: Mailpit is disabled by default. Enable Mailpit to inspect mail in non-production environments. It captures every message and delivers none of them. For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL keeps data on a 20 GB data volume. A backup is a gzipped SQL dump of the environment's database. It carries no role names and no grants, so you can import it into a database with another name and other users. A database import replaces the whole data volume. The Valkey service has no backups or imports. See Application Backups and Application Imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text: In a development workspace, Gunicorn runs with its polling reloader, so a saved Python file is picked up without a restart. A change to dependencies needs setup again. File changes do not apply migrations: run manage.py migrate with the workspace's Python.

docs.title: Drupal stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Drupal catalog stack provides separate Drupal 10 and Drupal 11 entries. The current service composition and version choices are documented in wodby/stack-drupal.

Start with the Drupal CMS or Vanilla Drupal boilerplate offered by the stack, or connect a compatible Composer-based repository. The default Drupal root subdirectory is web; change the PHP app service's Drupal root subdirectory setting when your repository uses a different layout.

docs.title: Install Drupal
docs.text:
After the first deployment, open the app's main domain and finish the Drupal installer. Until the installation has finished, Drupal PHP image r16 and newer answer every other page with a 503 and the message Drupal is being installed, so nothing else can reach a half-installed site. If you left the installer, open /core/install.php to continue.

A site installed on an earlier image can show No route found, lose its theme styles, or fail when saving a form right after installation. To fix it, run Rebuild all cache from the PHP app service.

docs.title: Runtime configuration
docs.text:
The Drupal PHP runtime generates wodby.settings.php from the app environment's current environment and linked services. The runtime setup adds this file to the active Drupal site's settings.php when it initializes the site.

The generated settings provide:

  • database connection values from the selected database link
  • public, private, temporary, and configuration-sync paths
  • trusted-host patterns from the app environment routes
  • generated hash and file-sync salts
  • optional Valkey or Redis cache configuration when the Drupal Redis module is present
  • the password override used by the Drupal Solr integration

Do not edit the generated file inside a running container. Put application-specific overrides in your repository's settings.php after the Wodby include. If a custom repository replaces settings.php, keep this include:

include getenv('CONF_DIR') . '/wodby.settings.php';

docs.title: Files and configuration sync
docs.text:
The Drupal PHP service mounts shared file storage and links it to the active site's public files directory. Private files and Wodby's default configuration-sync directory use the same persistent storage.

The generated sync directory contains a stable per-app salt. You can override $settings['config_sync_directory'] in your own settings.php when configuration belongs in the application repository instead.

Use application imports for service files and database imports for database content. Use the web terminal when you need interactive access to a running container.

docs.title: Cron and application actions
docs.text:
The Drupal PHP service defines an hourly Drush cron schedule using the app environment's primary URL. You can change the schedule or run it manually from the app environment's Cron page.

The service also exposes actions to:

  • rebuild Drupal caches
  • generate a one-time login link
  • apply pending database updates

Run these from the app service operations in the dashboard. Use the web terminal for other one-off Drush or Composer commands.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, the PHP service gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. Add the OpenTelemetry PHP SDK with Composer; it then starts without code changes. See PHP applications and OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Optional services
docs.text:
The catalog stack can link Drupal to a database, shared files, Valkey, mail, Gotenberg, and Solr. Optional services and their defaults can change over time, so review the selected stack entry during app creation instead of relying on a static container list.

For search setup, see Connect Drupal to Solr.

docs.title: Connect Drupal to Solr
docs.text:
The Wodby Drupal catalog stack supports SolrCloud with ZooKeeper. Both the solr and zookeeper stack services are disabled by default, so enable both services and deploy them before configuring Drupal.

Solr creates a collection named default with its generic _default configset. Drupal's Search API Solr module must replace that configset before the collection can index Drupal content.

docs.title: Install Search API Solr
docs.text:
Add the module to your Composer project and enable its administration module:

composer require drupal/search_api_solr
vendor/bin/drush en search_api_solr search_api_solr_admin -y

Deploy the updated code, then go to Configuration > Search and metadata > Search API in Drupal and add a server.

docs.title: Configure the server
docs.text:
Name the server Solr so its machine name is solr. Select the Solr backend and the Solr Cloud with Basic Auth connector, then enter:

Setting Value HTTP protocol http Solr node solr Solr port 8983 Solr path / Default Solr collection default Solr host context solr Username solr Password Leave blank when the server machine name is solr

The Drupal PHP service receives the internal Solr hostname and generated password through its stack link. Wodby's generated wodby.settings.php applies the password to the Search API server whose machine name matches the linked Solr service. It does not replace the connector's Solr node value, so enter solr explicitly.

localhost points back to the Drupal PHP container. A server saved with localhost cannot reach the separate Solr app service.

docs.title: Upload the Drupal configset
docs.text:
After saving the server, an incompatible-schema warning is expected while the collection still uses _default.

  1. Open the Search API server's detail page.
  2. Select Upload configset.
  3. Confirm that the configset may be uploaded or overwritten.
  4. Use one shard.
  5. Submit the upload.

The Search API Solr Admin module uploads a configuration generated for the installed module version and updates the default collection. Create and configure a Search API index after the server and collection both report as available.

Upload the configset again whenever Search API Solr reports that the schema is outdated, then reindex the affected indexes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Check Server cannot be reached Solr node is solr, not localhost; both Solr and ZooKeeper are enabled and deployed Server is reachable but collection is unavailable Default Solr collection is default Authentication fails Server machine name is solr, the generated Wodby settings file is included, and username is solr Schema is incompatible Upload or overwrite the configset from the Search API server page

See the Solr catalog guide for collection and authentication behavior and the Search API Solr project for module releases and compatibility.

docs.title: Elasticsearch stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Elasticsearch catalog stack runs a single-node Elasticsearch with Kibana. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-elasticsearch.

docs.title: Connect an application
docs.text:
Link your application's app service to the Elasticsearch app service. See Links. The app service receives the host, port and password in variables named by the linking service. Read them in code. Do not copy the password into your repository.

  • URL: http://<app service name>:9200. Security is on and TLS is off, so use plain http:// with HTTP Basic authentication.
  • User: elastic, the built-in superuser. Its password is the password token on the Elasticsearch app service's Configuration > Tokens tab.
  • Port 9200 is private, and Wodby creates no route for it. Port 9300 is the transport port. Applications do not use it.

Wodby also generates a kibana_password token for the built-in kibana_system user. Kibana uses it. Do not use it from applications, and do not give Kibana the elastic password.

docs.title: Sign in to Kibana
docs.text:
Kibana is the main app service, so the app environment's root route opens it. Sign in with user elastic and the Elasticsearch password token. kibana_system cannot sign in.

The link from Kibana to Elasticsearch is required and is set up by the stack. Kibana stays unready until Elasticsearch is up. If Kibana reports that the server is not ready, check the Elasticsearch app service first.

Wodby generates three encryption keys for Kibana and keeps them stable across deployments. Replacing them signs users out and makes encrypted saved objects, such as connector secrets, unreadable.

docs.title: Single node and resources
docs.text:
Elasticsearch runs as a single node and does not scale. An index with replicas stays yellow because there is no second node, so create indices with zero replicas.

The stack requests 1 CPU and 2048 MiB for Elasticsearch and limits it to 2 CPU and 4096 MiB. The JVM heap is fixed at -Xms1g -Xmx1g by default (ES_JAVA_OPTS). If you raise the heap, keep the container memory limit above it. Kibana requests 0.5 CPU and 1024 MiB and is limited to 1 CPU and 2048 MiB. Change resources under Runtime > Resources.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
Set Elasticsearch settings as environment variables on its app service, named exactly like the setting, for example cluster.name. Do not mount an elasticsearch.yml. See Environment variables. Turning security off or HTTP TLS on changes how every linked service connects, Kibana included.

Kibana settings are variables in the image's form: the setting name in upper case with dots replaced by underscores. Do not mount a kibana.yml.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
The stack adds a 20 GiB Elasticsearch data volume. Kibana has no volume. Dashboards, data views and other saved objects live in Elasticsearch.

The services have no backup or import support. Snapshots need a repository configured in Elasticsearch itself.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
In a web terminal on the Elasticsearch app service, run:

curl -s -u "elastic:$ELASTIC_PASSWORD" http://localhost:9200/_cluster/health?pretty

docs.title: FastAPI stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby FastAPI catalog stack runs a Python (FastAPI) app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and Cloud PostgreSQL services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-fastapi.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the FastAPI boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

To use a managed database instead of the PostgreSQL container, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The container runs Gunicorn with Uvicorn workers on port 8080. Do not add a uvicorn start command to the Dockerfile and do not change the port.
  • GUNICORN_APP is main:app: the object app in main.py at the root of the repository. Set the variable on the app service if your application lives elsewhere.
  • Gunicorn and uvicorn-worker are not in the image. Add both to your dependencies, or Gunicorn fails to start.
  • Set the number of workers with GUNICORN_WORKERS. Other Gunicorn settings are GUNICORN_* variables on the app service. A Gunicorn configuration file in the repository is not loaded.
  • The service's Dockerfile installs requirements.txt when the file exists. A Dockerfile from your repository replaces it and must install the dependencies itself. See Application builds.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
The application reads these variables itself. FastAPI has no settings convention of its own, so read these names. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail transport without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 20 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • The application starts with Uvicorn and --reload, so a saved Python file is picked up without a restart.
  • Run workspace preparation again after changing dependencies.

docs.title: Flask stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Flask catalog stack runs a Python (Flask) app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and Cloud PostgreSQL services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-flask.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the Flask boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

To use a managed database instead of the PostgreSQL container, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• Gunicorn serves the application on port 8080. Do not add a flask run command or an app.run() call for deployment.
  • GUNICORN_APP is app:app: the object app in the module or package app at the root of the repository. Set the variable on the app service if your application lives elsewhere, for example to call an application factory.
  • Flask and Gunicorn are not in the image. Add both to your dependencies.
  • Set the number of workers with GUNICORN_WORKERS. Other Gunicorn settings are GUNICORN_* variables on the app service. A Gunicorn configuration file in the repository is not loaded.
  • FLASK_DEBUG is true in environments of type dev only. Wodby sets no other FLASK_* variable and no secret key. If your application uses sessions, add its SECRET_KEY as a secret variable on the app service.
  • The service's Dockerfile installs requirements.txt when the file exists. A Dockerfile from your repository replaces it and must install the dependencies itself. See Application builds.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
Flask does not read these variables on its own: your application code must read them. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail transport without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 20 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • Gunicorn reloads when you save a Python file.
  • Run workspace preparation again after changing dependencies.

docs.title: Forgejo stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Forgejo catalog stack runs Forgejo, a self-hosted Git service, with PostgreSQL and an optional OpenSMTPD service. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-forgejo.

Forgejo and PostgreSQL are required. OpenSMTPD is selected by default, and you can leave it out when you create the app.

docs.title: Administrator account
docs.text:
Set the administrator in the Forgejo service's settings when you create the app:

Setting What it sets Admin username The administrator's username, forgejo_admin by default. Some names, such as admin, are reserved Admin password Required. The administrator's password, at least 8 characters Admin email The administrator's email address. When empty, it is the username at the main domain

Forgejo creates this account on its first start. The web installer is never shown, so nobody else can claim the site. Open the app's main domain and sign in with these credentials.

If the password is missing or shorter than 8 characters, Forgejo stops with an error and the deployment fails. Fix the setting and deploy again.

The settings are only used while Forgejo has no administrator. Changing them later changes nothing; change the password in Forgejo.

Registration is closed. Add accounts in Forgejo's Site Administration, or open sign-up by setting the environment variable FORGEJO__service__DISABLE_REGISTRATION to false and deploying the service.

docs.title: Clone repositories
docs.text:
HTTPS works through the main domain without extra setup. Git LFS is on. The route has no request timeout, so long clones and large pushes are not cut off.

Forgejo takes its address from the main domain. After you change the main domain, Wodby marks the Forgejo service for redeployment; deploy it so that Forgejo and its clone URLs use the new address.

SSH needs a published port. Until you publish it, SSH is off and Forgejo shows only HTTPS clone URLs.

  1. Open the app environment's Endpoints > Ports page and publish the Forgejo ssh port. See Publishing ports.
  2. Wodby assigns a public port from the range 31222-32222 and deploys Forgejo again. Forgejo turns SSH on and shows SSH clone URLs with the main domain and that port, for example ssh://git@forgejo.example.com:31222/owner/repository.git.
  3. Add your public SSH key in Forgejo under your user Settings > SSH / GPG Keys. Wodby SSH keys are not used for Git.

The SSH user is git. The cluster must support TCP port publishing; the Ports page says so if it doesn't.

docs.title: Mail delivery
docs.text:
The OpenSMTPD service is optional. While the Forgejo app service is linked to it, Forgejo sends mail through it from noreply@<main domain>. To send from another address, set the FORGEJO__mailer__FROM environment variable on the Forgejo service.

Attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD for production delivery, and make sure the provider accepts the sender domain. Without a relay, mail leaves directly from the cluster address, and recipient providers often reject it. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

Without OpenSMTPD, Forgejo sends no mail.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
Forgejo reads FORGEJO__<section>__<KEY> environment variables, for example FORGEJO__service__DISABLE_REGISTRATION for the DISABLE_REGISTRATION key in the [service] section. On every start it writes them to its app.ini configuration file. The keys are listed in Forgejo's configuration cheat sheet.

Add or edit the variables on the Forgejo app service and deploy it. See Environment variables.

  • Removing a variable does not remove its key from app.ini. Set the value you want instead. For example, if you remove the mail link from an existing app, set FORGEJO__mailer__ENABLED to false.
  • Wodby sets the site address, the database connection, mail while the link exists, and the app's title as the site name. Leave these to Wodby.
  • Users, organizations, and other data you manage in Forgejo are kept in the database and are not affected.

Wodby generates Forgejo's secret key and internal tokens and keeps them stable across deployments. They are on the Forgejo app service's Configuration > Tokens tab. Do not change secret_key: Forgejo can no longer read two-factor authentication secrets and other values it encrypted with it.

docs.title: Run CI jobs
docs.text: Forgejo Actions is available, but the stack includes no runner. To run workflows, register an external Forgejo Runner with Forgejo through the main domain.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• The Forgejo volume (20 GB by default) holds repositories, Git LFS objects, packages, attachments, avatars, Actions logs and artifacts, the SSH host keys, and app.ini.
  • Everything else, such as users, issues, and pull requests, is in PostgreSQL, which has its own 20 GB volume.

Back up the database and the Forgejo volume together as one recovery set. The Forgejo service has no backup or import operation in Wodby. The PostgreSQL service does. See Backups.

docs.title: Versions and upgrades
docs.text:
The Forgejo service offers two versions: the current release by default, or the long-term support release, which gets fixes for longer. Choose the version when you create the app environment.

Do not switch an existing environment from the current release to the long-term support release. Forgejo refuses to start on a database written by a newer version. See Forgejo's upgrade guide.

When a new stack revision brings a newer Forgejo, upgrade the app environment's stack. See Upgrade. Forgejo migrates its database when it starts, and Wodby waits up to 15 minutes for it to answer. Back up first.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The Forgejo service is fixed to one replica. Its data is on a single volume, so it can't be scaled.
  • No Forgejo Runner is included.
  • Forgejo requests 0.2 CPU and 512 MiB of memory and is limited to 2 CPU and 2048 MiB. Change resources under Runtime > Resources.

docs.title: FRP Server stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby FRP Server catalog stack runs an frps server for workloads that are outside the cluster. An external frpc client connects to the server's published control port and registers one or more HTTP hostnames. Wodby terminates public TLS for those hostnames and forwards HTTP to FRPS, which sends the requests through the tunnel to the external workload.

This application stack is separate from the FRPC infrastructure component installed on Kubernetes machines. It does not configure cluster connectivity or require Kubernetes permissions.

docs.title: Deploy and expose FRPS
docs.text:
1. Create an app from the FRP Server catalog stack and deploy it.
  2. Open Apps > [App] > [Environment] > Endpoints > Ports, select the proxy endpoint, and publish its control TCP port. Wodby assigns a public port in the cluster's published port range.
  3. Record the public hostname and assigned port. Open the FRPS app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal its generated auth_token value. Every FRPC client must use the same token.
  4. Add a custom route for every hostname listed in an FRPC proxy's customDomains. Target the FRPS service's proxy endpoint and proxy-http port.

The dashboard port on the proxy endpoint has separate generated dashboard_user and dashboard_password token values. Its port-specific technical Wodby route is suitable for administration; do not reuse the dashboard password as the FRPC token.

docs.title: Configure an FRPC client
docs.text:
The following client configuration exposes a dashboard and API running on an external server. Replace the example hostname, published port, and token with the values from the Wodby app:

serverAddr = "tunnel.example.com"
serverPort = 31500

auth.method = "token"
auth.token = "replace-with-the-generated-auth-token"
transport.tls.enable = true

[[proxies]]
name = "dashboard"
type = "http"
localIP = "127.0.0.1"
localPort = 3000
customDomains = ["tunnel.example.com"]

[[proxies]]
name = "api"
type = "http"
localIP = "127.0.0.1"
localPort = 8080
customDomains = ["api.tunnel.example.com"]

Create routes for both tunnel.example.com and api.tunnel.example.com. Point their DNS records at the Wodby cluster before enabling Let's Encrypt. Do not publish the proxy-http port manually; HTTP traffic enters through Wodby routes.

When a client workload itself moves into Wodby, route directly to that app service instead of tunneling it back through FRPS.

docs.title: Ghost stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Ghost catalog stack combines Ghost, MySQL, and OpenSMTPD services. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-ghost.

docs.title: Before you create the app
docs.text:
Set Email sender on the Ghost app service. It is required. Use the form Ghost <ghost@example.com>, with an address that your mail relay accepts.

Ghost needs MySQL, which the stack includes. MariaDB is not supported.

docs.title: First sign-in
docs.text: Wodby does not create an administrator account. Open /ghost/ on the app's main route and create the owner account in the browser.

docs.title: Mail delivery
docs.text:
Ghost sends mail through the stack's OpenSMTPD service. Password resets, staff invitations, and member email need working mail delivery. Recipient mail servers often reject mail sent directly from a cluster, so attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD for production. See the OpenSMTPD guide for relay setup and testing.

Ghost also has the Verify new devices by email setting on the app service's Configuration > Settings tab. It is false by default. When it is true, staff who sign in from a new device must enter a code sent by email. Turn it on only after you have confirmed that mail is delivered. Otherwise staff cannot sign in.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
Add or change environment variables on the Ghost app service, then deploy it. Use Ghost's section__key form, for example mail__from. Database and mail connection values come from the stack links. Do not set them elsewhere. See Environment variables.

Ghost builds its links from the environment's primary URL, so they change when the primary host changes.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• The Content volume (20 GB by default) holds images, themes, and other content files.
  • Posts, users, and settings are in the MySQL database.

The Ghost content backup and content import cover only the volume. They accept tar, tar.gz, tgz, and zip archives for imports. They do not include the database, so also back up MySQL. See Backups and Imports.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Ghost runs as one replica. Use an external CDN or cache for more delivery capacity instead of adding replicas.
  • The route accepts request bodies up to 50 MiB.
  • A new major Ghost version can change where content is stored and need an explicit storage migration. Read Ghost's upgrade notes before you move to a new major version, and do not treat it as a routine update.

docs.title: Gitea stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Gitea catalog stack runs Gitea, a self-hosted Git service, with PostgreSQL and an optional OpenSMTPD service. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-gitea.

Gitea and PostgreSQL are required. OpenSMTPD is selected by default, and you can leave it out when you create the app.

docs.title: Administrator account
docs.text:
Set the administrator in the Gitea service's settings when you create the app:

Setting What it sets Admin username The administrator's username, gitea_admin by default. Some names, such as admin, are reserved Admin password Required. The administrator's password, at least 8 characters Admin email The administrator's email address. When empty, it is the username at the main domain

Gitea creates this account on its first start. The web installer is never shown, so nobody else can claim the site. Open the app's main domain and sign in with these credentials.

If the password is missing or shorter than 8 characters, Gitea stops with an error and the deployment fails. Fix the setting and deploy again.

The settings are only used while Gitea has no administrator. Changing them later changes nothing; change the password in Gitea.

Registration is closed. Add accounts in Gitea's Site Administration, or open sign-up by setting the environment variable GITEA__service__DISABLE_REGISTRATION to false and deploying the service.

docs.title: Clone repositories
docs.text:
HTTPS works through the main domain without extra setup. Git LFS is on. The route has no request timeout, so long clones and large pushes are not cut off.

Gitea takes its address from the main domain. After you change the main domain, Wodby marks the Gitea service for redeployment; deploy it so that Gitea and its clone URLs use the new address.

SSH needs a published port. Until you publish it, SSH is off and Gitea shows only HTTPS clone URLs.

  1. Open the app environment's Endpoints > Ports page and publish the Gitea ssh port. See Publishing ports.
  2. Wodby assigns a public port from the range 31222-32222 and deploys Gitea again. Gitea turns SSH on and shows SSH clone URLs with the main domain and that port, for example ssh://git@gitea.example.com:31222/owner/repository.git.
  3. Add your public SSH key in Gitea under your user Settings > SSH / GPG Keys. Wodby SSH keys are not used for Git.

The SSH user is git. The cluster must support TCP port publishing; the Ports page says so if it doesn't.

docs.title: Mail delivery
docs.text:
The OpenSMTPD service is optional. While the Gitea app service is linked to it, Gitea sends mail through it from noreply@<main domain>. To send from another address, set the GITEA__mailer__FROM environment variable on the Gitea service.

Attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD for production delivery, and make sure the provider accepts the sender domain. Without a relay, mail leaves directly from the cluster address, and recipient providers often reject it. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

Without OpenSMTPD, Gitea sends no mail.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
Gitea reads GITEA__<section>__<KEY> environment variables, for example GITEA__service__DISABLE_REGISTRATION for the DISABLE_REGISTRATION key in the [service] section. On every start it writes them to its app.ini configuration file. The keys are listed in Gitea's configuration cheat sheet.

Add or edit the variables on the Gitea app service and deploy it. See Environment variables.

  • Removing a variable does not remove its key from app.ini. Set the value you want instead. For example, if you remove the mail link from an existing app, set GITEA__mailer__ENABLED to false.
  • Wodby sets the site address, the database connection, mail while the link exists, and the app's title as the site name. Leave these to Wodby.
  • Users, organizations, and other data you manage in Gitea are kept in the database and are not affected.

Wodby generates Gitea's secret key and internal tokens and keeps them stable across deployments. They are on the Gitea app service's Configuration > Tokens tab. Do not change secret_key: Gitea can no longer read two-factor authentication secrets and other values it encrypted with it.

docs.title: Run CI jobs
docs.text: Gitea Actions is available, but the stack includes no runner. To run workflows, register an external Gitea Actions runner with Gitea through the main domain.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• The Gitea volume (20 GB by default) holds repositories, Git LFS objects, packages, attachments, avatars, Actions logs and artifacts, the SSH host keys, and app.ini.
  • Everything else, such as users, issues, and pull requests, is in PostgreSQL, which has its own 20 GB volume.

Back up the database and the Gitea volume together as one recovery set. The Gitea service has no backup or import operation in Wodby. The PostgreSQL service does. See Backups.

docs.title: Versions and upgrades
docs.text:
The Gitea service offers the current Gitea release.

When a new stack revision brings a newer Gitea, upgrade the app environment's stack. See Upgrade. Gitea migrates its database when it starts, and Wodby waits up to 15 minutes for it to answer. Back up first.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The Gitea service is fixed to one replica. Its data is on a single volume, so it can't be scaled.
  • No Actions runner is included.
  • Gitea requests 0.2 CPU and 512 MiB of memory and is limited to 2 CPU and 2048 MiB. Change resources under Runtime > Resources.

docs.title: GitLab stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby GitLab catalog stack runs GitLab Community Edition from the official GitLab Helm chart, with PostgreSQL, Valkey, OpenSMTPD, and an optional GitLab Runner. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-gitlab.

GitLab, PostgreSQL, Valkey, and OpenSMTPD are required. The GitLab Runner service is disabled until you enable it.

docs.title: Before you create the app
docs.text:
• Prepare S3-compatible object storage and a variable integration for it, as described below. GitLab can't be created without it.
  • Plan capacity. GitLab names 16 GB of memory and 8 vCPU as the baseline for a single-node installation. The cluster must fit GitLab's web, background job, Git, SSH, Registry, and toolbox pods together with PostgreSQL, which requests 0.5 CPU and 2.5 GiB of memory, with limits of 2 CPU and 4 GiB. CI jobs add their own pods. See the GitLab installation requirements.
  • Set up a custom domain as the main domain if you want GitLab, its clone URLs, and its mail to use your own hostname. See Endpoints.

docs.title: Prepare object storage
docs.text:
GitLab keeps CI artifacts, Git LFS objects, uploads, packages, Container Registry images, and backup archives in object storage. Create seven buckets with distinct names before you create the app: artifacts, LFS, uploads, packages, Registry, backups, and temporary restore data. GitLab serves artifact, LFS, upload, and package downloads itself.

The GitLab app service requires an S3-compatible object storage integration that supplies these variables:

Variable Secret Value GITLAB_OBJECT_STORAGE_CONNECTION Yes GitLab's object storage connection in YAML, such as provider, region, keys, and endpoint GITLAB_REGISTRY_STORAGE_CONFIG Yes The contents of the Registry storage block, with an S3 driver and the Registry bucket GITLAB_BACKUP_S3_CONFIG Yes An s3cmd configuration file for the backup tool GITLAB_ARTIFACTS_BUCKET No Bucket for CI artifacts GITLAB_LFS_BUCKET No Bucket for Git LFS objects GITLAB_UPLOADS_BUCKET No Bucket for uploads GITLAB_PACKAGES_BUCKET No Bucket for packages GITLAB_REGISTRY_BUCKET No Bucket for Container Registry images, the same one named in the Registry configuration GITLAB_BACKUPS_BUCKET No Bucket for backup archives GITLAB_BACKUPS_TMP_BUCKET No Bucket for temporary restore data

The formats are described in GitLab's external object storage guide.

To supply the variables, create a custom variable provider with New from manifest, create an integration from it with your values, and select that integration for GitLab when you create the app. Secret variables must come from secret fields. For example:

name: gitlab-object-storage
title: GitLab object storage
icon: variable

kinds:
  - name: s3
    title: S3-compatible object storage for GitLab
    type: variable
    fields:
      - type: textarea_upload
        secret: true
        name: connection
        label: Object storage connection
        variable: GITLAB_OBJECT_STORAGE_CONNECTION
      - type: textarea_upload
        secret: true
        name: registry_storage
        label: Registry storage configuration
        variable: GITLAB_REGISTRY_STORAGE_CONFIG
      - type: textarea_upload
        secret: true
        name: backup_s3cfg
        label: Backup s3cmd configuration
        variable: GITLAB_BACKUP_S3_CONFIG
      - type: text
        name: artifacts_bucket
        label: Artifacts bucket
        variable: GITLAB_ARTIFACTS_BUCKET
      - type: text
        name: lfs_bucket
        label: LFS bucket
        variable: GITLAB_LFS_BUCKET
      - type: text
        name: uploads_bucket
        label: Uploads bucket
        variable: GITLAB_UPLOADS_BUCKET
      - type: text
        name: packages_bucket
        label: Packages bucket
        variable: GITLAB_PACKAGES_BUCKET
      - type: text
        name: registry_bucket
        label: Registry bucket
        variable: GITLAB_REGISTRY_BUCKET
      - type: text
        name: backups_bucket
        label: Backups bucket
        variable: GITLAB_BACKUPS_BUCKET
      - type: text
        name: backups_tmp_bucket
        label: Temporary restore bucket
        variable: GITLAB_BACKUPS_TMP_BUCKET

See Variable integration for how integrations are attached.

docs.title: First sign-in
docs.text:
Wodby generates the password of GitLab's root administrator when the app is created.

  1. Open the GitLab app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal root_password. See Tokens.
  2. Open the app's main domain and sign in as root with that password.
  3. Change the password in your user settings.

GitLab uses the token only when it creates its database during the first deployment. Changing the token later does not change the password.

By default, anyone who can open GitLab can register an account, and an administrator must approve each new account. Review this under Admin area > Settings > General > New user account restrictions.

GitLab takes its address from the main domain when it is deployed. After you change the main domain, deploy the app environment so GitLab, its clone URLs, and the runner use the new address.

docs.title: Clone repositories
docs.text:
HTTPS works through the main domain without extra setup. GitLab shows the clone URL on each project page.

SSH needs a published port. GitLab's SSH endpoint isn't reachable from outside the cluster until you publish it:

  1. Open the app environment's Endpoints > Ports page and publish the GitLab ssh port. See Publishing ports.
  2. Wodby assigns a public port from the range 31222-32222 and deploys GitLab again, so that GitLab's SSH clone URLs show the main domain with that port, for example ssh://git@gitlab.example.com:31222/group/project.git.
  3. Add your public SSH key to your GitLab user settings. Wodby SSH keys are not used for Git.

Before the port is published, GitLab shows SSH clone URLs on port 22, which don't work. The cluster must support TCP port publishing; the Ports page says so if it doesn't.

docs.title: Container Registry
docs.text:
The Container Registry has its own public domain, separate from the main domain. Each project's container registry page in GitLab shows the registry address and the docker login, build, and push commands.

The Registry domain has a 15-minute request timeout. If pushing a large image layer takes longer, raise request_timeout and backend_request_timeout for that domain. See HTTP settings.

docs.title: Run CI jobs
docs.text:
The GitLab Runner service is disabled by default. To enable it:

  1. In GitLab, create a runner and copy its authentication token, which begins with glrt-. Registration tokens are not supported.
  2. On the Runner app service, set Runner authentication token to that token. See Settings tab.
  3. Enable the Runner app service and deploy it.

The runner connects to GitLab through the main domain. Configure tags, protected-branch access, and whether untagged jobs run on the runner in GitLab.

How jobs run:

  • Each job runs in its own pod, in the same Kubernetes namespace as GitLab. Up to four jobs run at once.
  • Jobs without an image use a small Alpine Linux image.
  • A job container requests 0.1 CPU and 256 MiB of memory, with limits of 2 CPU and 2 GiB. A job cannot raise these limits.
  • Job containers are unprivileged, so Docker-in-Docker is not available. Build container images with a builder that doesn't need privileged mode.
  • No distributed cache is configured, so CI cache entries are not kept between jobs. Artifacts are kept in object storage.

docs.title: Mail delivery
docs.text:
GitLab sends mail through the stack's OpenSMTPD service, from gitlab@<main domain> with a reply-to address of noreply@<main domain>. Attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD for reliable delivery, and make sure the provider accepts that sender domain. Without a relay, mail leaves directly from the cluster address, and recipient providers often reject it. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

To send from another address, override the GitLab chart value global.email.from on the GitLab app service's Configuration > Helm tab and deploy it. See Helm tab.

Incoming email, such as replying to notifications by email, is disabled.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• Git repositories and wikis are on the GitLab repositories volume (50 GB by default).
  • Database data is on the PostgreSQL volume (20 GB by default).
  • Valkey keeps its data on a 10 GB volume with persistence on. It can use up to 1 GB of memory and never removes keys to free memory, because it holds GitLab's background jobs and sessions.
  • Artifacts, LFS objects, uploads, packages, and Registry images are in your object storage.

GitLab creates a backup archive every day at 01:00 in the cluster's time zone and uploads it to the backups bucket. The archive contains the database, repositories and wikis, Registry images, and the object storage data. Runs don't overlap and are stopped after six hours. Each run uses a temporary 100 GiB volume, so the cluster must be able to provision one.

These archives are not Wodby backups. They don't appear on the app environment's Backups page, and Wodby doesn't remove old ones. Set retention and replication on the backups bucket.

GitLab leaves its Rails secrets out of the archive. A restore needs them, so keep a separately protected copy. See GitLab's Back up the secrets.

The PostgreSQL service also has a Wodby database backup and import. Use them as an extra layer for the database only. They don't contain repositories or object storage data, so they can't restore GitLab on their own. See Backups and Imports.

docs.title: Restore or move GitLab
docs.text: To restore an archive, or to move an existing GitLab installation into this stack, follow GitLab's Helm restore procedure. The archive must come from the same GitLab version, the Rails secrets must be restored too, and GitLab's web and background job pods must be stopped while the restore runs.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text:
Upgrade GitLab by upgrading the app environment's stack when a new revision changes the GitLab version. GitLab must pass its required upgrade stops. Before each upgrade, check that background migrations have finished in the Admin area and take a backup you have tested.

New non-production environments upgrade their stack automatically by default. Turn auto-upgrade off for GitLab environments whose upgrades you want to control.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• GitLab runs as a single instance and is not scalable. For high availability, see GitLab's Cloud Native Hybrid guidance.
  • GitLab Pages, the GitLab agent for Kubernetes server, incoming email, and the bundled monitoring are disabled.
  • Terraform state, CI/CD secure files, and the dependency proxy are not enabled.

docs.title: Go stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Go catalog stack runs a Go app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and Cloud PostgreSQL services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-go.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the Go boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

To use a managed database instead of the PostgreSQL container, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service's Dockerfile runs go mod download when go.mod exists, builds the package at the repository root with go build, and starts the binary. The main package must be at the root of the repository.
  • A Dockerfile from your repository replaces it and must still end with a command that starts the server. See Application builds.
  • The application must listen on port 8080 on all interfaces. Wodby sets no PORT variable in a deployed environment, so default to 8080 in the code.
  • Wodby sets no other variable for the application and generates no configuration file.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
The application reads these variables itself. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail transport without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 20 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • Wodby compiles the checkout and restarts the application after each change, usually within a few seconds. A failed build leaves the previous build running; read the compiler errors in the service's logs.
  • go.mod is required. A missing requirement or checksum fails the build, so fix it in the repository with go get or go mod tidy.
  • Set WORKSPACE_GO_PACKAGE on the app service to build a package other than ., such as ./cmd/server.
  • A repository with a go.work file is refused unless you set WORKSPACE_GO_COMMAND on the app service.

docs.title: Gotenberg stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Gotenberg catalog stack runs Gotenberg 8 for converting web pages, HTML, and office documents to PDF. The current service definition and version choices are documented in wodby/service-gotenberg.

Applications in the same app can reach the service through its private endpoint:

http://gotenberg:3000

Keep this endpoint private unless an external client must call it. After testing, disable the Gotenberg technical route under App environment → Endpoints → Routes. Internal service-to-service requests continue to work.

docs.title: Migrate from AthenaPDF
docs.text:
Gotenberg is not a drop-in replacement for AthenaPDF. AthenaPDF accepts requests through /convert with an authentication key, while Gotenberg 8 uses multipart POST requests to conversion-specific routes. Changing only the hostname or port does not migrate the application client or CMS configuration.

When the Wodby 1 migration CLI maps athenapdf to gotenberg, it:

  • adds the Gotenberg service to the target stack and preserves whether the source service is enabled
  • sets GOTENBERG_ENDPOINT on the target PHP service to the private in-cluster URL, normally http://gotenberg:3000
  • does not rewrite application code, Drupal configuration, WordPress plugin configuration, or custom AthenaPDF options

docs.title: Drupal
docs.text:
For Drupal, use the contributed Gotenberg module. It includes a Gotenberg client and an Entity Print backend, but it does not convert configuration or custom code from the older Athena PDF API module.

composer require drupal/gotenberg

The Drupal module stores its base URL in Drupal configuration and does not read GOTENBERG_ENDPOINT automatically. To use the endpoint supplied by Wodby, add an environment-specific override after the generated Wodby settings include:

$config['gotenberg.settings']['base_url'] =
  getenv('GOTENBERG_ENDPOINT') ?: 'http://gotenberg:3000';

After importing the Wodby 1 database, remove or replace the stored athenapdf_api configuration and validate the Gotenberg module configuration before switching traffic.

docs.title: WordPress and custom PHP
docs.text:
Wodby does not provide a WordPress-specific Gotenberg plugin. Use a plugin only if it explicitly supports the remote Gotenberg 8 API, or update custom code to use an appropriate client. Composer-managed PHP applications can use the official Gotenberg PHP client:

composer require gotenberg/gotenberg-php:^2

Application code must read GOTENBERG_ENDPOINT explicitly.

docs.title: Authentication variables
docs.text:
Do not copy GOTENBERG_HTTP_AUTH_USERNAME or GOTENBERG_HTTP_AUTH_PASSWORD from a custom Wodby 1 stack as though they were Drupal module settings. The module does not read them, and they are not Gotenberg 8 server configuration names.

If API basic authentication is required, configure Gotenberg 8 deliberately with GOTENBERG_API_BASIC_AUTH_USERNAME and GOTENBERG_API_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD and enable its basic-auth setting. Prefer the private service endpoint when only services inside the app need access.

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
1. Find every AthenaPDF dependency, including ATHENAPDF_URL, ATHENAPDF_PASSWORD, stored athenapdf_api configuration, custom clients, and calls to /convert.
  2. Install a Gotenberg-aware module or client and configure it to use GOTENBERG_ENDPOINT.
  3. Replace AthenaPDF requests with the corresponding Gotenberg multipart route. For example, use /forms/chromium/convert/url for a URL or /forms/chromium/convert/html with an index.html upload for HTML.
  4. Map paper size, margins, media type, backgrounds, headers, footers, cookies, timeouts, and JavaScript wait behavior explicitly. The migration CLI does not translate AthenaPDF request options.
  5. Replace AthenaPDF configuration stored in the imported database through a configuration import, deployment hook, or CMS administration page.
  6. Compare representative PDFs before switching traffic, including fonts, images, authenticated assets, page breaks, headers, backgrounds, file size, and failure behavior.

See the Gotenberg documentation for URL conversion, HTML conversion, and supported clients.

docs.title: Grafana stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Grafana catalog stack runs Grafana on its own. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-grafana.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
Open the Grafana domain listed under Endpoints for the app environment. Open the app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal admin_username (admin) and admin_password. See Tokens.

Grafana applies these values once, on the first start with an empty data volume. Changing the tokens later does not change the existing account.

docs.title: Add data sources
docs.text:
The stack ships no data sources. The Grafana service can be linked to Grafana Loki, Grafana Tempo, Prometheus, and VictoriaMetrics services. A link sets no variables and creates no data source by itself.

Declare data sources in the Grafana datasources file under Configuration > Configs. It is empty by default. A data source removed from the file is deleted from Grafana on the next start. Grafana reads the file at start, so deploy the service after a change. See Configs tab.

A linked service is reached at http://<its app service name>:<its port>. Loki uses port 3100, Tempo uses 3200, VictoriaMetrics uses 8428, and Prometheus uses 9090. To add data sources automatically, use a stack that provisions them. See the Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, and VictoriaMetrics guides.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text: Add or change GF_* environment variables on the app service, or edit the data sources file, then deploy. Do not edit grafana.ini in the container, because it is not on a volume. Wodby turns off usage reporting and update checks by default.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: The stack creates a 10 GB Grafana data volume, mounted at /var/lib/grafana. It holds Grafana's built-in SQLite database with dashboards, users, and settings, and installed plugins. Wodby defines no backups or imports for this service. Grafana is not scalable.

docs.title: Check that Grafana is running
docs.text: /api/health on port 3000 reports whether Grafana and its database are up.

docs.title: HTML stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby HTML catalog stack serves static HTML sites with Nginx or, optionally, Apache HTTP Server. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-html.

docs.title: Choose a web server
docs.text:
Nginx is enabled by default. Apache HTTP Server is available but disabled by default. Pick the one that matches how your site handles routes:

  • Nginx serves a directory request with the index file. A path that matches no file also falls back to the index file, which suits a single-page application.
  • Apache HTTP Server serves a directory request with index.html. A path that matches no file gets no fallback. Add your own rewrite rule to a .htaccess file when you need one. .htaccess overrides are allowed in the document root.

docs.title: Build and deployment
docs.text:
Start from the HTML boilerplate or connect your own repository. See Application Builds.

The build copies your repository into the image at /var/www/html. A changed file needs a new build and deployment.

Set the Nginx docroot subdir or Apache docroot subdir setting when the site is in a subdirectory of the repository. Leave it empty to serve the repository root.

docs.title: Defaults you should know about
docs.text:
Both web servers answer /.healthz with status 204 and deny paths that start with a dot. Nginx still allows /.well-known/. Both deny wodby.yml and Makefile. Apache also denies files ending in .sh, .sql, .mysql, .po, .tpl, .make or .test, and it keeps directory listings off.

Nginx adds the X-XSS-Protection, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options and Content-Security-Policy headers. The default policy only restricts framing. Set NGINX_HEADERS_CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY to change it.

docs.title: Change web server settings
docs.text: Do not add an nginx.conf or httpd.conf to the repository. Set NGINX_* or APACHE_* environment variables on the app service instead, or override the config files that the service declares. Changes apply with the next deployment.

docs.title: Java stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Java catalog stack runs a Java app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and Cloud PostgreSQL services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-java.

Use it for applications built into a runnable jar with Maven or Gradle, such as ones on Quarkus, Micronaut, Javalin, or no framework. For Spring Boot applications, use the Spring Boot stack, which also sets Spring Boot's own connection settings.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the Java boilerplate, a small web application on the JDK's built-in HTTP server with no other dependencies, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

Choose the Java version with the app service's version. To use a managed database instead of the PostgreSQL container, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service's Dockerfile builds the repository with its own build setup and keeps only the runnable jar:
    • Maven, when pom.xml is at the repository root: the Maven wrapper (mvnw) when the repository has one, or else Maven from the image, runs package without compiling or running tests. The jar is taken from target/.
    • Gradle, when build.gradle or build.gradle.kts is at the root: the Gradle wrapper (gradlew) runs assemble. The jar is taken from build/libs/. A Gradle project without the wrapper fails to build.
  • Run tests in your pipeline, as the boilerplate does with ./mvnw test.
  • Jars ending in -sources, -javadoc, -tests or -plain, and Maven's original-*.jar, are ignored. When the build leaves more than one other jar, such as in a multi-module project, add a build variable JAVA_BUILD_JAR to the app service with the path of the jar to run, such as app/target/app.jar. JAVA_BUILD_ARGS adds arguments to Maven or Gradle, and JAVA_BUILD_COMMAND replaces the build command.
  • The image keeps only that jar and starts it with java -jar, so the jar needs a Main-Class in its manifest and its dependencies inside it: a "fat" or "uber" jar, such as one built by the Maven Shade plugin or Gradle's Shadow plugin. Quarkus builds one with quarkus.package.jar.type=uber-jar; its default layout, a jar with a separate lib/ directory, does not work.
  • A Dockerfile from your repository replaces the service's, as in the boilerplate. It must still end with a command that starts the server. See Application builds.
  • The application must listen on port 8080 on all interfaces. Wodby sets no PORT variable in a deployed environment, so default to 8080 in the code.
  • The service is ready when port 8080 answers HTTP with a status below 500 at /. To check a health endpoint instead, add JAVA_READY_PATH to the app service, such as /health; that path must then answer 200.
  • The JVM sizes its heap from the container's memory limit (JAVA_OPTS is -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0). Set the app service's memory limit instead of -Xmx.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
The application reads these variables itself. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION), DATABASE_URL Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

DATABASE_URL is a URL such as postgresql://user:password@host:5432/db, not a JDBC URL. Build the JDBC URL from the other variables, such as jdbc:postgresql://${DB_HOST}:${DB_PORT}/${DB_NAME}, and pass DB_USERNAME and DB_PASSWORD to the driver separately. Add the database's JDBC driver to your project.

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail client without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 20 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • Wodby builds the checkout as above and restarts the application with the new build after each change, usually within a few seconds. A failed build leaves the previous build running; read the compiler errors in the service's logs.
  • Setup downloads the project's dependencies with Maven or the Gradle wrapper. Dependencies and the build are kept in .wodby-workspace/ in the checkout, so a restart downloads nothing again. Maven and Gradle in an SSH session use the same locations.
  • JAVA_BUILD_JAR, JAVA_BUILD_ARGS and JAVA_BUILD_COMMAND apply here too when they have the runtime scope.
  • target/, build/, .gradle/ and .wodby-workspace/ stay out of Git status without changes to .gitignore.
  • Set WORKSPACE_JAVA_WATCH to 0 on the app service to stop rebuilding on changes, or WORKSPACE_JAVA_COMMAND to replace the start command.

docs.title: Apache Kafka stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Apache Kafka catalog stack runs a single Apache Kafka node. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-kafka.

docs.title: What the stack runs
docs.text:
The node runs in KRaft mode and acts as both broker and controller. There is no ZooKeeper service, and the service cannot be scaled to more than one node. Do not pair it with the ZooKeeper stack.

Wodby generates the cluster ID once. The internal offsets and transaction topics use a replication factor of 1, so a topic that needs a replication factor above 1 cannot be created.

docs.title: Connect an application
docs.text:
Use these values from a service in the same app environment:

  • Bootstrap server: <app service name>:9092
  • Security protocol: PLAINTEXT

The broker has no TLS, no username, no password, and no certificate. The port is private, so Wodby creates no public route for it. The broker advertises the app service name as its address, so a client must be able to resolve that name. This works for services in the same environment.

A service linked to Kafka receives the host and port in variables named by the linking service. Read those variables instead of hardcoding the host.

docs.title: Change broker settings
docs.text:
Set broker properties as environment variables on the Kafka app service. Use the KAFKA_* form: a broker property in upper case with dots replaced by underscores. Do not mount a server.properties file.

Do not change the listener, advertised listener, node ID, or controller quorum variables. Doing so breaks the single-node setup.

docs.title: Data
