docs.text: Log segments and cluster metadata are stored on the Kafka data volume. The stack creates it with a size of 20 GB. Wodby defines no backups or imports for this service.

docs.title: Check that the broker is running
docs.text:
Open a web terminal for the Kafka app service and run:

/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list

/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-broker-api-versions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 also answers when the broker is up.

docs.title: Keycloak stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Keycloak catalog stack runs Keycloak in production mode with a PostgreSQL database. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-keycloak.

docs.title: Your own themes and providers
docs.text: To add your own login, account or email themes, or custom providers, use the buildable Keycloak stack instead. You keep them in a Git repository started from the Keycloak boilerplate, and Wodby builds Keycloak with them on every push. Select a theme for a realm under Realm settings > Themes.

docs.title: First sign-in
docs.text:
Open the app's main route. Sign in with the admin_username token, which is admin, and the generated admin_password token. Find both on the Keycloak app service's Configuration > Tokens tab. See Tokens.

Keycloak creates this account only on the first start with an empty database, and marks it as temporary. Changing the tokens later does not change an existing account.

docs.title: Hostname and TLS
docs.text: Keycloak uses the environment's primary URL for the addresses it issues, such as token issuers and redirects. TLS ends at Wodby's router.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
Add or change KC_* environment variables on the app service and deploy it. Environment variables take precedence over conf/keycloak.conf, which is not stored on a volume. Database connection values come from the PostgreSQL link. See Environment variables.

Manage realms, clients, and users in the Keycloak administration console or its API.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: Keycloak has no volume. All of its data is in the linked PostgreSQL database (20 GB volume by default), so back up that database. See Backups.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Keycloak serves health and metrics on a private management port (9000). It has no public route.
  • The Keycloak service is not scalable.

docs.title: Keycloak (buildable) stack guide
docs.text:
The buildable Keycloak stack runs Keycloak built from your Git repository: the repository holds your own login, account, email or admin themes and your custom providers. The stack has the same services as the Keycloak stack: Keycloak and PostgreSQL. Its composition is documented in wodby/stack-keycloak-buildable.

Everything in the Keycloak guide applies, from the administrator account to the hostname and backups. This page covers what differs.

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
Start the repository from the Keycloak boilerplate and connect it when you create the app.

Path Purpose themes/ Your themes, one directory per theme with a directory per type, such as login/theme.properties providers/ Your provider jars, such as authenticators, user storage, event listeners or protocol mappers

A login/theme.properties that extends Keycloak's theme can start with:

parent=keycloak.v2
import=common/keycloak
styles=css/login.css css/my-theme.css

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Choose the Keycloak version when you create the app. The build starts from the official Keycloak image of that version, adds your themes and providers, and runs Keycloak's build with the service's settings, so Keycloak starts without rebuilding.

The build fails when a theme has the name of one of Keycloak's own themes (base, keycloak, keycloak.v2) or has no theme.properties. Build provider jars for the Keycloak version you run.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
Select a theme for a realm in Keycloak's administration console, under Realm settings > Themes. Themes are part of the image, so changes reach Keycloak with the next deployment.

To run Keycloak without your own themes or providers, use the Keycloak stack.

docs.title: Kotlin stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Kotlin catalog stack runs a Kotlin app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and Cloud PostgreSQL services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-kotlin.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the Kotlin boilerplate, a Ktor application, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

The app service's version is the Java version. The Kotlin version is the one your Gradle build pins with the Kotlin Gradle plugin. To run on every Java version the service offers, compile for the oldest one with jvmTarget and Java's targetCompatibility, as the boilerplate does.

To use a managed database instead of the PostgreSQL container, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The repository must contain the Gradle wrapper (gradlew and gradle/wrapper/) and a build.gradle.kts or build.gradle at its root. Gradle itself is not installed in the image; the wrapper downloads the version your project pins.
  • The service's Dockerfile runs ./gradlew assemble. Tests are not compiled or run, so run them in your pipeline, as the boilerplate's .wodby/pipeline.yml does with ./gradlew test.
  • The build must leave exactly one runnable jar in build/libs/, with the application's dependencies inside and the main class in its manifest. Jars ending in -plain, -sources, -javadoc, or -tests are not counted. With the Shadow plugin, set the shadow jar's classifier to empty, the plain jar's to plain, and call mergeServiceFiles(), as the boilerplate does. Ktor's Gradle plugin can build such a jar with buildFatJar.
  • When the build leaves several jars, such as in a multi-project build, add a build variable JAVA_BUILD_JAR to the app service with the path of the one to run, such as server/build/libs/server-all.jar. A development workspace builds at runtime, so give the variable the runtime scope too.
  • A Dockerfile from your repository replaces the service's. Its last stage must start from the service image and run java-app, as in the boilerplate. See Application builds.
  • The application must listen on port 8080 on all interfaces. Wodby sets no PORT variable in a deployed environment, so default to 8080 in the code. With Ktor's embeddedServer, pass host = "0.0.0.0".
  • The JVM's heap follows the container's memory limit: JAVA_OPTS on the app service defaults to -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0. Change the service's memory limit rather than setting -Xmx.
  • The app service is ready when / answers with a status below 500. To check a health route instead, add a JAVA_READY_PATH variable with its path, such as /healthz from the boilerplate. That path must then answer 200.
  • Kubernetes stops the container with SIGTERM and waits up to 30 seconds. Ktor's embeddedServer finishes running requests and stops on its own.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
The application reads these variables itself. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION), DATABASE_URL Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

DATABASE_URL is a URL such as postgresql://user:password@host:5432/db, not a JDBC URL. For JDBC-based libraries such as Exposed, build the URL from the other variables, such as jdbc:postgresql://$DB_HOST:$DB_PORT/$DB_NAME, and pass the user name and password separately.

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail client without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 20 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • Wodby builds the jar from the checkout and runs it. After each change it builds again and restarts the application, usually within 10 to 20 seconds on a small cluster. A failed build leaves the previous build running; read the Kotlin compiler's errors in the service's logs. Reload the browser page yourself.
  • Setup downloads Gradle and the dependencies. They are kept in .wodby-workspace/ in the checkout, so a restart downloads nothing again, and builds keep Gradle running between changes.
  • build/ and .gradle/ stay out of Git status without changes to .gitignore. Add .kotlin/ to your .gitignore, as the boilerplate does: Kotlin's Gradle plugin keeps its state there.
  • Set WORKSPACE_JAVA_WATCH to 0 on the app service to stop rebuilding on changes, or WORKSPACE_JAVA_COMMAND to replace the start command.
  • A change to variables or linked services still needs a deployment of the environment.

docs.title: Laravel stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Laravel catalog stack runs Laravel on PHP-FPM behind Nginx, with MariaDB, Valkey, shared file storage and Mailpit. A queue worker, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg and managed databases are optional. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-laravel.

docs.title: Build and deployment
docs.text:
Start from Laravel on Wodby, which includes .wodby/pipeline.yml, or connect your own repository. The boilerplate is offered only for the PHP versions it supports. See Application Builds.

Only the document root (Nginx docroot, public by default) goes into the Nginx image. Put front-end build output there during the build. Code, vendor and .env stay in the PHP image.

Wodby does not provide a development workspace for the Laravel PHP service.

docs.title: Configuration and .env
docs.text:
When the container starts and /var/www/html/.env does not exist, the image writes one from the service's environment variables. Keep .env out of your repository. A committed .env is left as it is, and Wodby generates nothing.

To change a value, set the variable on the PHP service and deploy. Do not edit the generated file. It takes the app name, environment name and URL from Wodby. It takes APP_KEY, APP_DEBUG, DB_*, LOG_*, CACHE_DRIVER, SESSION_DRIVER, QUEUE_CONNECTION, MAIL_*, REDIS_*, AWS_* and PUSHER_* from variables of the same name. A name that is not in this list is not written to it.

APP_KEY is generated by Wodby. Find it in the PHP app service's Configuration > Tokens tab. APP_DEBUG is on in development environments and off elsewhere. See Environment variables.

docs.title: Database, Valkey and mail
docs.text:
Link What the PHP service receives DBMS DB_* variables, including DB_CONNECTION and DB_DATABASE Redis (Valkey) REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD, and QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis Mail Transfer Agent MSMTP_HOST and MSMTP_PORT, used as MAIL_HOST and MAIL_PORT unless you set those

Cache and sessions stay on files until you set CACHE_DRIVER and SESSION_DRIVER on the PHP service.

Valkey stores queued jobs, so the stack sets its policy to noeviction. Jobs are not evicted under memory pressure. When Valkey reaches its memory limit, new writes fail instead, so size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY (128m by default) for your queue on the Valkey app service.

A Valkey restart loses queued jobs

Valkey has no volume in this stack, so a restart or deployment of Valkey empties it.

To keep queued jobs across a restart, store them in MariaDB. Set QUEUE_CONNECTION to database on the PHP service and deploy. This also applies to the optional Laravel Queue service. Jobs need the jobs table, which the boilerplate includes through Laravel's default migrations. If your application does not have it, run php artisan make:queue-table and commit the migration. See Laravel's queue documentation.

Do not select Add volume on an existing Valkey app service. Kubernetes does not allow the change, so the deployment fails.

Do not use this Valkey instance for Laravel's cache. Cache pressure would block queue writes. Add a separate cache service with an LRU policy.

Mailpit captures every message and delivers none of them. Its web interface is protected with basic auth. Reveal the password in Endpoints > Auths. For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the PHP service's Mail Transfer Agent link at it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

To use a Cloud MariaDB or Cloud MySQL service, see Managed Databases. Laravel connects over TLS and verifies the server certificate when the server has one.

docs.title: After each deployment
docs.text:
• php artisan migrate --force runs after every deployment.
  • php artisan db:seed runs once, after the first deployment's migrations.
  • A cron job runs php artisan schedule:run at minute 0 of every hour. A service schedule cannot run more often, so tasks scheduled for other minutes do not run from it. Schedule tasks on the hour, or run php artisan schedule:work as a long-running process. See Application Cron Schedules.
  • The optional Laravel Queue service runs php artisan queue:listen.

Do not add migration or queue worker commands to the build or to a start script.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, the PHP service and the Laravel Queue service get the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. Add the OpenTelemetry PHP SDK with Composer; it then starts without code changes. To trace requests, queue jobs, and database queries, also add open-telemetry/opentelemetry-auto-laravel. See PHP applications and OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Files and storage
docs.text:
The PHP service requires a storage link and mounts a shared files volume at /mnt/files. The stack provides it as Files NFS storage. The PHP service's storage volume is 20 GB, and the NFS service's own data volume is 25 GB. See Application Persistent Storage.

On start, storage/app/public and public/storage become links to /mnt/files/public. Nginx serves those files under /storage/. This replaces php artisan storage:link, so do not run it in the build. The step fails when either directory holds anything other than a .gitignore.

Only storage/app/public is on the volume. Logs and file-based sessions and cache are in the container's file system and are lost when it restarts.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
A MariaDB backup is a gzipped SQL dump of the environment's database. The stack excludes the contents of the cache and cache_locks tables by default. They keep their definition and lose their rows. You can change this with the backup's Excluded table contents option. A database import replaces the whole data volume. The Valkey service has no backups or imports.

The Files NFS storage service has its own Files backup and Files import. See Application Backups and Application Imports.

docs.title: Grafana Loki stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Grafana Loki catalog stack runs Loki with Grafana as its interface. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-loki.

To collect traces, metrics, and logs in one app, with links between them in Grafana, use the Observability stack.

docs.title: Choose services when you create the app
docs.text: Loki is required. Grafana is enabled by default as the stack's main interface, with Loki provisioned as its default data source. The OpenTelemetry Collector is enabled by default as the public endpoint that applications send logs to. You can exclude Grafana when you need only the Loki API, and the Collector when only services in the same app environment write to Loki.

docs.title: Sign in to Grafana
docs.text: Open the Grafana app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal admin_username (admin) and admin_password. Grafana applies them once, on the first start with an empty data volume. Changing the tokens later does not change the existing account. See Tokens and the Grafana guide.

docs.title: Send logs from your applications
docs.text:
Applications send logs to the OpenTelemetry Collector over OTLP. The Collector's HTTP port has a public HTTPS domain, listed under Endpoints for the app environment, so applications in other app environments, other clusters, or outside Wodby can use it. Every request needs the Collector's ingest token: open the Collector app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal ingest_token. See Tokens.

Set the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables in the application that sends logs:

Variable Value OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT https://<Collector domain>, without a path OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL http/protobuf OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS Authorization=Bearer%20<ingest token>, stored as a secret OTEL_SERVICE_NAME A name for the application OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER otlp OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER, OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER none, because this Collector accepts logs only

The Collector forwards logs to Loki. In Grafana, find them by the service_name label, for example {service_name="api"}. To change what the Collector does, edit its Collector config under Configuration > Configs and deploy the service. See Configs tab and the Grafana Tempo guide for the same Collector used for traces.

Apps from the Wodby application stacks can instead forward logs through their own Collector: set its Logs link to this app's Collector, listed with the other apps you can link to. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Connect to Loki
docs.text:
Loki runs as a single instance and listens on port 3100. The port is private, so Wodby creates no public route for it. Other services in the app environment reach it at http://<Loki app service name>:3100.

Authentication is off, and Loki stores chunks, index, and rules on the local filesystem.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: The stack creates a 20 GB Loki data volume, mounted at /loki. Grafana has its own 10 GB volume. Wodby defines no backups or imports for these services.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Loki has no settings, links, or config files in Wodby. Its configuration file is part of the image and is not on a volume, so do not edit it in the container.
  • Loki is not scalable.

docs.title: Check that Loki is ready
docs.text: /ready on port 3100 answers when Loki can accept requests.

docs.title: Mailpit stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Mailpit catalog stack runs Mailpit, a mail catcher for development and testing. It accepts mail over SMTP and shows it in a web interface. It does not deliver mail to recipients. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-mailpit.

docs.title: Send mail to Mailpit
docs.text:
Use these values from a service in the same app environment:

  • SMTP host: the Mailpit app service name
  • SMTP port: 1025

Mailpit uses no TLS, no username, and no password, and Wodby generates no token. An application that requires SMTP authentication or TLS fails against it. Configure the application's mail transport without them.

Mailpit satisfies the mail link of application services. A linked PHP service receives MSMTP_HOST and MSMTP_PORT, and PHP's mail() then sends to Mailpit. Other runtimes receive variables named by their own service, such as SMTP_HOST and SMTP_PORT. Read those variables instead of hardcoding the host.

docs.title: Open the web interface
docs.text:
Port 8025 serves the web interface and Mailpit's REST API under /api/v1/. Use it to read, search, and delete messages.

Captured mail can include password reset links and other secrets, so Wodby protects the public domains with basic auth by default. Each Mailpit app service gets its own generated password. Reveal it under Endpoints > Auths for the app environment. See Auths. Services inside the environment reach port 8025 directly, without the password. A request to the REST API from outside the environment sends the same username and password.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
• Mailpit captures every message sent to it, whatever the recipient. Nothing leaves the environment, so mail never reaches real mailboxes.
  • For real delivery, the environment needs a relay such as OpenSMTPD.
  • Mailpit keeps a limited number of messages and deletes the oldest first.
  • Set Mailpit options as environment variables on the app service in Mailpit's MP_* form. Wodby sets none by default.

docs.title: Keep messages across restarts
docs.text: The optional Data volume is mounted at /data. Mailpit stores messages in a temporary file that is removed when it exits. Captured mail survives a restart only when the volume exists and MP_DATABASE is set to a path under /data. Wodby defines no backups or imports for this service.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text: Send a test message from the application, then open the web interface. From a service in the environment, you can also request GET http://<app service name>:8025/api/v1/messages.

docs.title: MariaDB stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby MariaDB catalog stack runs a MariaDB database server, with optional Adminer and phpMyAdmin. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-mariadb.

docs.title: Create an environment
docs.text:
MariaDB is enabled by default with a 20 GB data volume. Adminer and phpMyAdmin are disabled by default. Enable one when you want a browser interface for the database. Each is linked to the MariaDB service automatically.

Wodby creates the database and its user. Both are named after the app and the app environment, and the user has all privileges on that database only. The database uses the utf8mb4 charset by default. The application does not create them. A user you create by hand with a name Wodby later needs, but a different password, makes Wodby's create action fail. Add further DBs and users on Wodby.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
Wodby generates two tokens once per environment. Open the MariaDB app service's Configuration > Tokens tab to reveal them:

  • password: the password of the environment's database user.
  • root_password: the root password. The container also has it in MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD.

Use the database user, not root, in applications.

docs.title: Connect to the database
docs.text:
The server listens on TCP port 3306. Inside the app environment, the host is the name of the MariaDB app service. The database has no public route. To reach it from outside the cluster, publish its port. See Publishing ports.

An app service linked to MariaDB receives the host, port, database name, user name, and password as environment variables defined by its own link, for example DB_HOST and DB_PASSWORD on a PHP service. Read them in the application instead of hardcoding them.

To open a shell in the database container, use the web terminal. For example, mariadb -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e 'SHOW DATABASES;' lists the databases.

docs.title: Adminer and phpMyAdmin
docs.text:
Both have no persistent data. Wodby protects their public domains with basic auth by default. Reveal the generated password on the environment's Endpoints > Auths page. See Auths.

  • Adminer: the login form is prefilled with the system, server, and database. Type the user name and password.
  • phpMyAdmin: it connects only to the linked MariaDB server. Sign in with the environment's database user to see its database, or with root to see all databases.

docs.title: Server settings
docs.text:
The container rebuilds its configuration from environment variables on every start. Change a setting by setting a variable on the MariaDB app service. Do not edit the generated file. Common ones:

  • MYSQL_INNODB_BUFFER_POOL_SIZE, MYSQL_MAX_CONNECTIONS, MYSQL_MAX_ALLOWED_PACKET
  • MYSQL_CHARACTER_SET_SERVER, MYSQL_COLLATION_SERVER
  • MYSQL_WAIT_TIMEOUT, MYSQL_INNODB_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT, MYSQL_TRANSACTION_ISOLATION
  • MYSQL_SLOW_QUERY_LOG, MYSQL_LONG_QUERY_TIME, MYSQL_GENERAL_LOG

A change applies on the next deployment of the service. Host names are not resolved, and connections use the server character set.

docs.title: Backups and restore
docs.text:
Data is on the data volume. A backup is a gzipped SQL dump of the environment's database. In the backup's Excluded table contents option, list table names or SQL LIKE patterns. Those tables keep their definition and lose their rows. See Application backups.

To restore, run a database import from a backup or an uploaded file. See Application imports. The import accepts .gz, .tar.gz, .tgz, and .zip archives that contain exactly one .sql or .mysql file.

Warning

A database import replaces the contents of the data volume. Data that is not in the dump is not kept.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text: After a version upgrade, Wodby runs mariadb-upgrade and mariadb-check on the environment's database and on the mysql system database.

docs.title: Matomo stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Matomo catalog stack runs Matomo web analytics with MariaDB, shared NFS storage for Matomo's files, and OpenSMTPD for mail. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-matomo.

The stack runs Wodby's prebuilt Matomo image, so there's nothing to build and no repository to connect.

docs.title: Your own plugins
docs.text: To add your own Matomo plugins, use the buildable Matomo stack instead. You keep them in a Git repository started from the Matomo boilerplate, which also sets the Matomo release to run, and Wodby builds Matomo with them on every push. You decide when to upgrade Matomo, so watch Matomo's releases for security fixes.

docs.title: Superuser and first website
docs.text:
Matomo is installed during the app's first deployment, so you never use Matomo's web installer. Set the superuser and the first website in the Matomo service's settings when you create the app:

Setting Default What it sets Admin password none, required The superuser's password Admin email none, required The superuser's email address Admin username admin The superuser's login Website URL empty The address of the first website to track, such as https://www.example.com
  • The first website is named after the app's title. Without a website URL, Matomo asks for a website at the first sign-in.
  • These settings are only used when Matomo is installed. To change the superuser later, use Matomo.

If the first deployment can't install Matomo, for example because the admin password or email is missing, the deployment's post-deploy step fails with the reason. Fix it and deploy again. Later deployments update Matomo's database instead.

docs.title: Domains
docs.text: Matomo uses the app environment's main domain as its address and accepts requests for every domain of the app. After you add a domain or change the main domain, deploy the Matomo service again.

docs.title: Archiving
docs.text:
Matomo processes reports in the background, not when someone views them. The Matomo service defines an hourly Archive reports cron schedule, at five minutes past the hour, which also sends scheduled email reports. Change the schedule or run it manually from the app environment's Cron page.

Cron schedules require an active paid subscription. Without them, Matomo's reports are not updated.

docs.title: Plugins and updates
docs.text:
Install plugins from Matomo's Marketplace. They are kept on the shared files volume, so every replica loads them and they stay after updates. After you activate a plugin that changes Matomo's tracking code, restart the Matomo service so every replica serves the new code.

New Matomo releases arrive as updates of the Matomo service; see stack upgrades. The deployment after an update runs Matomo's database update. Matomo's own updater is turned off.

docs.title: Geolocation
docs.text: The Matomo image includes a GeoLite2 City database. In Matomo, open Administration > System > Geolocation, select the GeoIP 2 PHP provider, and save the setting.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text: Matomo sends mail through the stack's OpenSMTPD service. Attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD for production delivery. Direct delivery from a cluster IP is not a reliable production mail strategy. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• The files volume holds Matomo's settings file, custom logos and Marketplace plugins. Every Matomo replica and the archiving job share it through the NFS storage service.
  • The MariaDB database holds reports, visits, users and sessions.

Back up both the database and the files volume, and restore them together; see Application Backups. Use Matomo's UI for settings: changes made to files in a web terminal outside the files volume are lost when the container is replaced.

Matomo mixes a salt that Wodby generates for the Matomo service, the matomo_salt token in Configuration > Tokens, into every password, API token and session. Keep it. If it changes, existing passwords, API tokens and sessions stop working. A database restored into another app environment needs the same token. See Tokens.

docs.title: Apps created before the prebuilt image
docs.text: Earlier versions of the Matomo stack built Matomo from a repository and served it with a separate Nginx service. Apps created from them keep that setup, because a new major version of a service is never applied automatically. Archive their reports with an app-level cron schedule on the Matomo service that runs php console core:archive --url="${WODBY_PRIMARY_URL}" once an hour. To move to the prebuilt image, create a new app from the Matomo stack.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Matomo supports only MariaDB and MySQL.
  • Development workspaces are not available for Matomo.

docs.title: Matomo (buildable) stack guide
docs.text:
The buildable Matomo stack runs Matomo built from your Git repository: the repository pins the Matomo release and holds your own plugins. The stack has the same services as the Matomo stack: MariaDB, shared NFS storage for Matomo's files, and OpenSMTPD for mail. Its composition is documented in wodby/stack-matomo-buildable.

Everything in the Matomo guide applies, from the superuser settings to archiving, mail and backups. This page covers what differs.

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
Start the repository from the Matomo boilerplate and connect it when you create the app.

Path Purpose .matomo-version The Matomo release to run, such as 5.14.2. Required. plugins/ Your plugins, one directory per plugin, named like the plugin

Matomo 5 releases are supported. The build downloads the release from Matomo, checks its signature and installs it with your plugins on Wodby's PHP image for Matomo.

The build fails when .matomo-version is missing, when a directory in plugins/ has no plugin.json, or when a plugin has the name of one of Matomo's own plugins.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
On every deployment Wodby installs Matomo or updates its database, activates every plugin from the repository, and deactivates the plugins you removed from the repository since the last deployment. A plugin from the repository can't stay deactivated: remove it from the repository instead.

Plugins installed from Matomo's Marketplace work as on the Matomo stack: they are kept on the shared files volume, not in the repository.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Matomo's version changes only when you change .matomo-version and deploy; the deployment updates Matomo's database. Updates of the service bring PHP and Wodby's own changes, not a new Matomo. You decide when to upgrade, so watch Matomo's releases for security fixes.

To have Wodby keep Matomo up to date instead, use the Matomo stack.

docs.title: Mattermost stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Mattermost catalog stack runs Mattermost Team Edition with PostgreSQL and an optional OpenSMTPD service. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-mattermost.

docs.title: Before you create the app
docs.text:
• The stack is for simple, single-replica installations. The Mattermost service is fixed to one replica.
  • Mattermost must run on a linux/amd64 node.
  • Mattermost Calls is disabled. Calls on Kubernetes needs a separately managed RTCD service and direct TCP and UDP media routing.

docs.title: First sign-in
docs.text: Wodby creates no account. Open the app's main route and create the first system administrator in the browser.

docs.title: Mail delivery
docs.text: The OpenSMTPD service is optional. While the Mattermost app service is linked to it, Mattermost receives its SMTP settings from the link. Attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD for production delivery. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
Mattermost reads MM_<SECTION>_<SETTING> environment variables. They take precedence over config.json, and a setting given by a variable cannot be changed in the System Console.

Wodby sets variables for the site URL, the database, mail (while the link exists), the maximum file size, and logging. Change them as environment variables on the app service and deploy it. Change other settings in the System Console. They are saved to config.json on the volume. See Environment variables.

Mattermost limits files to 100 MB. The route has no size limit of its own, so you can raise the Mattermost file limit without changing the route. Do not set the route's request body size: it makes the route hold each request in memory until it is complete, and Mattermost's live updates stop working.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
The Mattermost volume (20 GB by default) holds uploaded files, config.json, server plugins, and web application plugins. Everything else is in PostgreSQL, which has its own 20 GB volume.

Back up the database and the Mattermost volume together as one recovery set. The Mattermost service has no backup or import operation in Wodby. The PostgreSQL service does. See Backups.

docs.title: Mautic stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Mautic catalog stack runs Mautic, the open source marketing automation platform, with MariaDB, shared NFS storage for Mautic's files, and OpenSMTPD for mail. Two workers run Mautic's cron jobs and its queue. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-mautic.

The stack runs Wodby's prebuilt Mautic image, so there's nothing to build and no repository to connect.

docs.title: Your own plugins and themes
docs.text: To add your own plugins or themes, use the buildable Mautic stack instead. You keep Mautic as a Composer project in a Git repository started from the Mautic boilerplate, and Wodby builds it on every push. Each deployment runs Mautic's database migrations and registers new plugins. You decide when to update Mautic, so watch Mautic's releases for security fixes.

docs.title: Administrator account
docs.text:
Mautic is installed during the app's first deployment, so you never use Mautic's web installer. Set the administrator account in the Mautic service's settings when you create the app:

Setting Default What it sets Admin password none, required The administrator's password, at least 6 characters Admin email none, required The administrator's email address Admin username admin The administrator's username
  • Mautic sends email from the admin email, with the app's title as the sender name. Change both in Mautic under Settings > Configuration > Email Settings.
  • These settings are only used when Mautic is installed. To change the administrator later, use Mautic.

If the first deployment can't install Mautic, for example because the admin password or email is missing, the deployment's post-deploy step fails with the reason. Fix it and deploy again. Later deployments update Mautic's database instead.

docs.title: Site address
docs.text: Mautic uses the app environment's main domain as its address, in links in emails and in cron jobs. The address saved in Mautic's settings is ignored. When you change the main domain, deploy the Mautic service again so Mautic picks up the new address. To use another address, set the MAUTIC_SITE_URL environment variable on the Mautic service.

docs.title: Cron jobs and queue
docs.text:
• The cron worker runs Mautic's cron jobs, such as segment and campaign updates, sending scheduled emails and broadcasts, imports, webhooks and scheduled reports, one after another every five minutes. You don't need to add a cron schedule.
  • The worker worker sends queued email and records queued page hits.

Both start working once Mautic is installed, and let the current job finish when they stop. Their logs show each run.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text: Mautic sends mail through the stack's OpenSMTPD service. For production delivery, attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD, and set a sender address your provider accepts in Mautic's email settings. See the OpenSMTPD guide. You can also enter another mail server in Mautic's email settings.

docs.title: Plugins and updates
docs.text:
Mautic's code is part of the image, so you can't add plugins or themes. Mautic's built-in plugins, such as its CRM and social integrations, are available.

New Mautic releases arrive as updates of the Mautic service; see stack upgrades. The deployment after an update migrates Mautic's database. Back up the app before you upgrade.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• The files volume holds Mautic's settings file, uploaded files and images, language packs, imports, logs and sessions. The Mautic service and both workers share it through the NFS storage service.
  • The MariaDB database holds everything else.

The settings file holds Mautic's secret key and every setting saved in Mautic. Without it, Mautic can't use its database, and the next deployment refuses to install Mautic over the existing data. Back up both the database and the files volume, and restore them together; see Application Backups.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Mautic supports only MariaDB and MySQL, and can't connect to a database server over TLS. A database that requires TLS connections can't be used.
  • Uploads are limited to 64 MB. Mautic's own limit for assets is 6 MB until you change it in Mautic's settings.
  • Development workspaces are not available for Mautic.

docs.title: Mautic (buildable) stack guide
docs.text:
The buildable Mautic stack runs Mautic built from your Git repository: a Mautic Composer project whose lock file pins Mautic and the plugins and themes you install with Composer. The stack has the same services as the Mautic stack: MariaDB, shared NFS storage for Mautic's files, cron and queue workers, and OpenSMTPD. Its composition is documented in wodby/stack-mautic-buildable.

Everything in the Mautic guide applies, from the administrator settings to workers, mail and backups. This page covers what differs.

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
Start the repository from the Mautic boilerplate, Mautic's recommended Composer project with a composer.lock, and connect it when you create the app.

  • Add plugins and themes with Composer, for example composer require mautic/helloworld-bundle.
  • Or commit a plugin or theme of your own under docroot/plugins/ or docroot/themes/, and re-include it in .gitignore, such as !/docroot/plugins/MyPluginBundle/.

Don't commit config/local.php: Mautic writes its settings there, and Wodby keeps that file on the shared files volume.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
The build runs composer install, which installs Mautic and your packages, runs npm and generates Mautic's assets, then adds Wodby's settings on top of Wodby's PHP image for Mautic.

The build fails when composer.json or composer.lock is missing, or when the repository has a config/local.php.

docs.title: Plugins and updates
docs.text:
After every deployment Wodby runs Mautic's database migrations and reloads its plugins, so new plugins are installed and updated ones are upgraded. The cron and queue workers run the same build.

To update Mautic, run composer update "mautic/*" --with-all-dependencies, commit composer.lock and deploy. You decide when to update, so watch Mautic's releases for security fixes.

To have Wodby keep Mautic up to date instead, use the Mautic stack.

docs.title: Meilisearch stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Meilisearch catalog stack runs Meilisearch, a search engine for websites and apps, as a single instance. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-meilisearch.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Every Meilisearch request except GET /health needs an API key, sent as Authorization: Bearer <key>.

Wodby generates the master key when the app is created. It is the master_key token on the Meilisearch app service's Configuration > Tokens tab, and the MEILI_MASTER_KEY variable inside the container. See Tokens. Use the master key only to manage API keys, and keep it on your servers. Never put it in browser code or in a repository.

Meilisearch creates default keys from the master key. List them with the master key:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <master key>" https://<meilisearch domain>/keys
  • Give browsers and mobile apps the Default Search API Key. It can only search.
  • Give backends that add or update documents the Default Admin API Key, or a narrower key you create with POST /keys.

See Meilisearch's security guide.

Changing the master key changes every key derived from it. The default keys and every key you created stop working, and your clients need the new keys.

docs.title: Connect to Meilisearch
docs.text:
Meilisearch has a public HTTPS domain, so browsers and mobile apps can search it directly. Services in the same app environment can use http://<app service name>:7700 instead.

Wodby does not protect the Meilisearch domain with basic auth, and you should not add one under Endpoints > Auths. Meilisearch reads its API key from the Authorization header, the same header basic auth uses, so search and indexing requests would fail. The API keys protect the domain.

Meilisearch accepts document batches of up to 100 MB. The domain allows 5 minutes per request so that large batches can finish uploading. Do not set the route's request body size: it makes the route hold each request in memory until it is complete. See HTTP settings.

docs.title: Development and production mode
docs.text:
The mode follows the app environment's type:

  • In dev environments, Meilisearch runs in development mode. Opening the domain in a browser shows Meilisearch's search preview, where you can try searches with an API key.
  • In prod, staging, test, and feature environments, Meilisearch runs in production mode, without the search preview.

In both modes, every request except GET /health needs an API key.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
Meilisearch settings are MEILI_* environment variables on the Meilisearch app service. Change them and deploy the service. See Environment variables and Meilisearch's configuration reference.

Index settings, such as searchable, filterable, and sortable attributes, ranking rules, and synonyms, are set per index through the API.

Meilisearch's telemetry is off.

docs.title: Version updates
docs.text:
A Meilisearch database opens only with the version that wrote it. When a stack upgrade brings a newer Meilisearch, Meilisearch upgrades the database in place when it starts. See Upgrade. Searches keep working during the upgrade, and new tasks wait until it is done. Follow it with GET /tasks?types=upgradeDatabase.

Meilisearch warns that this upgrade is not atomic and can, rarely, corrupt the database. Before you upgrade a production environment, create a dump with POST /dumps, or make sure you can reindex from your application's own data. A failed or stuck upgrade task can be cancelled, which rolls the database back. See Meilisearch's update guide.

New non-production environments upgrade their stack automatically by default. Turn auto-upgrade off for environments whose upgrades you want to control.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
The Meilisearch volume (10 GB by default) holds the database. Dumps and snapshots that you create with the API are written to the same volume and use its space. Raise the volume size for large datasets.

The Meilisearch service has no backup or import operation in Wodby. Create dumps or snapshots with the API, or keep the source data in your application so that you can reindex it.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The Meilisearch service is fixed to one replica. It runs one instance on one volume and can't be scaled.
  • The stack requests 0.2 CPU and 512 MiB of memory for Meilisearch and limits it to 2 CPU and 2048 MiB. Indexing uses up to two thirds of the memory limit, so raise the limit for large indexing batches. Change resources under Runtime > Resources.

docs.title: Memcached stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Memcached catalog stack runs a single Memcached service. The current composition and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-memcached.

docs.title: Connect an application
docs.text:
The service listens on TCP port 11211. UDP is switched off. It has no HTTP endpoint, so Wodby creates no route for it.

Link your application's app service to the Memcached app service. See Links. The app service receives the host and port in variables named by the linking service. Read them in code instead of hardcoding the host.

Memcached has no password, and Wodby generates no token for it. Access is limited to the environment's internal network.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Change these under Configuration > Settings on the Memcached app service. Do not use a command or a configuration file.

Setting Variable Default Cache memory (MB) MEMCACHED_MEMORY 64 Worker threads MEMCACHED_THREADS 4 Maximum connections MEMCACHED_MAX_CONNECTIONS 1024

Cache memory (MB) covers cached items only. The process uses more, so set the container memory limit higher under Runtime > Resources.

docs.title: Data loss
docs.text: Memcached stores nothing on disk, and the service has no volume. Every restart and every deployment empties the cache, because the service is replaced rather than updated in place. When the item memory is full, Memcached evicts the least recently used items. Do not keep data here that you cannot rebuild.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
Open a web terminal on the Memcached app service and run:

make check-ready -f /usr/local/bin/actions.mk
printf 'stats\r\nquit\r\n' | nc localhost 11211

The first command reports whether the server answers. The second shows limit_maxbytes, curr_items and evictions.

docs.title: Metabase stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Metabase catalog stack runs Metabase, the open source business intelligence tool, with PostgreSQL and an optional OpenSMTPD service for mail. Metabase uses the official open source edition image. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-metabase.

docs.title: Administrator account
docs.text:
Set the first administrator in the Metabase service's settings when you create the app. Both settings are required:

Setting What it sets Admin email The email address the administrator signs in with Admin password The administrator's password

The first deployment creates this administrator before Metabase accepts any requests, so Metabase's setup page is never shown and nobody else can claim a new installation. The site name is set to the app's title, and Metabase's anonymous usage tracking is turned off. You can change both in Metabase's admin settings.

The password must meet Metabase's password rules: by default, at least 6 characters with at least one digit. If Metabase refuses the password, Metabase does not start, and the Metabase service log shows Metabase's reason. Fix the setting and deploy again.

The settings are only used when the application database has no users. Changing them later does not change the account. Change the password, and add other people, in Metabase.

docs.title: Site URL
docs.text: Metabase's site URL is the Metabase service's primary domain. Metabase uses it in emails, sharing links, and embeds. Because Wodby sets it, it can't be changed in Metabase's admin settings. After you add a domain or change the primary domain, deploy the Metabase service. See Domains.

docs.title: Connect your data
docs.text:
The stack's PostgreSQL service is Metabase's application database. It holds Metabase's own data: users, questions, dashboards, saved connections, and settings. Do not use it for the data you want to analyze.

Add the databases you want to analyze in Metabase, under Admin settings > Databases > Add a database. Metabase connects to them over the network, so they must be reachable from the cluster. They are not Wodby links.

Metabase encrypts the saved connection details with a key Wodby generates for the Metabase service, the encryption_key token in Configuration > Tokens. Keep it. If the key changes, Metabase can no longer read the saved connections. See Tokens.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Metabase sends invitations, password resets, and dashboard subscriptions by email. The OpenSMTPD service is disabled by default. Either enable it, or enter your own SMTP server in Metabase's email settings.

While Metabase is linked to OpenSMTPD, it gets the SMTP server's host and port from the link, and these can't be changed in Metabase. Attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD for production delivery. Metabase sends from notifications@metabase.com by default, so set a sender address your provider accepts in Metabase's email settings. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
The Metabase container requests 0.5 CPU and 1.5 GB of memory and is limited to 2 CPUs and 3 GB. Metabase's Java heap uses up to 75% of the memory limit, so keep a memory limit when you change resources in Runtime > Resources. See Resources tab.

You can run several Metabase replicas. They share the application database, and each one gets these resources. See Replicas.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
PostgreSQL (10 GB by default) holds all of Metabase's data. The Metabase service has no volume. The databases you analyze are not part of the app and are not backed up with it.

The Metabase service has no backup or import operation in Wodby. The PostgreSQL service does. See Backups and Imports. A database restored into another environment needs the same encryption_key token, or Metabase can't read the saved connections.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text:
Metabase migrates its application database when a newer version starts, and an older version can't use the migrated database. Back up the PostgreSQL database before you choose a newer version on the General configuration tab or upgrade the stack.

You can't move back to an older version: Metabase refuses to start on a database that a newer version migrated. Restore the backup instead.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Every deployment stops all Metabase replicas before the new ones start, so Metabase is unavailable while its service is deployed.
  • The stack runs Metabase's open source edition. Features of Metabase's paid plans are not available.

docs.title: MongoDB stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby MongoDB catalog stack runs a MongoDB database server from the official MongoDB image, with an optional Mongoku web interface. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-mongodb.

docs.title: Create an environment
docs.text:
MongoDB is enabled by default with a 10 GB data volume. Mongoku is disabled by default. Enable it when you want a browser interface for the database. It is linked to the MongoDB service automatically.

Wodby creates the database and its user. Both are named <app>_<environment>, after the app and the app environment. The application does not create them. Wodby creates the database by adding a collection named __wodby to it. Leave that collection in place.

Add further DBs and users on Wodby. A user gets the readWrite role on each DB it has access to, and no other permissions.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
Wodby generates two tokens once per environment. Open the MongoDB app service's Configuration > Tokens tab to reveal them:

  • password: the password of the environment's database user.
  • root_password: the password of the administrator root.

Authentication is always on. Do not connect as root from an application.

docs.title: Connect to the database
docs.text:
The server listens on TCP port 27017. Inside the app environment, the host is the name of the MongoDB app service.

Database users are stored in the admin database, not in the application database. A client must authenticate against admin, so add authSource=admin to the connection string:

mongodb://<user>:<password>@<host>:27017/<database>?authSource=admin

Without authSource=admin, MongoDB refuses a correct password. URL-encode the user name and password.

An app service linked to MongoDB receives the connection details as environment variables defined by its own link. Read them in the application instead of hardcoding them. A connection URL that Wodby builds for a link already includes authSource=admin. If you assemble the URL from separate host, port, user and password variables, add it yourself.

To open a shell in the database container, use the web terminal. For example, this lists the databases:

mongosh --quiet -u "$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME" -p "$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD" \
  --authenticationDatabase admin --eval 'db.adminCommand({listDatabases: 1})'

docs.title: Access from outside the cluster
docs.text:
The database has no public domain. To reach it from outside the cluster, publish its port. See Publishing ports.

Warning

The server does not use TLS. On a published port, passwords and data cross the network unencrypted. Unpublish the port when you no longer need it.

docs.title: Mongoku
docs.text:
Mongoku gets its own technical domain. Find it under Endpoints > Domains. See Technical domains. Mongoku is configured with the app service's primary URL, so open it at its primary domain.

Mongoku asks for its own user name and password. This sign-in is part of Mongoku, separate from the basic auth you can add under Endpoints > Auths. Sign in with:

  • user name: admin
  • password: the admin_password token on the Mongoku app service's Configuration > Tokens tab. See Tokens tab.

Mongoku then opens the linked MongoDB server as the environment's database user, without asking for database credentials. It has the same access as that user. The admin, config and local databases are hidden.

To prevent changes from the interface, turn on the Read-only mode setting on the Mongoku app service. See Settings tab.

Mongoku has no volume. Servers you add in it are lost when its container is replaced.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The MongoDB service runs a single standalone server, not a replica set. MongoDB does not support transactions on a standalone server, so application code that needs transactions does not work with this service.
  • The service has no settings or configuration files to override. MongoDB runs with its default configuration.
  • On x86-64 nodes, MongoDB needs a CPU with AVX support.

docs.title: Backups and restore
docs.text:
Data is on the data volume. A backup is a .tar.gz archive. It holds a gzipped mongodump archive of the environment's database, dump.archive.gz, and the script Wodby uses to restore it. The backup does not include users or other databases. See Application backups.

The backup is first written to the data volume and then uploaded, so keep free space on the volume for a compressed copy of the database.

To restore a downloaded backup outside Wodby, extract it and run mongorestore --archive=dump.archive.gz --gzip with your connection options.

To restore on Wodby, run a database import from a backup or an uploaded file. See Application imports. The import accepts .tar.gz and .tgz backups made by the MongoDB service on Wodby. Collections are restored into this environment's database, even when the backup comes from an environment with another database name.

Warning

A database import replaces the contents of the data volume. Data that is not in the backup is not kept.

docs.title: Moodle stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Moodle catalog stack runs Moodle LMS with Nginx, MariaDB, shared NFS storage for Moodle's files, OpenSMTPD for mail, and an optional Valkey service for sessions. A separate worker runs Moodle's cron. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-moodle.

The stack runs Wodby's prebuilt Moodle image, so there's nothing to build and no repository to connect.

docs.title: Your own plugins and themes
docs.text: To add your own plugins or themes, use the buildable Moodle stack instead. You keep them in a Git repository started from the Moodle boilerplate, which also sets the Moodle release to run, and Wodby builds Moodle with them on every push. Each deployment installs new plugins and upgrades changed ones. You decide when to upgrade Moodle, so watch Moodle's releases for security fixes.

docs.title: Administrator account
docs.text:
Moodle is installed during the app's first deployment, so you never use Moodle's web installer. Set the administrator account in the Moodle service's settings when you create the app:

Setting Default What it sets Admin password none, required The administrator's password Admin username admin The administrator's username Admin email empty The administrator's email address
  • A password that doesn't meet Moodle's password policy works for the first sign-in, and Moodle then asks for a new one.
  • Without an email, Moodle asks for it at the first sign-in.
  • The site's full name and short name start as the app's title and name. Change them in Moodle under Site administration > Site home > Site home settings.

These settings are only used when Moodle is installed. To change the administrator later, use Moodle.

If the first deployment can't install Moodle, for example because the admin password is missing, the deployment's post-deploy step fails with the reason. Fix it and deploy again.

docs.title: Site address
docs.text: Moodle uses the app environment's main domain as its address and redirects other domains of the app to it. When you change the main domain, deploy the Moodle service again so Moodle picks up the new address. To use another address, set the MOODLE_WWWROOT environment variable on the Moodle service.

docs.title: Configuration and plugins
docs.text:
Moodle's config.php reads the database, address, data directory and session settings from the app environment.

Moodle's code is part of the image, so you can't add plugins or themes. Installing them from Moodle's web interface is turned off, because the next deployment would remove them.

docs.title: Updates and upgrades
docs.text: New Moodle releases arrive as updates of the Moodle service; see stack upgrades. The deployment after an update runs Moodle's upgrade, and Moodle switches to maintenance mode while it upgrades. Back up the app before you upgrade.

docs.title: Cron
docs.text: The cron service keeps Moodle's cron running all the time, as Moodle requires. You don't need to add a cron schedule. When the cron service stops, it lets the running task finish first.

docs.title: Mail and sessions
docs.text:
Moodle sends mail through the stack's OpenSMTPD service. For production delivery, attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD; see the OpenSMTPD guide.

Sessions are stored as files in Moodle's data directory. Enable the Valkey service to keep them in Valkey instead.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• The moodledata volume holds uploaded files and Moodle's file caches. The Moodle service and its cron worker share it through the NFS storage service.
  • The MariaDB database holds everything else.

Back up both the database and the moodledata volume; see Application Backups.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Each Moodle release supports only certain PHP and MariaDB versions. The stack's defaults match; check Moodle's release notes before you change either version.
  • Uploads are limited to 256 MB.

docs.title: Moodle (buildable) stack guide
docs.text:
The buildable Moodle stack runs Moodle built from your Git repository: the repository pins the Moodle release and holds your own plugins and themes. The stack has the same services as the Moodle stack: Nginx, MariaDB, shared NFS storage for Moodle's data, a cron worker, OpenSMTPD and optional Valkey. Its composition is documented in wodby/stack-moodle-buildable.

Everything in the Moodle guide applies, from the administrator settings to cron, sessions and backups. This page covers what differs.

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
Start the repository from the Moodle boilerplate and connect it when you create the app.

Path Purpose .moodle-version The Moodle release to run, such as 5.3.1. Required. public/ Your plugins and themes, at their place in Moodle's public/ tree, such as public/local/myplugin .wodby/pipeline.yml The pipeline, which puts Moodle together before building the images

Moodle 5.1 and later 5.x releases are supported.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Before building the images, the pipeline runs moodle-install-release. It downloads the release with its Composer packages and adds your public/ files and Wodby's settings file. The Moodle and Nginx images are then built from the same code, so Nginx serves your plugins' and themes' files.

The build fails when .moodle-version is missing, or when a file in public/ is already part of Moodle: your plugins are added next to Moodle's code and never replace it.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
Each deployment installs or upgrades Moodle, installs plugins that are new in the repository and upgrades those whose version went up. The cron worker runs the same build, so your plugins' scheduled tasks run too.

Uninstall a plugin in Moodle's administration before you remove it from the repository. Plugins can't be installed from Moodle's web interface, because the code is part of the image.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Moodle's version changes only when you change .moodle-version and deploy; the deployment upgrades the database. Updates of the service bring PHP and Wodby's own changes, not a new Moodle. You decide when to upgrade, so watch Moodle's releases for security fixes.

To have Wodby keep Moodle up to date instead, use the Moodle stack.

docs.title: MySQL stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby MySQL catalog stack runs a MySQL database server, with an optional phpMyAdmin. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-mysql.

docs.title: Create an environment
docs.text:
MySQL is enabled by default with a 20 GB data volume. phpMyAdmin is disabled by default. Enable it when you want a browser interface for the database. It is linked to the MySQL service automatically.

Wodby creates the database and its user. Both are named after the app and the app environment, and the user has all privileges on that database only. The database uses utf8mb4 with the utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci collation. The application does not create them. A user you create by hand with a name Wodby later needs, but a different password, makes Wodby's create action fail. Add further DBs and users on Wodby.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
Wodby generates two tokens once per environment. Open the MySQL app service's Configuration > Tokens tab to reveal them:

  • password: the password of the environment's database user.
  • root_password: the root password. The container also has it in MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD, and root may connect from any host.

Use the database user, not root, in applications.

docs.title: Connect to the database
docs.text:
The server listens on TCP port 3306. Inside the app environment, the host is the name of the MySQL app service. The database has no public route. To reach it from outside the cluster, publish its port. See Publishing ports.

An app service linked to MySQL receives the host, port, database name, user name, and password as environment variables defined by its own link, for example DB_HOST and DB_PASSWORD on a PHP service. Read them in the application instead of hardcoding them.

To open a shell in the database container, use the web terminal. For example, mysql -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e 'SHOW DATABASES;' lists the databases.

docs.title: phpMyAdmin
docs.text: phpMyAdmin has no persistent data and connects only to the linked MySQL server. Wodby protects its public domains with basic auth by default. Reveal the generated password on the environment's Endpoints > Auths page. See Auths. On the phpMyAdmin login page, sign in with the environment's database user to see its database, or with root to see all databases.

docs.title: Server settings
docs.text:
On every start the container writes its configuration from a template and environment variables. Do not edit the generated file. Use one of these instead:

  • Set a variable on the MySQL app service: MYSQL_INNODB_BUFFER_POOL_SIZE, MYSQL_MAX_CONNECTIONS, MYSQL_MAX_ALLOWED_PACKET, MYSQL_WAIT_TIMEOUT, MYSQL_TRANSACTION_ISOLATION, MYSQL_CHARACTER_SET_SERVER, or MYSQL_COLLATION_SERVER. These are applied only when you set them: MYSQL_SQL_MODE, MYSQL_SLOW_QUERY_LOG, MYSQL_LONG_QUERY_TIME, MYSQL_PERFORMANCE_SCHEMA, MYSQL_INNODB_REDO_LOG_CAPACITY, MYSQL_INNODB_IO_CAPACITY, MYSQL_LOWER_CASE_TABLE_NAMES.
  • Override the service's MySQL config file for a setting that no variable covers. It replaces the template. See Configs tab.

A change applies on the next deployment of the service.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The MySQL service runs a single instance.

docs.title: Backups and restore
docs.text:
Data is on the data volume. A backup is a gzipped SQL dump of the environment's database. In the backup's Excluded table contents option, list table names or SQL LIKE patterns. Those tables keep their definition and lose their rows. See Application backups.

To restore, run a database import from a backup or an uploaded file. See Application imports. The import accepts a .sql or .mysql file, or a .gz, .tar.gz, .tgz, or .zip archive that contains exactly one such file.

Warning

A database import replaces the contents of the data volume. Data that is not in the dump is not kept.

docs.title: n8n stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby n8n catalog stack runs n8n, the workflow automation tool, from the official Community Edition image, with PostgreSQL and an optional OpenSMTPD service for mail. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-n8n.

docs.title: Owner account
docs.text:
Set the owner account in the n8n service's settings when you create the app:

Setting Default What it sets Owner email none, required The email address the owner signs in with Owner password none, required The owner's password, at least 8 characters Timezone UTC The default timezone of schedules and date functions, such as Europe/Berlin

n8n applies the owner's email and password on every start, so its setup page is never shown and nobody else can claim a new installation. Open the app's domain and sign in with these credentials.

You can't change the owner's email or password in n8n. Change them in the service's Configuration > Settings and deploy the n8n service. The owner is then signed out and signs in with the new values. If the password is shorter than 8 characters, n8n does not start, and the n8n service log says why. See Settings tab.

To let other people in, invite them in n8n. Invitations are sent by email; see Mail.

docs.title: Webhooks and the editor URL
docs.text:
n8n builds webhook URLs and editor links from the n8n service's primary domain. After you add a domain or change the primary domain, deploy the n8n service so that n8n shows webhook URLs with the new domain. If you remove the old domain, update the webhook URLs in the systems that call them. See Domains.

The route has no request timeout, so a webhook can wait for its workflow to finish before it answers. Do not set the route's request body size: it makes the route hold each request in memory until it is complete, and the editor's live connection stops working. See HTTP settings.

docs.title: Code nodes
docs.text:
JavaScript and Python Code nodes run in a separate task runner container next to n8n, at the same version as n8n. A Code node may run for up to 5 minutes.

Which modules Code nodes may import is set in the runner image. By default, Python Code nodes can't import standard-library modules, and JavaScript Code nodes can use crypto and moment. Environment variables you add to the n8n service do not reach the runner.

The runner has its own CPU and memory, up to 1 CPU and 1 GB by default. Raise them in Runtime > Resources if Code nodes process large data. See Resources tab.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
n8n sends user invitations and password resets by email. The owner account doesn't need mail, so the OpenSMTPD service is disabled by default. Enable it to send n8n's mail, and attach an SMTP provider integration to it for production delivery. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

While n8n is linked to OpenSMTPD, mail is sent from noreply@ the n8n service's primary hostname. If your provider accepts only other senders, set the N8N_SMTP_SENDER environment variable on the n8n service, for example n8n <automation@example.com>, and deploy it. See Environment variables.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL (10 GB by default) holds workflows, credentials, executions, users, and settings.
  • The n8n volume (10 GB by default) holds community nodes, binary data, and n8n's own files.

n8n encrypts saved credentials with a key Wodby generates for the n8n service, the encryption_key token in Configuration > Tokens. Keep it and keep a copy. If the key changes, n8n can no longer read saved credentials. A database restored into another environment needs the same key. See Tokens.

Back up the database and the n8n volume together as one recovery set. The n8n service has no backup or import operation in Wodby. The PostgreSQL service does. See Backups and Imports.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text: n8n migrates its database when a newer version starts, for example after a stack upgrade, and an older version can't use the migrated database. Back up the PostgreSQL database before you upgrade.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The n8n service is fixed to one replica. n8n's queue mode, with Redis and separate worker processes, is not set up by this stack.
  • n8n is unavailable for a short time while its service is deployed.
  • n8n's Sustainable Use License allows use for your own internal business purposes or for non-commercial or personal use. Check it before you offer n8n to others.

docs.title: NetBird stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby NetBird catalog stack runs a self-hosted NetBird server: a WireGuard-based private network that connects your devices and servers wherever they are. One app service runs the management server, sign-in, the relay and the NetBird dashboard. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-netbird.

Everything runs over HTTPS, so it works on any cluster and you don't need to publish ports.

docs.title: Create the app
docs.text:
1. Create an app from the NetBird catalog stack.
  2. Set the required Admin email and Admin password settings. The first deployment creates this administrator, so the dashboard never offers a public setup page.
  3. Deploy. The first start downloads location databases used by posture checks and can take a few minutes before the app is ready.

Sign in to the dashboard at the app's main domain with the administrator's email and password. Changing the settings later has no effect: change passwords, invite users and add single sign-on providers in the dashboard.

docs.title: Connect devices
docs.text:
1. In the dashboard, create a setup key under Setup Keys, or let people sign in from the NetBird client.
  2. Install the NetBird client on each device.

  3. Point the client at your server's main domain:

    netbird up --management-url https://prod.myapp.example.com

    Add --setup-key <key> on devices without a browser. In the desktop apps, enter the same URL as the management URL in the settings.

Use the app's main domain as the management URL, the same address as the dashboard.

docs.title: Domains
docs.text:
The NetBird app service has two domains:

  • The main domain of the netbird endpoint serves the dashboard and everything clients use to sign in and stay connected. Add your own domain to this endpoint if you want one.
  • The relay endpoint has its own domain, relay.<service>.<environment domain>. The server tells clients about it; nobody enters it.

After you add a domain and make it primary for an endpoint, deploy the app service so the server uses the new address. If the main domain changes, run netbird up with the new management URL on every device.

See Endpoints.

docs.title: How devices connect
docs.text:
Devices connect to each other directly when their networks allow it. To find their public addresses they use Cloudflare's public STUN server (stun:stun.cloudflare.com:3478). NetBird's own STUN server isn't used: behind the cluster's gateway it can't see the devices' addresses. To use other STUN servers, set the NETBIRD_STUN_URIS environment variable to a space-separated list of stun: URLs, or to an empty value for none, and deploy the app service.

When a direct connection isn't possible, traffic goes through the relay on your cluster, and it counts toward your cluster's bandwidth.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
The data volume holds the accounts, devices, network settings, users and activity log, in SQLite databases. If you lose the volume, every device has to be set up again. The stack runs one replica.

Wodby generates the keys that encrypt sensitive data and sign-in sessions when the app is created. They stay the same across deployments.

docs.title: Nextcloud stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Nextcloud catalog stack runs Nextcloud file storage and sharing with PostgreSQL, Redis, and an optional OpenSMTPD mail relay. Nextcloud uses the official Nextcloud Apache image. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-nextcloud.

docs.title: Before you create the app
docs.text:
• Nextcloud, PostgreSQL, and Redis are required. OpenSMTPD is optional and selected by default. You can leave it out when you create the app.
  • Enter Admin username and Admin password on the Nextcloud service. Nextcloud creates this administrator account during the first deployment. Both values are stored as secrets and Wodby does not show them again, so keep a copy.
  • Choose volume sizes now. The Nextcloud volume is 50 GB and the PostgreSQL volume is 20 GB by default. A volume cannot be resized from the app service settings after it is created. See Application persistent storage.
  • If file contents should be stored in a bucket instead of the Nextcloud volume, set that up before the first deployment. See Object storage for files.

docs.title: First sign-in
docs.text:
Nextcloud installs itself when it first starts. After the first deployment, open the app's main domain and sign in with the administrator username and password you entered.

Changing Admin username or Admin password later does not change the account. Change the password in Nextcloud, or reset it with an occ command.

docs.title: Domains
docs.text:
Nextcloud accepts requests only for its trusted domains. Wodby sets them from the app environment's domains, including Private App Access hostnames, each time Nextcloud starts. This list replaces trusted domains set in Nextcloud's own configuration, so manage domains in Wodby.

After you add or remove a domain, or change the main domain, deploy the Nextcloud service. Until then, Nextcloud rejects requests for a new hostname with an untrusted domain error. Links that Nextcloud creates in background jobs, such as email notifications, use the primary domain. See Domains.

The optional Trusted proxies setting lists proxy IP addresses or CIDR ranges, separated by spaces, whose forwarded client address headers Nextcloud trusts. Do not enter a range wider than your cluster's proxy network.

docs.title: Background jobs
docs.text: A cron container in the Nextcloud pod runs Nextcloud's background jobs every five minutes. On the first run, Nextcloud switches its background jobs setting to Cron. You do not need a Wodby cron schedule. Keep Cron selected under Administration settings > Basic settings > Background jobs.

docs.title: Mail delivery
docs.text:
While the Nextcloud service is linked to OpenSMTPD, Nextcloud sends mail through it and takes its email server settings from Wodby. The sender address is built from two Nextcloud service settings: Mail sender, nextcloud by default, and Mail domain, the app's primary hostname by default.

Recipient mail servers often reject mail sent directly from a cluster. For production, attach an SMTP provider integration to OpenSMTPD and set Mail sender and Mail domain to an address your provider accepts. Then deploy the Nextcloud service. See the OpenSMTPD guide for relay setup and testing.

Without the OpenSMTPD link, set up an email server in Nextcloud under Administration settings > Basic settings.

docs.title: Uploads and timeouts
docs.text:
The Nextcloud domain passes uploads through to Nextcloud as they arrive, and its request and backend timeouts are one hour. The PHP upload limit setting is 3G, and the Apache request body limit setting is 0, which means no Apache limit. Nextcloud clients normally upload large files in smaller parts, so these limits apply to each part.

To accept larger single requests, raise the PHP upload limit, then deploy the Nextcloud service. Do not set the request_body_size HTTP setting on the Nextcloud domain: it makes the route hold each upload in memory until it is complete. PHP memory limit is 512M by default.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Nextcloud keeps a local cache in its own container and uses Redis for the shared cache, file locking, and browser sessions. In this stack, Redis has no volume and keeps nothing on disk. It can use up to 512 MB of memory and never removes keys to free memory, so file locks and sessions are not lost while Redis runs. When Redis restarts or is deployed, its data is cleared, and people signed in through the browser may need to sign in again. See the Redis guide.

docs.title: Object storage for files
docs.text:
Nextcloud can store file contents in Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, or Backblaze B2 instead of the Nextcloud volume. Set it up before the first deployment:

  1. Create an empty bucket used only by this app environment's Nextcloud. For Amazon S3, create it in the region selected in the AWS integration.
