  2. Create an AWS, Cloudflare R2, or Backblaze B2 integration whose credentials can read, write, and delete objects in that bucket.
  3. On the Nextcloud service, attach the integration to S3 primary storage on the Integrations tab and enter the bucket name in the S3 bucket setting. Nextcloud uses the bucket only when both are set.

Data loss

Do not enable object storage on an installation that already has files: files stored on the volume become inaccessible. For the same reason, do not detach the integration or clear S3 bucket later, or the files in the bucket become inaccessible.

The bucket holds file contents under internal names. Folder structure and file names are stored in PostgreSQL, so you cannot browse users' folders in the bucket. Do not store anything else in it, including Wodby backups.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• The Nextcloud volume holds the Nextcloud installation, its configuration, installed apps, themes, and, without object storage, all user files.
  • PostgreSQL holds accounts, shares, file records, and app data.
  • Redis holds only temporary data.

The Nextcloud service has no backup or import operation in Wodby. The PostgreSQL service does: a backup is a compressed SQL dump of the database, and an import replaces the whole database. See Backups and Imports.

A PostgreSQL backup on its own does not restore Nextcloud: the database records which files exist, so a restored database does not match the files on the volume or in the bucket. Wodby cannot back up the Nextcloud volume, so copy it, and the bucket if you use one, with your own tools together with a PostgreSQL backup, and restore them together. To keep the copies consistent, turn on maintenance mode while you make them.

docs.title: Run occ commands
docs.text:
Open a web terminal on the Nextcloud service, choose the nextcloud container, and run occ as the www-data user:

su -s /bin/sh www-data -c 'php /var/www/html/occ status'

For example, use maintenance:mode --on and maintenance:mode --off around a backup, or user:resetpassword <user> to set a new password for an account.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text:
Nextcloud upgrades itself when it starts with a newer version, for example after you change the version on the General configuration tab or after a stack update. Nextcloud's built-in web updater is turned off. The upgrade runs before Nextcloud serves requests, and Wodby gives it about 15 minutes before the container is restarted.

  • Back up before you upgrade.
  • Upgrade one major version at a time. If you skip a major version, Nextcloud does not start.
  • You cannot return to an older version. Nextcloud does not start when its data is newer than the selected version. Restore a backup instead.
  • Apps that are not compatible with the new version are disabled during the upgrade. The Nextcloud service log lists them.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Nextcloud runs as one replica, and the old pod stops before the new one starts. Nextcloud is unavailable while its service is deployed.
  • The stack does not include an online office server, such as Collabora Online.

docs.title: Next.js stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Next.js catalog stack runs a Node.js (Next.js) app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, and Gotenberg services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-nextjs.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text: Start from the Next.js Boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service's Dockerfile copies your build context, runs npm run build while the image is built, and starts the container with npm run start. package.json must define both scripts, normally next build and next start.
  • The Dockerfile does not install dependencies. Install them in your pipeline before the image is built, for example with wodby ci run -- npm ci, so that node_modules is part of the image. See CI/CD.
  • Runtime variables are not available to npm run build. That includes link variables and secrets. Render pages that need them at request time instead of prerendering them during the build.
  • The application must listen on port 3000, which next start does by default.
  • NODE_ENV is production in every environment type, including dev, because the container runs a production build. Do not set it to development for a deployed environment.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
Server-side code reads these variables. They are not exposed to the browser. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail transport without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 10 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • The app service runs next dev directly from node_modules, so options in the dev script of package.json do not apply. With Next.js 16 or later it adds --webpack.
  • NODE_ENV is development there, and saved files are picked up without a restart. The npm run build step does not run.

docs.title: Node.js stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Node.js catalog stack runs a Node.js app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and Cloud PostgreSQL services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-node.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the Express.js boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

To use a managed database instead of the PostgreSQL container, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The container runs npm run start from the application directory. package.json must define a start script.
  • The application must listen on port 3000 on all interfaces. Wodby sets NODE_PORT to 3000 and does not set PORT. Read NODE_PORT, or default to 3000.
  • NODE_ENV is development in environments of type dev and production in every other type.
  • The service's Dockerfile only copies your build context. It does not run npm install. Install dependencies and produce any compiled output in your pipeline before the image is built, for example with wodby ci run -- npm ci, so that node_modules is part of the image. See CI/CD.
  • A Dockerfile from your repository replaces the service's Dockerfile.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
The application reads these variables itself. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail transport without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 10 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • The app service runs the dev script when package.json has one, otherwise start. Set WORKSPACE_NODE_COMMAND to use another command.
  • NODE_ENV is always development there. Run workspace preparation again after changing dependencies.

docs.title: Nuxt stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Nuxt catalog stack runs a Node.js (Nuxt) app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and OpenTelemetry Collector services. The app renders pages and runs server routes on Nuxt's Node.js server. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-nuxt.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the Nuxt Boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, Mailpit for mail, and the OpenTelemetry Collector for telemetry. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

The app service's version is the Node.js version. The boilerplate includes a health endpoint at /healthz and checks it after each deployment.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service's Dockerfile copies your build context, runs npm run build while the image is built, and starts the container with npm run start. package.json must define both scripts.
  • Build with Nuxt's default Node.js server output: nuxt build to build and node .output/server/index.mjs to start. Do not set another Nitro preset, and do not use nuxt generate as the build script. The boilerplate is set up this way.
  • The Dockerfile does not install dependencies. Install them in your pipeline before the image is built, for example with wodby ci run -- npm ci, so that node_modules is part of the image. See CI/CD. Keep the postinstall: nuxt prepare script from Nuxt's starter; it needs no runtime variables.
  • Runtime variables are not available to npm run build. That includes link variables and secrets. nuxt.config.ts is evaluated during the build, so values read there are fixed in the image. Read runtime values in server routes, server middleware, or server plugins when a request is handled.
  • The application must listen on port 3000, the Nitro server's default. Do not set PORT or NITRO_PORT.
  • NODE_ENV is production in every environment type, including dev, because the container runs a production build. Do not set it to development for a deployed environment.
  • The image build leaves out .nuxt, .output, and .data; nuxt build creates them again.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Configure the application
docs.text:
Use Nuxt's runtime config for settings that differ between environments. Declare each key in runtimeConfig in nuxt.config.ts with an empty or default value. Then add a variable to the app service named NUXT_ plus the key path in upper snake case, such as NUXT_API_SECRET for runtimeConfig.apiSecret. See Environment variables.

  • Only declared keys are overridden.
  • Keys under runtimeConfig.public use the NUXT_PUBLIC_ prefix and are sent to the browser. Never put secrets there.
  • Values such as true, numbers, and JSON are parsed, so they do not arrive as strings.
  • The production server does not read .env files.

Wodby generates NUXT_APP_SECRET, Nuxt's application secret, for each environment. It stays the same across deployments and differs between environments. Nuxt's sessions (useSession), deriveSecret, and modules built on them need it and fail when a request uses them without it. Changing the secret ends existing sessions and invalidates anything signed with secrets derived from it.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
Server routes read these variables from process.env. They do not reach the browser. They have no NUXT_ prefix, so they do not override runtime config. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

The database link sets no DATABASE_URL. If your database library needs a URL, build it from these variables in server code and URL-encode the user name and password.

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail transport without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
When you select the OpenTelemetry Collector, the app service's link to it sets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL (http/protobuf), and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS (the Collector's ingest token). An OpenTelemetry SDK in your application exports to the Collector without further configuration. Set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME on the app service to name the application. The Collector is reachable only inside the environment.

The Collector stores nothing. It forwards traces, metrics, and logs over OTLP/HTTP to another Collector or backend. On the Collector app service, under Configuration > Settings, set Upstream OTLP endpoint to the receiver's base URL and Upstream Authorization header to the header it expects, such as Bearer <ingest token>. See Settings tab.

The Grafana Tempo, Loki, and VictoriaMetrics stacks each accept one kind of data. Turn off the other exports in the application, for example with OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none and OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none when you send to Tempo.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 10 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

The app service has no volume, backup, or import of its own.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • Setup installs dependencies from the lockfile. Run setup again after you change dependencies.
  • The app service runs nuxt dev from node_modules, not the dev script in package.json. Options in that script do not apply. nuxt must be a dependency of the project.
  • The server listens on port 3000. Do not change the port in your Nuxt configuration.
  • The development server answers 403 for host names it does not know. Allow the environment's hosts in vite.server.allowedHosts of nuxt.config.ts. WODBY_HOSTS holds them as a JSON array; the boilerplate's nuxt.config.ts reads it.
  • NODE_ENV is development. Saved files, new pages, and new server routes are picked up without a restart. The npm run build step does not run.
  • A change to nuxt.config.ts restarts the development server only if you add watch: ['../nuxt.config.ts'] to it, as the boilerplate does when CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING is set.
  • .nuxt, .output, .data, and node_modules are kept out of Git status.
  • To start the server another way, set WORKSPACE_NODE_COMMAND on the app service. The command must listen on $HOST:$PORT and poll for file changes itself.
  • A change to variables or linked services still needs a deployment of the environment.

docs.title: Observability stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Observability catalog stack collects traces, metrics, and logs from your applications in one app. The OpenTelemetry Collector receives all three on one endpoint. Grafana Tempo stores traces, VictoriaMetrics stores metrics, Grafana Loki stores logs, and Grafana shows them together. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-observability.

Use this stack when you want all three signals in one place. To collect only one of them, use the Grafana Tempo, Grafana Loki, or VictoriaMetrics stack instead.

docs.title: Choose services when you create the app
docs.text: Tempo, Loki, VictoriaMetrics, and the OpenTelemetry Collector are required. Grafana is enabled by default as the stack's main interface. You can exclude Grafana when you query the data from another Grafana.

docs.title: Send telemetry from your applications
docs.text:
Applications send traces, metrics, and logs to the Collector over OTLP. The Collector's HTTP port has a public HTTPS domain, listed under Endpoints for the app environment, so applications in other app environments, other clusters, or outside Wodby can use it.

Every request needs the Collector's ingest token. Open the Collector app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal ingest_token. See Tokens. Requests without the token are refused with 401.

Set the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables in the application that sends telemetry:

Variable Value OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT https://<Collector domain>, without a path OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL http/protobuf OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS Authorization=Bearer%20<ingest token>, stored as a secret OTEL_SERVICE_NAME A name for the application, shown in Grafana

The space after Bearer is written as %20 because SDKs URL-decode header values. On Wodby, add the variables to the sending app service. See Environment variables.

The Collector sends traces to Tempo, metrics to VictoriaMetrics, and logs to Loki, so you don't need to turn off any signal in the SDK. If your SDK or agent doesn't export metrics or logs by default, set OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp and OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp.

Inside the same app environment, services can also send to http://<Collector app service name>:4318, or over gRPC to port 4317, with the same token.

Apps from the Wodby application stacks can instead forward telemetry through their own Collector: set its Upstream link to this app's Collector, listed with the other apps you can link to. On the same cluster the data stays on the private network. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: View telemetry in Grafana
docs.text:
Open the Grafana domain listed under Endpoints. Open the Grafana app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal admin_username (admin) and admin_password. Grafana applies them once, on the first start with an empty data volume. See the Grafana guide.

Grafana has three data sources:

  • VictoriaMetrics, the default, for metrics. VictoriaMetrics keeps OpenTelemetry attribute names, so queries quote them in label filters, for example {"service.name"="api"}.
  • Loki for logs. Find them by the service_name label, for example {service_name="api"}.
  • Tempo for traces. Search them with Explore or Drilldown > Traces.

The data sources are linked:

  • From a span in Tempo, open Logs for this span to see the Loki logs of the same trace, from 5 minutes before the span to 5 minutes after it.
  • A log line written during a trace shows a View trace link in its details that opens the trace in Tempo.

The links work when the application writes logs through the OpenTelemetry SDK while a trace is active, so each log record carries the trace ID.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
The Collector config, Tempo config, and Grafana data sources are files under their app service's Configuration > Configs tab. See Configs tab. After a change, deploy the app service. Wodby restarts it so the new file takes effect.

Common changes:

  • Send data to another backend as well. Add an exporter to the Collector config, for example otlp_http with the backend's endpoint and headers. In each pipeline that should send to it, replace the exporter list ${env:OTLP_<SIGNAL>_EXPORTERS:-[nop]} with both exporters, such as [otlp_http/logs, otlp_http/<name>]. Put the backend's key in a secret environment variable of the Collector and refer to it as ${env:NAME} in the file.
  • Keep traces longer. See Grafana Tempo.

Keep the token check on the Collector's receivers while its HTTP port has a public domain.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: The stack creates a 20 GB data volume each for Tempo, Loki, and VictoriaMetrics. Grafana has its own 10 GB volume with its dashboards, users, settings, and plugins. Tempo deletes traces after 7 days. Wodby sets no retention for VictoriaMetrics, so it keeps the upstream default. Wodby defines no backups or imports for these services.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Tempo, Loki, and VictoriaMetrics each run as a single instance and are not scalable. The stack suits development environments and low to moderate volumes.
  • Their ports are private: query them through Grafana or from another service in the app environment.
  • The Collector can run several replicas with the default configuration.

docs.title: Check that the services are ready
docs.text:
• Tempo: /ready on port 3200.
  • Loki: /ready on port 3100.
  • VictoriaMetrics: /-/ready on port 8428.
  • Collector: port 13133 answers 200 when every pipeline has started.
  • Send a test request to the Collector domain with the token: a POST of {} with Content-Type: application/json to https://<Collector domain>/v1/traces, /v1/metrics, or /v1/logs returns 200.

docs.title: Odoo stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Odoo catalog stack runs Odoo Community Edition 20, 19 or 18 with Nginx, PostgreSQL, shared NFS storage for Odoo's files, and an optional OpenSMTPD service for mail. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-odoo.

The stack needs no repository: Odoo and every Community app come with the service's image. Install apps from Odoo's Apps menu, or list them in the Apps to install setting when you create the app.

docs.title: Your own modules
docs.text: To add your own or community modules, use the buildable Odoo stack instead. You keep the modules and their Python packages in a Git repository started from the Odoo boilerplate, and Wodby builds Odoo with them on every push. Installed modules whose files change are updated when you deploy; new modules appear in the Apps menu.

docs.title: Administrator account
docs.text:
Odoo is installed during the app's first deployment. Its database manager is turned off, so databases can't be created, copied or dropped from the web. Set up the installation in the Odoo service's settings when you create the app:

Setting Default What it sets Admin password none, required The administrator's password Admin login admin The administrator's login Admin email empty The administrator's email address Language English A language to install and give the administrator, such as fr_FR Apps to install none Apps installed with Odoo, such as crm,sale_management
  • The company starts with the app's title as its name. Change it in Odoo's settings.
  • No demo data is loaded.

These settings are only used when Odoo is installed. To change the administrator later, use Odoo.

If the first deployment can't install Odoo, for example because the admin password is missing, the deployment's post-deploy step fails with the reason. Fix it and deploy again.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Odoo updates arrive with new revisions of the service's image. After each deployment, Odoo updates the installed apps whose version went up. To update every installed app, run the Update all modules action of the Odoo service.

To add your own or community modules, use the buildable Odoo stack.

docs.title: Workers and live updates
docs.text: Each Odoo replica runs 2 worker processes and 1 process for scheduled actions by default; change the Workers and Scheduled action workers settings to match the service's memory. A separate process serves live updates such as chat and notifications, and the Nginx service sends them to it. Keep at least 1 worker.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text: Enable the OpenSMTPD service to send Odoo's mail through it, and attach an SMTP provider integration for production delivery; see the OpenSMTPD guide. You can also set up an outgoing mail server in Odoo's settings.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• The filestore volume holds uploaded files and sessions. Every Odoo replica shares it through the NFS storage service.
  • The PostgreSQL database holds everything else.

Back up both the database and the filestore volume; see Application Backups. Back up the app before you move to a new major Odoo version: Odoo doesn't migrate a database between major versions by itself.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Odoo Community Edition only. Enterprise modules need the buildable Odoo stack, like your own modules.
  • One database per app environment.
  • Uploads are limited to 128 MB.

docs.title: Odoo (buildable) stack guide
docs.text:
The buildable Odoo stack runs Odoo Community Edition 20, 19 or 18 built from your Git repository: the repository holds your own and community modules and the Python packages they need. The stack has the same services as the Odoo stack: Nginx, PostgreSQL, shared NFS storage for Odoo's files, and an optional OpenSMTPD service. Its composition is documented in wodby/stack-odoo-buildable.

Everything in the Odoo guide applies, from the administrator settings to workers, mail and backups. This page covers what differs.

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
Start the repository from the Odoo boilerplate and connect it when you create the app.

Path Purpose addons/ Your modules, one directory per module with its __manifest__.py requirements.txt Python packages your modules need

Modules can also live in other directories up to three levels deep, for example one directory per module collection copied from a community repository. Every directory that holds modules is added to Odoo's addons path; the build log shows the addons path and the modules it found.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Choose the Odoo version when you create the app. The build starts from Wodby's Odoo image for that version, copies the repository into it and installs requirements.txt. Lines like git+https://... work. The image has no compiler, so packages need prebuilt wheels.

The build fails when a module has the name of one of Odoo's own modules, because Odoo would ignore it.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
• The first deployment installs Odoo with the apps in the Apps to install setting, which can include your own modules.
  • Later deployments update the installed modules whose files changed in the repository, or whose manifest version went up.
  • New modules appear in Odoo's Apps menu; install them there.
  • Uninstall a module in Odoo before you remove it from the repository.

Odoo Enterprise modules go in the repository like any other module; they need an Odoo Enterprise subscription.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Odoo's exact build comes from the service's Odoo image, not from the repository. It moves forward with service updates, and the app's next build uses it.

To run Odoo without your own modules, use the Odoo stack.

docs.title: Open WebUI stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Open WebUI catalog stack runs Open WebUI, a self-hosted chat interface for AI models, with PostgreSQL. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-open-webui.

Open WebUI does not run models itself. It connects to model APIs: a hosted provider such as OpenAI, or your own OpenAI-compatible server.

docs.title: Administrator account
docs.text:
Set the administrator in the Open WebUI service's settings when you create the app. Both settings are required:

Setting What it sets Admin email The email address the administrator signs in with Admin password The administrator's password

Open WebUI creates this account on its first start and then turns public sign-up off, so nobody else can register. Open the app's domain and sign in with these credentials.

The settings are only used when the database has no users. To change the password later, use Open WebUI. To let other people in, add their accounts in Admin Panel → Users, or turn sign-up back on in Admin Panel → Settings → General.

docs.title: Connect models
docs.text:
Add a model connection in Admin Panel → Settings → Connections: an API key for a hosted provider, or the URL and key of an OpenAI-compatible server, for example https://your-server/v1. The models it offers then appear in the chat.

In a custom stack, the Open WebUI service's optional OpenAI-compatible API link can connect it to a service in the same app that offers such an API, such as vLLM, including the service's API key. The link only takes effect on Open WebUI's first start; see the next section.

docs.title: Settings saved by Open WebUI
docs.text:
On its first start, Open WebUI saves most of its configuration in the database, including model connections, sign-up, and its own address. After that, it ignores the environment variables for those settings, and changes made in Admin Panel → Settings survive deployments. As a result, a model link added to an existing app does not add a connection; add it in Open WebUI instead.

Setting the environment variable RESET_CONFIG_ON_START to true makes Open WebUI read the variables again on the next start, but it also discards every setting changed in the admin panel. See Environment variables.

docs.title: Domains
docs.text:
Only the app's own domains can open the chat's live connection or call Open WebUI's API from a browser. When you add or remove a domain, Wodby marks the Open WebUI service for redeployment; deploy it to apply the change. To allow other origins, set the CORS_ALLOW_ORIGIN environment variable on the service to a list of origins separated by ;, such as https://chat.example.com;https://intranet.example.com. It replaces the computed list.

Answers stream for as long as the model writes, so the route has no request timeout. Do not set the route's request body size: it makes the route hold each request in memory until it is complete, and the chat's live connection stops working. See HTTP settings.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL holds users, chats, settings, models, and prompts.
  • The Open WebUI volume (10 GB by default) holds uploaded files, the document search index, and caches.

Back up the database and the Open WebUI volume together as one recovery set. The Open WebUI service has no backup or import operation in Wodby. The PostgreSQL service does. See Backups.

Document search runs its embedding model inside the Open WebUI container, using the models that come with the image. Large documents need memory and CPU in that container.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The Open WebUI service is fixed to one replica. Several replicas would need pgvector, Redis, and storage shared between replicas, which this stack does not set up.
  • There is no Ollama service in the catalog, so Open WebUI's Ollama connection is turned off.
  • Open WebUI's license requires keeping its branding in larger deployments. Wodby runs the official image unchanged.

docs.title: OpenClaw stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby OpenClaw catalog stack runs the OpenClaw gateway and its Control UI. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-openclaw.

docs.title: Before you create the app
docs.text:
The stack requires Protected access with the Private network type for the entire app. Select a compatible Private App Access integration when you create the app. You cannot change these choices. Private App Access needs an active paid subscription. See Private App Access.

Wodby publishes no public route for the gateway. You reach it through the Access provider. Services in the same app environment reach it directly on port 18789.

docs.title: Open the Control UI
docs.text:
Wodby sets up the private address after the first successful deployment.

  1. Connect your device to the provider's private network: join the tailnet for Tailscale, or use the Cloudflare One Client for Cloudflare.
  2. Open the address listed under Apps > [App] > [Environment] > Endpoints > Domains.
  3. Find the gateway_token token on the OpenClaw app service's Configuration > Tokens tab, and paste it into Gateway secret. See Tokens.

  4. Approve the browser. A new browser waits for a one-time approval. In a web terminal, run these commands, and the page connects by itself:

    openclaw devices list
openclaw devices approve <requestId>

Each browser profile needs its own approval. A private window asks again after it closes.

Other clients of the gateway authenticate with the same token.

docs.title: Turn on agents and channels
docs.text:
Add these environment variables to the OpenClaw app service, then deploy it. See Environment variables.

Variable Effect OPENAI_API_KEY adds the agents openai and openai-code ANTHROPIC_API_KEY adds the agent claude GEMINI_API_KEY or GOOGLE_API_KEY adds the agent gemini TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN enables the Telegram channel DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN enables the Discord channel

The first provider present, in the order of this table, is the default agent. Without a provider key, the configuration has no agent list.

Optional variables set agent models and workspaces: OPENCLAW_OPENAI_MODEL, OPENCLAW_OPENAI_CODE_MODEL, OPENCLAW_CLAUDE_MODEL, OPENCLAW_GEMINI_MODEL, OPENCLAW_AGENTS_WORKSPACE, and OPENCLAW_<AGENT>_WORKSPACE.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text: OpenClaw writes its configuration file from the app service's environment variables on every start. Do not edit the file. To change anything the variables do not cover, edit the OpenClaw config template on the app service's Configuration > Configs tab, then deploy.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: The Data volume (1 GB by default) holds the OpenClaw state directory. Agent workspaces default to directories that are not on this volume. Point the workspace variables at a path on the volume to keep them.

docs.title: Check the result
docs.text: In a web terminal, run openclaw health --json. It reports "ok": true when the gateway is up.

docs.title: OpenSearch stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby OpenSearch catalog stack runs a single-node OpenSearch with OpenSearch Dashboards. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-opensearch.

docs.title: Connect an application
docs.text:
Link your application's app service to the OpenSearch app service. See Links. The app service receives the host, port and password in variables named by the linking service. Read them in code. Do not copy the password into your repository.

  • URL: https://<app service name>:9200. OpenSearch serves the image's self-signed demo certificate. Your client must skip certificate verification or trust that certificate. Plain http:// requests are refused.
  • User: admin. Its password is the password token on the OpenSearch app service's Configuration > Tokens tab.
  • All OpenSearch ports are private, and Wodby creates no route for them. Applications use port 9200 only.

The image's other demo accounts have public passwords, so they are removed each time the node starts. The kibanaserver account remains for Dashboards, with its own generated dashboards_password token. Create your own users through the security API instead of reusing these names.

docs.title: Sign in to Dashboards
docs.text:
OpenSearch Dashboards is the main app service, and it has a public HTTPS address. Sign in as admin with the OpenSearch password token. Create other users under Security in Dashboards.

The address accepts sign-ins from anywhere. Do not turn on Wodby Basic Auth for it, because Dashboards reads the Authorization header for its own login. To restrict who can reach the address, use Private App Access.

The Dashboards version must match the OpenSearch version in major and minor. Wodby generates a cookie_password token once to encrypt session cookies. Replacing it signs users out.

docs.title: Single node and resources
docs.text:
OpenSearch runs as a single node and does not scale. An index with replicas stays yellow because there is no second node, so create indices with zero replicas.

The stack requests 1 CPU and 2048 MiB for OpenSearch and limits it to 2 CPU and 4096 MiB. The JVM heap is fixed at -Xms1g -Xmx1g by default (OPENSEARCH_JAVA_OPTS). If you raise the heap, keep the container memory limit above it. Dashboards requests 0.5 CPU and 1024 MiB and is limited to 1 CPU and 2048 MiB. Change resources under Runtime > Resources.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
Set OpenSearch settings as environment variables on its app service, named exactly like the setting, for example cluster.name. Do not mount an opensearch.yml. See Environment variables. Disabling the security plugin changes the scheme to http:// and removes authentication for every linked service.

Dashboards has a config file, opensearch_dashboards.yml, that you can override under Configuration > Configs. Keep opensearch_security.cookie.secure: true, because the public address always uses HTTPS. Environment variables set by the link take precedence over the same settings in the file.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
The stack adds a 20 GiB OpenSearch data volume. Dashboards has no volume. Dashboards, index patterns and other saved objects live in OpenSearch.

The services have no backup or import support. Snapshots need a repository configured in OpenSearch itself.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
In a web terminal on the OpenSearch app service, run:

curl -sk -u "admin:$OPENSEARCH_INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD" https://localhost:9200/_cluster/health?pretty

docs.title: OpenSMTPD stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby OpenSMTPD catalog stack provides an SMTP relay service on internal port 25. It can also be included in application stacks such as Drupal, WordPress, and Matomo. The current service definition is documented in wodby/stack-opensmtpd.

docs.title: Production delivery
docs.text:
Do not rely on direct delivery from a Kubernetes node or cloud-cluster IP for production mail. Recipient providers may reject or classify mail from those addresses as spam.

Create an SMTP provider integration, then attach it to the OpenSMTPD app service's Third-party SMTP server for Relay integration. Wodby supplies the relay host, port, protocol, username, and password from the selected provider.

Applications in the same app environment should connect through their stack link. The usual internal connection is the OpenSMTPD app-service hostname on port 25; linked PHP services receive that connection automatically through their mail-transfer-agent link.

docs.title: Send a test message
docs.text:
Open a web terminal on the OpenSMTPD service, then send a small message:

printf 'Subject: Wodby SMTP test

OpenSMTPD relay test.
' | \
  sendmail -v -f verified-sender@example.com recipient@example.com

Use a sender accepted by the configured provider. The verbose output confirms whether OpenSMTPD accepted the message; use the app logs and your provider's delivery logs to diagnose later relay or delivery failures.

Add the optional spool volume when queued mail must survive pod replacement.

docs.title: PHP stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby PHP catalog stack runs a PHP-FPM service behind Nginx, with MariaDB and Mailpit enabled by default. Apache HTTP Server, PostgreSQL, Valkey, OpenSMTPD and Gotenberg are available as optional services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-php.

docs.title: Build and deployment
docs.text:
Start from the Composer boilerplate or connect your own repository. The web server has no repository of its own. Its image is built from the PHP service's source, so both images contain the code at the same path. A changed static file needs a new build and deployment. See Application Builds.

The Nginx docroot setting defaults to public. It must be the directory that holds your front controller. Nginx passes a path that is not a file to index.php, so the application needs no rewrite rules. A path with a static file extension that matches no file returns 404 instead. Nginx does not read .htaccess files. The HTTPd docroot setting of Apache HTTP Server has no default, so Apache serves the repository root until you set it, for example to public or web. Apache reads .htaccess, and routing every path to index.php comes from your own .htaccess.

docs.title: Database and mail
docs.text:
Do not hardcode connection settings. The PHP service receives these variables from its links, and only while the link exists and the linked service is enabled:

Link Variables DBMS (MariaDB by default; MySQL or PostgreSQL) DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Mail Transfer Agent (Mailpit by default) MSMTP_HOST, MSMTP_PORT

PHP's mail() is delivered through the linked mail service, so no SMTP library or credentials are needed.

Mailpit captures every message and delivers none of them. Use it to inspect mail in non-production environments. Its web interface is protected with basic auth. Reveal the password in Endpoints > Auths. For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the PHP service's Mail Transfer Agent link at it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

Valkey and Gotenberg are disabled by default, and the PHP service has no link to either one. Wodby sets no variables for them. Put their addresses in your application's configuration. Valkey listens on port 6379 and always requires its generated password token. Gotenberg listens on port 3000 without authentication. Both are reachable at the name of their app service inside the environment.

docs.title: PHP settings
docs.text:
Set PHP_* variables on the PHP service, such as PHP_MEMORY_LIMIT, PHP_MAX_EXECUTION_TIME or PHP_FPM_PM_MAX_CHILDREN, instead of adding a php.ini to the repository. Changes apply with the next deployment. Uploads are limited by both NGINX_CLIENT_MAX_BODY_SIZE on Nginx and the PHP settings.

WODBY_HOSTS is a JSON array of the environment's hosts. Use WODBY_PRIMARY_URL for links generated outside a request. WODBY_ENV_TYPE tells a development environment from a production-like one. See Environment variables.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, the PHP service gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. Add the OpenTelemetry PHP SDK with Composer; it then starts without code changes. See PHP applications and OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
The PHP service has no volume. Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

MariaDB and PostgreSQL keep data on a 20 GB data volume. A backup is a gzipped SQL dump of the environment's database. A database import replaces the whole data volume. See Application Backups and Application Imports.

docs.title: PostGIS stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby PostGIS catalog stack runs a PostgreSQL database server that bundles PostGIS. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-postgis. It has one service, with a 20 GB data volume. It has no Adminer or pgAdmin option.

The service is based on PostgreSQL. The database, user, passwords, ownership, connection, server settings, backups, and imports work as described in the PostgreSQL guide.

docs.title: PostGIS extensions
docs.text:
Wodby creates these extensions in a database when it creates the database. The application does not run CREATE EXTENSION postgis.

  • postgis
  • postgis_raster
  • postgis_sfcgal
  • fuzzystrmatch
  • address_standardizer
  • address_standardizer_data_us
  • postgis_tiger_geocoder
  • postgis_topology

Setting POSTGRES_DB_EXTENSIONS on the service replaces this whole list. To add an extension such as vector, repeat the PostGIS extensions you need and append the new one. See Extensions in the PostgreSQL guide.

docs.title: Check the PostGIS version
docs.text:
Open a web terminal for the service and run:

PGPASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" psql -h localhost -U postgres -d <database> -c 'SELECT postgis_full_version();'

docs.title: PostgreSQL stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby PostgreSQL catalog stack runs a PostgreSQL database server, with optional Adminer and pgAdmin. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-postgres. For PostGIS, see the PostGIS guide.

docs.title: Create an environment
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is enabled by default with a 20 GB data volume. Adminer and pgAdmin are disabled by default. Enable one when you want a browser interface for the database. Each is linked to the PostgreSQL service automatically.

Wodby creates the database and its user. Both are named after the app and the app environment. The database uses the UTF8 encoding and the en_US.utf8 locale. The application does not create them. A role you create by hand with a name Wodby later needs, but a different password, makes Wodby's create action fail. Add further DBs and users on Wodby.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
Wodby generates two tokens once per environment. Open the PostgreSQL app service's Configuration > Tokens tab to reveal them:

  • password: the password of the environment's database user.
  • root_password: the password of the administrator postgres.

Do not connect as postgres from an application.

docs.title: Connect to the database
docs.text:
The server listens on TCP port 5432. Inside the app environment, the host is the name of the PostgreSQL app service. The database has no public route. To reach it from outside the cluster, publish its port. See Publishing ports.

An app service linked to PostgreSQL receives the host, port, database name, user name, and password as environment variables defined by its own link, for example DB_HOST and DB_PASSWORD on a PHP service. Read them in the application instead of hardcoding them.

To open a shell in the database container, use the web terminal. For example, PGPASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" psql -h localhost -U postgres -c '\l' lists the databases and their owner roles.

docs.title: Ownership inside a database
docs.text:
Each managed database is owned by its own role, named <database>:owner, which cannot log in. Granting a user access to the database makes that user a member of the role, and the user's sessions in that database act as the role.

  • Objects are created in the public schema and belong to the owner role, whichever user created them. All users with access share the database's data.
  • In such a session, current_user is the owner role and session_user is the user that logged in. Code that compares current_user with the login name sees the owner role.
  • Only users granted access can connect to the database.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text: Wodby creates extensions as the administrator. Set POSTGRES_DB_EXTENSIONS on the PostgreSQL app service to a comma-separated list of extensions to create in a database when Wodby creates it. pgvector is bundled with the image but not enabled. Add vector to the list to enable it. To list the extensions in a database, run PGPASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" psql -h localhost -U postgres -d <database> -c '\dx' in the web terminal.

docs.title: Adminer and pgAdmin
docs.text:
Wodby protects their public domains with basic auth by default. Reveal the generated password on the environment's Endpoints > Auths page. See Auths.

  • Adminer: it has no persistent data. The login form is prefilled with the system, server, and database. Type the user name and password.
  • pgAdmin: it has its own login, which is not a database credential. Sign in with the administrator email user@domain.com and the password in the pgAdmin app service's admin_password token. pgAdmin registers the linked database as a server named PostgreSQL. It connects as the environment's database user, not as postgres, and asks for no password. Wodby rewrites this server on every start, so changes to it inside pgAdmin do not last. The optional pgAdmin configuration volume keeps pgAdmin's own preferences and servers you add. Without it, they are lost when the container is replaced.

docs.title: Server settings
docs.text:
The container rebuilds its configuration from a template and environment variables on every start. Do not edit the generated file. Use one of these instead:

  • Set a variable on the PostgreSQL app service: POSTGRES_MAX_CONNECTIONS, POSTGRES_SHARED_BUFFERS, POSTGRES_WORK_MEM, POSTGRES_MAINTENANCE_WORK_MEM, POSTGRES_EFFECTIVE_CACHE_SIZE, POSTGRES_MAX_WAL_SIZE, POSTGRES_TIMEZONE, or POSTGRES_SHARED_PRELOAD_LIBRARIES.
  • Override the service's PostgreSQL config file for a setting that no variable covers. It replaces the template. See Configs tab.

A change applies on the next deployment of the service.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The PostgreSQL service runs a single instance.

docs.title: Backups and restore
docs.text:
Data is on the data volume. A backup is a gzipped SQL dump of the environment's database. In the backup's Excluded table contents option, list table patterns. Matching tables keep their definition and lose their rows. See Application backups.

A backup carries no role names and no grants. You can import it into a database with another name and other users.

To restore, run a database import from a backup or an uploaded file. See Application imports. The import accepts .gz, .tar.gz, .tgz, and .zip archives. Wodby hands the imported objects to the database's owner role. Roles that a dump names, which this server does not have, exist only while the dump is loaded.

Warning

A database import replaces the contents of the data volume. Data that is not in the dump is not kept.

docs.title: Prometheus stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Prometheus catalog stack runs Prometheus and an optional Grafana service. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-prometheus.

docs.title: Choose services when you create the app
docs.text: Prometheus is the stack's main service. Grafana is enabled by default and can be excluded when you create the app. Wodby provisions a Prometheus data source in Grafana for you, and the Prometheus service is linked to it. Apps created before Grafana became a default keep their choice; enable the Grafana app service there to add it.

docs.title: Open Prometheus
docs.text: Prometheus listens on port 9090. Wodby protects the service's public domains with basic auth by default. Each app service gets its own generated password. Reveal it under Endpoints > Auths for the app environment. See Auths.

docs.title: Change the Prometheus configuration
docs.text: The Prometheus config file is available under the app service's Configuration > Configs tab. Its default comes from the service image. An app override replaces the default, and Reset override restores the image's file on the next deployment. See Configs tab.

docs.title: Sign in to Grafana
docs.text:
When Grafana is enabled, open the Grafana app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal admin_username (admin) and admin_password. Grafana applies them once, on the first start with an empty data volume. Changing the tokens later does not change the existing account. See Tokens.

The Prometheus data source is the default. It is defined in Grafana's Grafana datasources config file. A data source removed from that file is deleted from Grafana on the next start. See the Grafana guide.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
The stack creates a 10 GB Data volume for Prometheus. Grafana, when enabled, has its own 10 GB volume with its dashboards, users, settings, and plugins. Wodby defines no backups or imports for Grafana.

Prometheus is not scalable.

docs.title: Python stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Python catalog stack runs a Python web application with Gunicorn. PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg and Cloud PostgreSQL are available as optional services, all disabled by default. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-python.

docs.title: Build and deployment
docs.text:
Start from the Python boilerplate or connect your own repository. The code is copied to /usr/src/app. The service's Dockerfile runs pip install -r requirements.txt when that file exists and does nothing else. If your pipeline passes a Dockerfile from the repository, that file installs the dependencies instead. See Application Builds.

The container runs Gunicorn on port 8080 with a configuration that Wodby writes on every start:

  • Set GUNICORN_APP on the app service to your WSGI callable as module:callable. The default is myapp.wsgi:application.
  • Gunicorn must be one of your application's dependencies. The image does not include it.
  • Do not add a Gunicorn configuration file to the repository. The container does not load it. Set GUNICORN_WORKERS, GUNICORN_WORKER_CLASS, GUNICORN_TIMEOUT or the other GUNICORN_* variables on the app service instead. Changes apply with the next deployment.

The app service has no volume. Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Database, Valkey and mail
docs.text:
Nothing in the image reads link variables. Your application reads them. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. With the defaults, no link variables are set.

Link Variables DBMS (PostgreSQL) DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Mail Transfer Agent SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT Redis (Valkey) REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD

The mail link carries no credentials. Mailpit captures every message and delivers none of them, and an application that requires SMTP authentication or TLS fails against it. For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

Valkey is a cache by default. It evicts keys when its memory limit is reached and starts empty after a restart unless you add its data volume. For a job queue or other data you must keep, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY on the Valkey app service.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: WODBY_HOSTS is a JSON array of the environment's hosts, not a comma-separated string. Use WODBY_PRIMARY_URL for links generated outside a request. Other services reach the application at WODBY_APP_SERVICE_NAME on port 8080. See Environment variables.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL keeps data on a 20 GB data volume. A backup is a gzipped SQL dump of the environment's database. It carries no role names and no grants, so you can import it into a database with another name and other users. A database import replaces the whole data volume. See Application Backups and Application Imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace, setup installs dependencies into .wodby-workspace/venv with uv sync --locked when uv.lock exists, otherwise with pip install -r requirements.txt. One of the two files must exist. Run setup again after you change dependencies.

The server starts with python -m gunicorn --reload on $HOST:$PORT (0.0.0.0:8080 by default). The generated Gunicorn configuration and the GUNICORN_* tuning variables are not used. Set WORKSPACE_PYTHON_COMMAND on the app service to replace the start command. A custom command must reload by itself. A change to variables or linked services still needs a deployment.

docs.title: RabbitMQ stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby RabbitMQ catalog stack runs a single RabbitMQ service with the management UI. The current composition and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-rabbitmq.

docs.title: Connect an application
docs.text:
Link your application's app service to the RabbitMQ app service. See Links. The app service receives the host, port and the account tokens in variables named by the linking service. Read them in code. Do not copy the password into your repository.

Port Use 5672 AMQP, without TLS 15672 Management UI and HTTP API 15692 Prometheus metrics at /metrics, internal only

The account tokens are on the RabbitMQ app service's Configuration > Tokens tab:

  • username: wodby
  • password: generated by Wodby
  • vhost: /

Applications do not need the generated erlang_cookie token.

docs.title: Management UI
docs.text: The management port is an HTTP endpoint, so Wodby generates a technical route for it. Sign in with the username and password tokens above. To stop serving the route, disable it under Endpoints. See Endpoints.

docs.title: Manage accounts
docs.text: RabbitMQ applies the default user, password and virtual host only when it first creates its database. Changing the tokens later does not change the account. Change accounts in RabbitMQ itself, with rabbitmqctl in a web terminal or in the management UI.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Set these variables on the app service under Configuration > Variables. See Environment variables.

Variable Setting Default RABBITMQ_CHANNEL_MAX channel_max 2047 RABBITMQ_HEARTBEAT heartbeat 60 RABBITMQ_VM_MEMORY_HIGH_WATERMARK_RELATIVE Memory high watermark, as a share of available memory 0.4 RABBITMQ_DISK_FREE_LIMIT disk_free_limit.absolute 50MB

Do not edit the generated RabbitMQ configuration file; it is rewritten on every start.

docs.title: Data and limits
docs.text:
The stack adds a 5 GB Data volume. It holds definitions, queues and messages. Without the volume, everything, including users and queues created at runtime, is lost when the container is replaced. A message survives a restart only when the volume exists, the queue is durable and the message is persistent.

RabbitMQ runs as a single node and does not scale. The service has no backup or import support.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
In a web terminal on the RabbitMQ app service, run:

rabbitmq-diagnostics -q ping
rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages consumers
rabbitmqctl list_users

docs.title: Rails stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Rails catalog stack runs a Ruby (Rails) app service with a Sidekiq worker, PostgreSQL, and Valkey. Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and Cloud PostgreSQL are optional. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-rails.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text: Start from the Rails boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service, PostgreSQL, and Valkey are required and cannot be excluded. Select Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, or Cloud PostgreSQL when you create the environment if your application uses them. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service. To use a managed database, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Application settings
docs.text:
• RAILS_ENV is development in environments of type dev and production in every other type. An environment of type test is a deployed application, not Rails' test environment.
  • SECRET_KEY_BASE is a secret that Wodby generates. Rails reads it by itself, so do not generate or commit another one. Find it on the app service's Configuration > Tokens tab as secret_key_base.
  • RAILS_MASTER_KEY is not set. If your application uses encrypted credentials, add the key as a secret variable on the app service. See Environment variables.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service's Dockerfile installs vips, runs bundle install, and runs rails assets:precompile with RAILS_ENV=production and a dummy secret key when the application has that task. Runtime variables and the database are not available during the build.
  • The container runs Puma on port 8080 with a configuration Wodby generates. A config/puma.rb in the repository is not loaded. Set PUMA_WORKERS, PUMA_THREADS, and the other PUMA_* variables on the app service instead.
  • Puma and a config.ru at the repository root are required. Add Puma to your Gemfile.
  • After every deployment Wodby runs bundle exec rails db:prepare, which prepares the schema and runs pending migrations. During the first deployment only, it then runs bundle exec rails db:seed. Your start command and pipeline do not need to run migrations.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Host authorization
docs.text: Wodby mounts a config named Host authorization at config/initializers/wodby_host_authorization.rb. It is not part of your repository. Change it as a config of the app service on Wodby. It adds every host of the environment and the service's internal host name to config.hosts, and it excludes requests to /healthz from host authorization. Do not add the environment's hosts to config.hosts in the code. Serve your health endpoint at /healthz.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
Rails reads DATABASE_URL by itself, and its values take precedence over config/database.yml. Do not put a host, user, or password in database.yml. The app service also receives the DB_* and REDIS_* variables with the same connection details in separate parts. Never print or commit the values of the URL variables, because they contain passwords.

Link Variables Database DATABASE_URL Valkey REDIS_URL (database 0) Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

Wodby does not configure a job queue, cache, or mailer for your application. Your application decides what to do with REDIS_URL, SMTP_HOST, and SMTP_PORT, and must start without them when a link is absent.

The Sidekiq worker runs bundle exec sidekiq instead of Puma and reads REDIS_URL by itself. Add sidekiq to your Gemfile. The Rails boilerplate uses Sidekiq, and its worker is enabled by default.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail transport without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 20 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. By default they keep the definitions of solid_cache_entries and solid_cable_messages but omit their rows. See Excluding table contents.
  • An import into PostgreSQL replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application imports.
  • Valkey stores queue data on a data volume of 5 GB with persistence on and the noeviction memory policy. The Valkey service declares no backups or imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • The application starts with bundle exec rails server on port 8080, and RAILS_ENV is development whatever the environment type.
  • Starting the server does not run migrations or seeds. Keep Rails' default config.file_watcher, ActiveSupport::FileUpdateChecker, because an evented file watcher is not reliable on the checkout's network storage.

docs.title: React stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby React catalog stack serves a built React application with Nginx. The current service and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-react.

docs.title: Build and deployment
docs.text:
Start from the React boilerplate or connect your own repository. The deployed app service runs no Node.js process. The pipeline installs dependencies, runs the production build, and builds the image from the output directory only (dist in the boilerplate). Source files and node_modules are not in the image.

If you change the name or location of the build output, change the pipeline's wodby ci build --from step too. Otherwise the image is built from the wrong directory. See Application Builds.

Nginx answers requests for paths that are not files with index.html, so client-side routes work without extra configuration. /.healthz returns status 204.

docs.title: Configuration reaches the build, not the browser
docs.text: The application runs in the browser. Environment variables of the app service, including WODBY_*, do not reach it at run time. Put the values it needs into the build, or have the application fetch them from an API.

docs.title: Web server settings
docs.text: Set NGINX_* environment variables on the app service to change Nginx, such as NGINX_HEADERS_CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY or NGINX_STATIC_EXPIRES. Do not add an nginx.conf to the repository. Changes apply with the next deployment.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace, the app service runs the Vite development server in a Node.js image instead of Nginx. Expect these differences:

  • Setup installs dependencies from the lockfile. Run setup again after you change dependencies.
  • The server starts through Vite's API with your Vite configuration file, not with the dev script in package.json. Options in that script do not apply. vite must be a dependency of the project.
  • The server listens on port 8080 and the container's health checks probe that port. Do not change the port.
  • Vite rejects host names it does not know. Allow the environment's hosts in server.allowedHosts of your Vite configuration.
  • To start the server another way, set WORKSPACE_NODE_COMMAND on the app service. The command must listen on $HOST:$PORT and poll for file changes itself.

docs.title: Redis stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Redis catalog stack runs a single Redis service. The current composition and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-redis.

docs.title: Connect an application
docs.text:
The Redis service listens on port 6379. It has no HTTP endpoint, so Wodby creates no route for it.

  1. Link your application's app service to the Redis app service. See Links.
  2. Read the connection values from the environment variables your app service receives. The linking service chooses their names, for example REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT and REDIS_PASSWORD, or a single REDIS_URL.

A password is always required. Wodby generates it as the password token. Open the Redis app service's Configuration > Tokens tab to see it. Do not hardcode the host or copy the password into your repository.

docs.title: Choose cache or storage behavior
docs.text:
With the defaults, Redis is a cache. It holds up to 128 MB (REDIS_MAXMEMORY). After that it evicts any key, including keys without an expiry (REDIS_MAXMEMORY_POLICY is allkeys-lru).

If you store a job queue, sessions or other data that must not disappear, set REDIS_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction and raise REDIS_MAXMEMORY. Otherwise Redis drops data silently under memory pressure.

Set these variables on the Redis app service under Configuration > Variables. See Environment variables. They apply on the next deployment. Do not edit the generated configuration file; it is rewritten on every start.

Variable Effect Default REDIS_MAXMEMORY Memory limit 128m REDIS_MAXMEMORY_POLICY Eviction policy allkeys-lru REDIS_DATABASES Number of databases 16 REDIS_TIMEOUT Idle client timeout, in seconds 300 REDIS_NOTIFY_KEYSPACE_EVENTS Keyspace notifications empty

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
The stack does not add the optional Data volume. Without it nothing is written to disk, and every restart or deployment starts with an empty Redis. To keep data, add the volume under Runtime > Volumes on the Redis app service and redeploy. Wodby then turns persistence on. Once added, the volume cannot be resized or removed. See Volumes.

The service has no backup or import support.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
Open a web terminal on the Redis app service and run:

redis-cli -a "$REDIS_PASSWORD" ping

The answer is PONG. Use config get maxmemory-policy and config get appendonly to see the eviction policy and whether persistence is on. info stats shows evicted_keys.

docs.title: Ruby stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Ruby catalog stack runs a Ruby app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and Cloud PostgreSQL services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-ruby.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the Ruby boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

To use a managed database instead of the PostgreSQL container, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The container runs Puma on port 8080. The repository needs a config.ru at its root, or set PUMA_RACKUP to its path.
  • Puma is not in the image. Add it to your Gemfile.
  • Wodby generates the Puma configuration. A config/puma.rb in the repository is not loaded. Set PUMA_WORKERS, PUMA_THREADS, PUMA_WORKER_TIMEOUT, PUMA_WORKER_BOOT_TIMEOUT, PUMA_PRELOAD_APP, PUMA_PRUNE_BUNDLER, PUMA_QUIET, or PUMA_TAG on the app service instead.
  • PUMA_ENVIRONMENT defaults to development, and Wodby sets neither it nor RACK_ENV. If your application depends on them, set them on the app service or in your Dockerfile.
  • The service's Dockerfile runs bundle install when a Gemfile exists. A Dockerfile from your repository replaces it and must install the gems itself. See Application builds.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
The application reads these variables itself. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail transport without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 20 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • The application starts with bundle exec puma. Puma does not watch files, so restart the service after a code change.
  • Gemfile.lock must be committed. Preparation fails without it. Run preparation again after changing dependencies.

docs.title: Rust stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Rust catalog stack runs a Rust app service on the latest stable Rust release, with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and Cloud PostgreSQL services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-rust.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the Rust boilerplate, an axum web application, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

To use a managed database instead of the PostgreSQL container, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service's Dockerfile builds the project with cargo build --release and starts the binary. The project must build exactly one binary, or name one with default-run in Cargo.toml. A project with a Cargo.toml at the repository root is required.
  • Commit Cargo.lock. When it is present, the build uses it as is and fails if it is out of date; update it with cargo update and commit the result.
  • A Dockerfile from your repository replaces the service's, as in the boilerplate. It must still end with a command that starts the server. See Application builds.
  • The boilerplate's pipeline checks formatting with cargo fmt, lints with cargo clippy, and runs cargo test before it builds the image.
  • Binaries are built for Alpine Linux and linked statically. The image includes OpenSSL and pkg-config, so crates that link OpenSSL build without changes. For other C libraries, use your own Dockerfile and install their static packages.
  • A rust-toolchain.toml in the repository selects another Rust version. It is downloaded when the build starts.
  • The application must listen on port 8080 on all interfaces. Wodby sets no PORT variable in a deployed environment, so default to 8080 in the code.
  • The app service is ready when the application answers 200 at /. An application without a page at / is never served.
  • Wodby sets no other variable for the application and generates no configuration file.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
The application reads these variables itself. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail client without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: The boilerplate logs every request and reads the log level from RUST_LOG, info by default. Set RUST_LOG on the app service, for example to debug, to change it.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 20 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • Wodby compiles the checkout with cargo build and restarts the application after each change, usually within a few seconds. A failed build leaves the previous build running; read the compiler errors in the service's logs.
  • Setup downloads the project's crates and compiles it once, so the first start is quick. A compile error doesn't stop setup.
