  • Cargo.lock is never changed: an outdated lock file fails the build, so fix it in the repository with cargo update.
  • When the project builds several binaries and has no default-run, set WORKSPACE_RUST_BIN on the app service to the one to run, or WORKSPACE_RUST_PACKAGE to choose a member of a Cargo workspace. WORKSPACE_RUST_COMMAND replaces the start command.
  • Compiled files and downloaded crates stay out of Git status without changes to .gitignore. Running cargo yourself in the workspace terminal doesn't restart the application.
  • Compiling takes more memory and CPU than running the application. If builds are slow or stop, raise the app service's resources.

docs.title: RustDesk Server stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby RustDesk Server catalog stack runs the open-source RustDesk server, so your devices use your own server for remote desktop sessions instead of RustDesk's public one. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-rustdesk.

The server has no web interface: you use it from the RustDesk app on each device. Devices connect over WebSocket to the app's HTTPS domain, so it works on any cluster and you don't need to publish ports. The domain also shows a page with these setup steps.

docs.title: Set up devices
docs.text:
1. Create an app from the RustDesk Server catalog stack and deploy it.
  2. On the RustDesk app service, run the Show client settings action. See Actions. The task log shows the values to enter.
  3. In the RustDesk app on each device, open Settings > Network:
    1. Turn on Use WebSocket.
    2. Under ID/Relay server, enter the ID server, API server and Key from the task log, and leave Relay server empty.

The ID server is the app's main domain, for example prod.myapp.example.com, and the API server is the same domain with https://. The RustDesk app needs the API server to connect securely; the server has no accounts or address book.

The key is the server's public key: devices without it can't use the server, so share it only with people who should use your server. The page on the app's domain shows the other values, but not the key.

docs.title: Connect devices without WebSocket
docs.text:
On K3s clusters and single-node clusters, devices can also connect without Use WebSocket:

  1. Open Apps > [App] > [Environment] > Endpoints > Ports, select the rustdesk endpoint, and publish the id TCP port, then the id-udp UDP port. The second one gets the same public port as the first. See Publishing ports.
  2. Publish the relay TCP port.
  3. Deploy the RustDesk app service again, so the server knows its public addresses.

Show client settings then also prints the ID server and relay server with their ports for these devices; their API server stays empty. On other clusters the id-udp port gets a different number, and devices without WebSocket can't sign in.

You don't need the nat port. Without it, the RustDesk app can't show which devices are online; sessions work normally.

docs.title: How sessions connect
docs.text:
Every session goes through the relay, and its traffic counts toward your cluster's bandwidth. Devices can't connect to each other directly through Wodby's gateway.

The relay limits each session to 128 Mbit/s and all sessions together to 1024 Mbit/s. To change that, set the SINGLE_BANDWIDTH and TOTAL_BANDWIDTH environment variables in Mbit/s, then deploy the app service.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
The data volume holds the server's key pair and its list of devices. If you lose the key pair, every device must be set up again with the new key. The stack runs one replica.

If the app's domain changes, update the ID server and API server on every device.

docs.title: Slack Inviter stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Slack Inviter catalog stack runs a public invitation page for a Slack community on the Node.js service. The source is the wodby/slack-inviter project. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-slack-inviter.

Warning

This stack needs an existing Slackin-compatible legacy administrator API token. Slack no longer issues these tokens. Ordinary Slack app and bot tokens do not work. Use the stack only to migrate a Slackin installation whose token is still active.

docs.title: Before you create the app
docs.text:
• Use the Slack Inviter repository as the build source, or connect your own compatible repository. See Application Builds.
  • Set Slack workspace to the workspace subdomain only, for example community for community.slack.com. It is required.
  • Attach a Slack integration to the Slack legacy API token slot. It is required and supplies SLACK_TOKEN. See Slack.
  • Optionally attach a Cloudflare integration with the Turnstile kind to the Cloudflare Turnstile slot. It supplies TURNSTILE_SITE_KEY and TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY. See Cloudflare.

The application refuses to start without the workspace and the token. The container log names the variable at fault. Put the token and keys in integrations, not in the repository or a .env file.

docs.title: Page content and limits
docs.text:
Set these on the app service's Configuration > Settings tab: Community name, Community headline, Community description, Community website URL, Community logo URL, Support URL, Privacy URL, and Social image URL. The logo and social image accept an HTTPS URL or a path starting with /.

The rate limits are Maximum invites per IP (10 per 3600 seconds by default) and Maximum invites per email (3 per 86400 seconds by default). Change the windows with IP rate-limit window in seconds and Email rate-limit window in seconds.

The rate limiter keeps its counters in the memory of one process. Replicas do not share them, and a restart resets them.

docs.title: Health check
docs.text: /healthz answers the health check.

docs.title: Solr stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Solr catalog stack runs SolrCloud with a required ZooKeeper service. The current service composition and Solr version are documented in wodby/stack-solr.

docs.title: Authentication and endpoints
docs.text:
Wodby generates a password for SolrCloud's solr administrator account. Applications connected through a stack link receive the internal hostname and generated credential defined by their service integration.

Solr exposes an HTTP endpoint on port 8983, so Wodby creates a technical route for its UI and API. Solr already uses HTTP Basic authentication. Do not add Wodby route-level basic authentication to this route because an HTTP client cannot send two independent Basic authorization headers.

docs.title: Default collection
docs.text:
The Solr post-deployment initialization creates a collection named default when the cluster has no collections. It uses Solr's _default configset.

_default is only a starting point. Applications that require a particular schema must install their own configset. For Drupal, follow Connect Drupal to Solr so Search API Solr generates and uploads a compatible configset.

docs.title: Create another collection
docs.text:
You can create collections from the Solr Admin UI. You can also open a web terminal on the Solr app service and use the image action:

make create-collection collection=my_collection num_shards=1 config=_default \
  -f /usr/local/bin/actions.mk

Replace my_collection, the shard count, and the configset for your application. The command uses the generated SOLR_CLOUD_PASSWORD automatically.

docs.title: Configsets
docs.text:
Keep custom configsets in a reproducible application or service workflow and upload them to ZooKeeper. Do not edit configsets bundled in the running image: those changes are tied to one container and disappear when it is replaced.

When a client integration can generate its own configset, prefer that workflow. After replacing a configset, follow the client's instructions for reloading the collection and reindexing data.

Use application backups for supported persistent service data and review volume settings before production use.

docs.title: Apache Spark stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Apache Spark catalog stack runs a Spark standalone cluster with a Spark master and Spark worker services. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-spark.

docs.title: What the stack runs
docs.text: Both services are required. The worker is linked to the master, and Wodby sets the master address on the worker for you, so do not set it elsewhere. The stack starts with one worker.

docs.title: Connect an application
docs.text: Applications reach the master at spark://<master app service name>:7077. This port is private: other services in the same app environment can reach it, and Wodby creates no public route for it.

docs.title: Open the master web interface
docs.text: The master web interface is on port 8080 and is protected with basic auth by default. Each app service gets its own generated password. Reveal it under Endpoints > Auths for the app environment. See Auths. Services inside the environment reach the master directly, without the password.

docs.title: Add workers and size them
docs.text:
The worker service is scalable: each replica is one worker. Set the replica count as described in Application Scalability.

Each worker offers CPU and memory to the master through these settings on the worker app service:

Setting Default Meaning Worker CPU cores 2 Cores that Spark applications may use on this worker Worker memory 2g Memory that Spark applications may use on this worker

These settings are separate from the container's CPU and memory resources. Keep them within the container's limits.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The master is not scalable and has no volume.
  • Workers have no volume. Application work directories are lost when a worker pod is replaced.
  • The worker web interface (port 8081) is not reachable from other services.
  • Other Spark settings are environment variables on the app service. The master's ports and listen address are fixed. See environment variables.

docs.title: Spring Boot stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Spring Boot catalog stack runs a Spring Boot app service with PostgreSQL, and optional Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and Cloud PostgreSQL services. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-spring-boot.

The Spring Boot service is based on the Java service: it builds and starts the application the same way, and adds the settings Spring Boot reads by itself.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the Spring Boot boilerplate, a Spring Boot web application that stores notes in PostgreSQL, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service and PostgreSQL are required. The other services are optional and not selected by default. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

Choose the Java version with the app service's version. To use a managed database instead of the PostgreSQL container, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service builds the repository with Maven or the Gradle wrapper and runs the jar, as described for the Java stack. Spring Boot's Maven and Gradle plugins build a runnable jar with its dependencies inside, so no extra build setup is needed. The boilerplate's pipeline runs ./mvnw test before it builds the image.
  • The application must listen on port 8080, Spring Boot's default.
  • The service is ready when /actuator/health answers 200, so add spring-boot-starter-actuator to the project. Without Actuator, set JAVA_READY_PATH on the app service to another path that answers 200, such as /.
  • Graceful shutdown is on by default in Spring Boot. Keep its timeout below 30 seconds, the time the container gets to stop.

docs.title: Environments and requests
docs.text:
• Development environments activate the dev profile, so application-dev.properties applies. Other environment types use the default profile. To choose profiles yourself, set SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE on the app service.
  • Wodby's gateway terminates HTTPS. On Kubernetes, Spring Boot uses the gateway's forwarded headers by itself, so redirects and generated links use the public domain and HTTPS. Don't add HTTPS redirection in the application: checks inside the environment use plain HTTP.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
The links set the variables Spring Boot reads by itself, so application.properties needs no datasource, Redis or mail connection settings. Variables override settings in application.properties, so local defaults there, such as jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/app, are fine. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL, SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME, SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD Valkey SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST, SPRING_DATA_REDIS_PORT, SPRING_DATA_REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SPRING_MAIL_HOST, SPRING_MAIL_PORT

SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL is a JDBC URL such as jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/db, without the username and password. It starts with jdbc:postgresql:, jdbc:mariadb: or jdbc:mysql: to match the linked database, so the project needs that database's JDBC driver. The Java stack's variables, such as DB_HOST, are set as well.

Valkey and mail are used only when the project has spring-boot-starter-data-redis or spring-boot-starter-mail. Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Database migrations
docs.text: Wodby runs no migration step. Add Flyway or Liquibase to the project: Spring Boot runs them at startup, so every deployment migrates the database before the application serves requests, and replicas starting together wait for each other. The boilerplate keeps its migrations in src/main/resources/db/migration and lets Hibernate only validate the schema.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail settings without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 20 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text: In a development workspace, Wodby rebuilds the checkout and restarts the application after each change, usually within a few seconds, as described for the Java stack. A failed build leaves the previous build running; read the compiler errors in the service's logs. The dev profile follows the environment type, as in other environments.

docs.title: Strapi stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Strapi catalog stack runs a Node.js (Strapi) app service with PostgreSQL and optional Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, and OpenTelemetry Collector services. Strapi keeps its content in PostgreSQL and uploaded media on a volume of the app service. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-strapi.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the Strapi Boilerplate, a Strapi project in TypeScript, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service and PostgreSQL are required. Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, and the OpenTelemetry Collector are optional and not selected by default. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Mailpit for mail, and the OpenTelemetry Collector for telemetry. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

The app service's version is the Node.js version.

docs.title: First sign-in
docs.text:
Wodby creates no Strapi account. After the first deployment, open the app's domain: Strapi redirects to the admin panel, where you create the first administrator. Do this right away, because until an administrator exists anyone who opens the admin panel can create one.

The boilerplate includes an example Article collection type. On its first start it lets the Public role read articles, so /api/articles answers without a token. To stop that, remove the permission under Settings > Users & Permissions > Roles > Public; it stays removed.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Wodby generates the secrets Strapi needs when the environment is created and sets them as secret variables: APP_KEYS, API_TOKEN_SALT, ADMIN_JWT_SECRET, TRANSFER_TOKEN_SALT, JWT_SECRET, and ENCRYPTION_KEY. They are tokens on the Strapi app service's Configuration > Tokens tab. See Tokens.

Each environment has its own values, and they stay the same across deployments and stack upgrades. Keep them unchanged unless you mean to rotate one. Changing a value has these effects:

Changed Effect APP_KEYS, ADMIN_JWT_SECRET, JWT_SECRET Everybody is signed out ENCRYPTION_KEY Stored API tokens can no longer be shown in the admin panel API_TOKEN_SALT Existing API tokens stop working TRANSFER_TOKEN_SALT Existing transfer tokens stop working

The same applies when you copy a database to another environment, which has different values.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service's Dockerfile copies your build context, runs npm run build while the image is built, and starts the container with npm run start. package.json must define both scripts, normally strapi build and strapi start.
  • The build compiles the TypeScript project and builds the admin panel. Changes to the admin panel, such as customizations in src/admin, take effect after a new build and deployment.
  • The Dockerfile does not install dependencies. Install them in your pipeline before the image is built, for example with wodby ci run -- npm ci, so that node_modules is part of the image. See CI/CD.
  • Runtime variables are not available to npm run build, and Strapi does not need them there. It reads the secrets and the database URL when it starts.
  • The application must listen on port 3000. The service sets HOST to 0.0.0.0 and PORT to 3000; config/server.ts must read them, as Strapi's generated file does.
  • The project must use PostgreSQL through the pg package.
  • NODE_ENV is production in every environment type, including dev, because the container runs a production build. Do not set it to development for a deployed environment.
  • Strapi's GET /_health answers without touching the database. The boilerplate checks it after each deployment.
  • The service sets STRAPI_TELEMETRY_DISABLED to true.

docs.title: Behind the gateway
docs.text:
Wodby's gateway terminates TLS. Strapi must trust its forwarded headers: set proxy: { koa: true } in config/server.ts. Without it, Strapi treats every request as plain HTTP. Its admin sign-in cookies are not marked secure, cookies that require HTTPS cannot be set, and every client address is the gateway's. The boilerplate trusts the headers and takes the client address from the last X-Forwarded-For entry, the one the gateway added.

The boilerplate's config/server.ts uses the environment's primary URL, WODBY_PRIMARY_URL, as Strapi's public URL, so links in emails are absolute. Set PUBLIC_URL on the app service to use another address. The admin panel works on every domain of the environment.

docs.title: Connect the database, mail, and telemetry
docs.text:
Link Variables Database DATABASE_URL, and also DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT OpenTelemetry Collector OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS

DATABASE_URL is a secret URL such as postgresql://user:password@host:5432/db, with the user name and password encoded. In your config/database.ts, use it as the connection string when it is set, and do not combine it with the separate variables. The boilerplate's file does this. The stack's PostgreSQL service does not use TLS.

A mail or telemetry variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

The OpenTelemetry variables are the standard SDK settings, so an OpenTelemetry SDK in your application exports to the Collector without further configuration. The boilerplate does not include one. The Collector accepts data only from inside the environment and forwards traces, metrics, and logs to the OTLP/HTTP endpoint in its Upstream OTLP endpoint setting, with the Upstream Authorization header setting if your backend needs one.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Strapi sends email such as password resets. The boilerplate's config/plugins.ts sends it through SMTP when SMTP_HOST is set, and otherwise keeps Strapi's default email provider. Set SMTP_FROM on the app service to choose the sender; it defaults to no-reply@ followed by the primary domain.

Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Uploaded media
docs.text:
Strapi's local upload provider stores media in public/uploads and serves it at /uploads/.... On Wodby, that directory is on the app service's uploads volume, 10 GB by default, so media survives deployments.

  • Files committed to public/uploads in your repository are not included in the image.
  • The boilerplate's config/plugins.ts accepts images, video, audio, PDF, Office documents, plain text, and CSV, and refuses SVG images and executables. Change the lists there to accept other types.
  • To keep media in object storage instead, use a Strapi upload provider such as @strapi/provider-upload-aws-s3. The volume then stays empty.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL holds content, users, roles, settings, and API tokens on its data volume of 10 GB.
  • The uploads volume holds uploaded media.

Back up the database and the uploads volume together as one recovery set. The PostgreSQL service has backups, which are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database, and imports, which replace the contents of its data volume. The Strapi app service has no backup or import operation in Wodby. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • Setup installs dependencies from the lockfile. Run setup again after you change dependencies.
  • The app service runs the dev script of package.json, strapi develop in the boilerplate. It serves the admin panel with hot reloading and restarts the server when you change code. The environment's domains work without configuration.
  • The Content-Type Builder works only here. Content types you create are written to src/api and src/components, and Strapi updates the type definitions in types/generated. Commit these files, then build and deploy them to your other environments.
  • A TypeScript error stops the server until you fix the file; it then restarts by itself.
  • NODE_ENV is development, so the admin panel's cookies are not marked secure. The npm run build step does not run.
  • The workspace uses its own environment's PostgreSQL database.
  • Media uploaded in a workspace is written to public/uploads in the checkout, not to the uploads volume.
  • .strapi/, dist/, build/, .tmp/, .strapi-updater.json, and public/uploads/ are kept out of Git status.
  • A change to variables or linked services still needs a deployment of the environment.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The Strapi app service is fixed to one replica, because the uploads volume can be attached to one container at a time.
  • During a deployment, the old container stops before the new one starts, so the app is briefly unavailable.

docs.title: Supabase stack guide
docs.text: The Supabase stack runs one self-hosted Supabase project per app environment, with a dedicated PostgreSQL database and the Auth, REST, Realtime, Storage and Studio components. The stack source defines its current services and defaults.

docs.title: Create an environment
docs.text:
Set these on the Supabase service:

  • Email sender address and an SMTP integration, both required. Supabase uses them for confirmation and recovery emails.
  • Application site URL, which is where users land after email links and sign-in. Set it to your application's URL. If you leave it empty, the public Supabase URL is used, which opens Studio and asks for its password.
  • Additional allowed redirect URLs, for any other redirect target, such as a custom domain of your application.

Exposed database schemas lists the schemas the API can reach. Keep the default unless your application uses a custom schema.

docs.title: Connect your application
docs.text:
Wodby routes HTTPS to the Supabase gateway, and the public Supabase URL follows the service's primary route. Find the generated keys on the Supabase app service's Configuration > Tokens tab:

  • publishable_key is for client applications, together with the public URL.
  • secret_key is for trusted server code only. It bypasses row level security and must not reach a browser build.

Sign in to Studio at the public URL with user name supabase and the dashboard_password token.

Don't generate Supabase keys by hand or copy them from another project. Data encrypted with the service's signing and encryption tokens can't be read after those tokens change.

docs.title: Social sign-in
docs.text:
To let users sign in with GitHub, Google or another provider, register an OAuth application with the provider and give Supabase Auth its credentials:

  1. In the provider's developer settings, create an OAuth application. Set its callback URL to the public Supabase URL followed by /auth/v1/callback, for example https://supabase.example.com/auth/v1/callback, and create a client secret.
  2. On the Supabase app service, add these environment variables, each scoped to the auth workload and the auth container. Replace GITHUB with the provider's name, such as GOOGLE or GITLAB.
Variable Value GOTRUE_EXTERNAL_GITHUB_ENABLED true GOTRUE_EXTERNAL_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID the application's client ID GOTRUE_EXTERNAL_GITHUB_SECRET the client secret, marked as secret GOTRUE_EXTERNAL_GITHUB_REDIRECT_URI the callback URL from step 1
  1. Deploy the app service. The provider then appears as enabled at /auth/v1/settings on the public Supabase URL.

In your application, start the sign-in with the Supabase client, for example supabase.auth.signInWithOAuth({ provider: 'github' }). After sign-in, users return to the Application site URL, or to a redirectTo address that matches the site URL or an Additional allowed redirect URL.

Supabase needs the user's email address. For a GitHub App, set the Email addresses account permission to read-only; a GitHub OAuth App has access by default. Without it, sign-in fails and the user returns to the site URL with an error in the address. GitLab and Keycloak also need GOTRUE_EXTERNAL_<PROVIDER>_URL for a self-hosted instance. The full list of providers and settings is in the Supabase Auth documentation.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: The database is always postgres. Its port is private and gets no public route. Manage tables and policies with Supabase migrations rather than adding databases or reserved roles. The database password and JWT secret belong to the Supabase PostgreSQL service, so change them there and never on the Supabase service alone.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: By default, Storage keeps objects on a persistent volume. To use S3, connect the optional S3 integration, which needs an access key, a secret key and a region. Set S3 bucket to a bucket that already exists, and S3 endpoint URL for storage other than AWS. Wodby doesn't back up an S3 bucket.

docs.title: Backups and restore
docs.text:
A consistent recovery point needs all of these together, taken with application writers stopped:

  • the database backup, which contains secrets
  • the stored objects: the objects backup, or your S3 bucket
  • the Supabase service's tokens

The database backup doesn't include storage objects or the Supabase service's tokens. The snippets backup holds Studio snippets.

The database import accepts only a .tar.gz or .tgz backup made by this service with the same Supabase bundle. An ordinary SQL dump isn't accepted. It restores into a new, empty data volume before the database accepts connections. If an initialization or import fails, the database won't start normally; run a new import on a fresh volume.

To restore files, run the Supabase service's objects import with the objects backup taken at the same point as the database backup. It replaces everything on the Storage volume with the backup's content, so files added after that backup are removed. Restore the database and the objects together: the database holds the file records, so a file without its record isn't visible, and a record without its file fails to download. The snippets import restores Studio snippets the same way. Objects in an S3 bucket are restored outside Wodby.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Components run as single replicas. Edge Functions, connection pooling, analytics and high-availability PostgreSQL aren't included. A rollback doesn't undo database migrations.

docs.title: SvelteKit stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby SvelteKit catalog stack runs a Node.js (SvelteKit) app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, Gotenberg, and OpenTelemetry Collector services. The app renders pages, runs form actions, and serves API routes on a Node.js server. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-sveltekit.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the SvelteKit Boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, Mailpit for mail, and the OpenTelemetry Collector for telemetry. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

The app service's version is the Node.js version, and every version the service offers runs SvelteKit. The boilerplate includes a health endpoint at /healthz and checks it after each deployment.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service's Dockerfile copies your build context, runs npm run build while the image is built, and starts the container with npm run start. package.json must define both scripts.
  • Build with the Node.js adapter: set adapter: adapter() from @sveltejs/adapter-node in the sveltekit() plugin in vite.config.ts, build with vite build, and start with node build. SvelteKit does not read svelte.config.js. The boilerplate is set up this way.
  • The Dockerfile does not install dependencies. Install them in your pipeline before the image is built, for example with wodby ci run -- npm ci, so that node_modules is part of the image. See CI/CD. SvelteKit, the adapter, Vite, and Svelte can stay in devDependencies: the adapter bundles them into build/.
  • Runtime variables are not available to npm run build. That includes link variables and secrets. See Environment variables for how to read them.
  • The application must listen on port 3000, the adapter's default. Do not set PORT.
  • NODE_ENV is production in every environment type, including dev, because the container runs a production build. Do not set it to development for a deployed environment.
  • The image build leaves out build/ and .svelte-kit/ and creates them again.
  • Request bodies are limited to 512 KB. For larger uploads, set BODY_SIZE_LIMIT on the app service, for example to 10M or Infinity.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Declare the variables your application reads in src/env.ts with defineEnvVars from @sveltejs/kit/env, and import them in server code from $app/env/private. Add your own variables to the app service, see Environment variables.

  • Keep variables dynamic, the default. A variable with static: true is fixed at build time, when runtime variables do not exist.
  • SvelteKit checks the declared variables during vite build as well as when the server starts. A variable declared without a schema must be set, so the image build fails. Give every runtime variable a schema that accepts a missing value, such as schema: (value) => value || undefined, as the boilerplate's src/env.ts does.
  • Variables declared with public: true reach the browser through $app/env/public. Never make a secret public.
  • Server code can also read process.env when a request is handled. The $env/dynamic/* and $env/static/* modules still work but are deprecated.

docs.title: Domains and form actions
docs.text:
Wodby's gateway handles HTTPS and passes each request to the app with its original host name. The app service sets the adapter's PROTOCOL_HEADER, ADDRESS_HEADER, and XFF_DEPTH for that, so:

  • url.origin is the scheme and host name the visitor used, on every domain of the environment. A request without the scheme header, such as a check from inside the environment, is treated as https.
  • Form actions pass SvelteKit's origin check on every domain of the environment. Do not set paths.origin in vite.config.ts: it is fixed at build time and allows only one domain. Use csrf.trustedOrigins only for other sites that must post to the application.
  • getClientAddress() returns the visitor's address. It throws for a request that did not pass the gateway, such as a check from inside the environment, so do not call it on every request in handle or in /healthz.
  • Do not set ORIGIN, HOST_HEADER, or PORT_HEADER. The Node.js adapter does not read ORIGIN.

On shutdown, open requests get 25 seconds to finish, set by SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT. Then the sveltekit:shutdown event runs, before the container is stopped.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
Declare the variables your application uses in src/env.ts with a schema that accepts a missing value: the links are optional, and the variables do not exist during the build. They do not reach the browser unless you declare them public. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

The database link sets no DATABASE_URL. If your database library needs a URL, build it from these variables in server code and URL-encode the user name and password.

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail transport without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
When you select the OpenTelemetry Collector, the app service's link to it sets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL (http/protobuf), and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS (the Collector's ingest token). An OpenTelemetry SDK in your application exports to the Collector without further configuration. Set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME on the app service to name the application. The Collector is reachable only inside the environment.

The Collector stores nothing. It forwards traces, metrics, and logs over OTLP/HTTP to another Collector or backend. On the Collector app service, under Configuration > Settings, set Upstream OTLP endpoint to the receiver's base URL and Upstream Authorization header to the header it expects, such as Bearer <ingest token>. See Settings tab.

The Grafana Tempo, Loki, and VictoriaMetrics stacks each accept one kind of data. Turn off the other exports in the application, for example with OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none and OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none when you send to Tempo.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 10 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

The app service has no volume, backup, or import of its own.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • Setup installs dependencies from the lockfile, which also runs the prepare script (svelte-kit sync in the boilerplate). Run setup again after you change dependencies.
  • The app service runs the Vite development server through Vite's API with your vite.config.ts, not with the dev script in package.json. Options in that script do not apply. vite must be a dependency of the project.
  • The server listens on port 3000. Do not change the port in your Vite configuration.
  • Vite rejects host names it does not know. Allow the environment's hosts in server.allowedHosts of vite.config.ts. WODBY_HOSTS holds them as a JSON array; the boilerplate's vite.config.ts reads it.
  • NODE_ENV is development. Saved files and new route files are picked up without a restart, and SvelteKit regenerates .svelte-kit/ with the route types. The npm run build step does not run, and the origin check of form submissions is off.
  • build/, .svelte-kit/, and node_modules are kept out of Git status.
  • To start the server another way, set WORKSPACE_NODE_COMMAND on the app service. The command must listen on $HOST:$PORT and poll for file changes itself.
  • A change to variables or linked services still needs a deployment of the environment.

docs.title: Symfony stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Symfony catalog stack runs Symfony on PHP-FPM behind Nginx, with PostgreSQL and Mailpit. OpenSMTPD and a managed PostgreSQL database are optional. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-symfony.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from Symfony on Wodby, a Symfony application with Doctrine, Twig, Mailer and a /healthz endpoint, or connect your own repository. The boilerplate is offered only for the PHP versions it supports; your own repository can use any PHP version the service offers.

PHP, Nginx and PostgreSQL are required. The PHP service links to PostgreSQL for the database and to Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the PHP app service. To use a managed database instead of the PostgreSQL container, see Managed databases.

docs.title: Build and deployment
docs.text:
The boilerplate's .wodby/pipeline.yml runs composer install with development packages, so the same build also works in a development environment, then builds the PHP and Nginx images. See Application builds.

Only the document root (Nginx docroot, public by default) goes into the Nginx image. Put front-end build output there during the build. Code and vendor stay in the PHP image. Runtime variables and the database are not available during the build, so don't warm the prod cache there.

After every deployment, php bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate --no-interaction --allow-no-migration runs on the PHP service. Commit your migrations and don't add migration commands to the build or a start script. The step fails when the application doesn't have Doctrine Migrations.

docs.title: Environments and requests
docs.text:
• Development environments run Symfony with APP_ENV=dev. Other environment types use prod; a test environment is a deployed application, not Symfony's test environment. APP_DEBUG follows APP_ENV unless you set it.
  • APP_SECRET is generated by Wodby. Find it in the PHP app service's Configuration > Tokens tab.
  • Variables set on the PHP service take precedence over your committed .env files. Keep .env with safe defaults only, and set secrets as environment variables.
  • Wodby's gateway terminates HTTPS. The service sets SYMFONY_TRUSTED_PROXIES and SYMFONY_TRUSTED_HEADERS, which Symfony reads, so request schemes, generated URLs and client addresses are those of the visitor.
  • The boilerplate sets DEFAULT_URI, used for URLs generated outside a request, to the environment's primary URL.
  • Symfony accepts any host name unless you set SYMFONY_TRUSTED_HOSTS on the PHP service.

docs.title: Database and mail
docs.text:
Link What the PHP service receives DBMS DATABASE_URL for Doctrine, and the PHP service's DB_* variables Mail Transfer Agent MAILER_DSN for Symfony Mailer, and MSMTP_HOST and MSMTP_PORT for PHP's mail()

A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. DATABASE_URL holds the password in encoded form. If you connect your own application:

  • Read it with %env(DATABASE_URL)%, not %env(resolve:DATABASE_URL)%, which fails on an encoded password.
  • The URL has no serverVersion and no charset. On PostgreSQL, set charset: utf8 or server_version under doctrine.dbal in config/packages/doctrine.yaml, or Doctrine fails before it connects. The boilerplate already handles both.

With a managed database that requires TLS, the boilerplate connects with the server's certificate, which Wodby mounts in the container. See Managed databases.

Mailpit captures every message and delivers none. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the PHP service's Mail Transfer Agent link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Files and sessions
docs.text: Symfony's var/ directory, with its cache, logs and file-based sessions, is in the container's file system and is lost when the container is replaced. File-based sessions are also not shared between replicas: store sessions in the database or a Redis-compatible service before you run more than one PHP replica. The stack has no files volume; add one for user uploads. See Application persistent storage.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, the PHP service gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. Add the OpenTelemetry PHP SDK with Composer; it then starts without code changes. To trace requests, also add open-telemetry/opentelemetry-auto-symfony. See PHP applications and OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 20 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • PHP serves the code from the checkout as it is on disk, so changes show on the next request. With APP_ENV=dev, Symfony rebuilds its cache when code or configuration changes, and the web profiler is available.
  • Setup runs composer install and then the Doctrine migrations. Deployments of a workspace don't run migrations: after adding one, run php bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate yourself.
  • After changing variables and deploying, run php bin/console cache:clear.
  • vendor/ stays out of Git status without changes to .gitignore.

docs.title: Kubernetes system stacks
docs.text:
Wodby deploys these stacks as infrastructure apps that operate a cluster. You don't create apps from them. Which ones a cluster runs depends on its provider and selected infrastructure features.

Stack What it does Source Envoy Gateway Provides the Kubernetes Gateway API and ingress control plane for clusters that use Envoy Gateway stack-envoy-gateway Monitoring Provides node, workload and Kubernetes object telemetry for cluster observability stack-monitoring Metrics Provides Kubernetes resource and object-state metrics for cluster operations stack-metrics AWS LB Controller Connects clusters that need it to AWS load balancers stack-aws-lb-controller FRPC Provides tunneling for cluster networking configurations that need an FRP client stack-frpc

To update them, see Cluster updates. To view the metrics they collect, see cluster observability.

The FRPC stack is separate from the FRP Server application stack, which you deploy yourself for workloads outside the cluster.

docs.title: T3 Code stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby T3 Code catalog stack runs the T3 Code server, a web interface for the Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode coding agents. The agents run inside the app service's container and work on repositories stored on its volume. The current composition is documented in wodby/stack-t3code.

docs.title: Before you create the app
docs.text:
• The stack has one service, T3 Code, which runs one replica. T3 Code keeps its state in a single SQLite database, so it cannot be scaled out.
  • The data volume is 20 GB by default. It holds your projects, agent sign-ins, and installed tools. Choose a size that fits them: a volume cannot be resized after it is created. See Volumes.
  • The container requests 0.5 CPU and 1 GiB of memory and is limited to 4 CPU and 8 GiB. Raise the limits if your agents run large builds or test suites. See Resources.
  • The cluster needs outbound internet access. Claude Code is downloaded from Anthropic on the first start, and the agents call their model providers.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
T3 Code has no password. Each browser or T3 Code app signs in once with a one-time pairing link, which expires after 5 minutes.

  1. Deploy the app, then run the Generate pairing link action on the T3 Code app service. See Actions.
  2. Open the link from the task log in the browser you want to sign in.

You can also run t3-pairing-link in a web terminal.

The link points to the app's main domain as it was at the last deployment. After you change the main domain, deploy the app service again. See Main and primary. Without a main domain, you get only a token: enter it on T3 Code's sign-in page.

T3 Code also prints a pairing link in the app service's log each time it starts. That link uses the container's internal address, so enter its token on the sign-in page instead of opening it.

To list and revoke signed-in devices, run these commands in a web terminal:

t3 auth session list
t3 auth session revoke <id>

docs.title: Sign in to the agents
docs.text:
Agent Command Where it comes from Codex codex included in the image OpenCode opencode included in the image Claude Code claude downloaded from Anthropic to the volume in the background on first start; updates itself

None of the agents is signed in. Choose one of these ways:

  • In T3 Code, open Settings → Providers.
  • In a web terminal, run codex login, claude auth login, or opencode auth login.
  • Add API keys such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY as environment variables on the T3 Code app service, mark them as secret, and deploy. The agents inherit them. See Secrets.
  • Enter API keys per provider in T3 Code's settings.

Sign-ins made in T3 Code or the web terminal are stored on the volume and survive restarts.

docs.title: Work with repositories
docs.text:
Projects live in ~/projects (/data/projects), the default working directory. Clone repositories there with git in a web terminal. Git credentials, such as SSH keys in ~/.ssh, are stored in the home directory on the volume.

To add another agent or a command-line tool, install it with npm install -g or into ~/.local/bin. Both locations are on the volume and take priority over the tools in the image.

docs.title: Agent permissions and sandboxing
docs.text:
New threads use Full access, T3 Code's default. Agents then run commands without asking for approval, and the container is the only boundary. An agent can read everything in the container, including its environment variables and the files on the volume. Keep credentials you do not want an agent to use out of the app service.

Codex's Supervised and Auto modes run commands in a sandbox that needs unprivileged user namespaces. If the cluster blocks them, those commands fail with a bwrap error. Use Full access for that thread.

T3 Code's built-in browser downloads itself to the volume on first use and needs the same namespaces for Chrome's sandbox. If a browser tab reports that the host blocks the sandbox, t3 browser setup cannot fix it inside the container. Setting T3CODE_SERVER_BROWSER_SANDBOX to 0 runs the browser without Chrome's sandbox. A compromised web page could then reach everything in the container.

docs.title: Who can reach it
docs.text:
The T3 Code domain is public. Anyone can open the sign-in page, but only a paired browser or app can do anything else.

  • Treat a pairing link like a password until it is used or expires.
  • A paired device can run agents with full access to the container. Revoke devices you no longer use.
  • Anyone who can run the app service's actions or open its web terminal in Wodby can sign a new device in. So can anyone who reads its log within 5 minutes of a start. Limit those permissions to people who should use T3 Code.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
Change environment variables on the T3 Code app service, then deploy it. See Environment variables.

  • T3CODE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED is false. Set it to true to send T3 Code's product usage data.
  • T3 Code reads other T3CODE_* variables. Keep T3CODE_HOST unchanged and T3CODE_PORT set to 3773. Without T3CODE_PORT, the server does not start.

Agent turns stream over a long-lived WebSocket connection. The domain's request timeouts are 0s for this reason. Keep them that way, and do not set request_body_size on the domain: the gateway then refuses WebSocket connections and T3 Code cannot connect. See HTTP settings.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
The data volume is mounted at /data, the home directory of the user T3 Code runs as. It holds T3 Code's database (~/.t3), agent sign-ins, Git credentials, tools you install, and ~/projects. Everything outside /data is reset when the container restarts.

The T3 Code service has no backup or import operation in Wodby. Push your work to a Git remote: if the volume is lost, every device and agent must sign in again and unpushed work is gone.

docs.title: Check the result
docs.text:
In a web terminal, run:

curl -fsS http://localhost:3773/.well-known/t3/environment

It reports the running version and needs no sign-in.

docs.title: Tailscale stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Tailscale catalog stack runs a persistent Tailscale node as an app service. The node joins your tailnet. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-tailscale.

docs.title: Before you create the app
docs.text:
The stack requires one Tailscale integration of the Tailscale Node type. Set up Tailscale and create the integration first. See Tailscale-side setup and Tailscale Node.

Wodby creates a scoped auth key for the app service, and the node uses it to join your tailnet.

docs.title: Node state
docs.text: The stack creates a State volume of 1 GB for the node. The volume is required.

docs.title: Serve another service
docs.text: The optional Service to serve link points the node at another service in the app environment. The stack contains only the node, so use this link in a custom stack that also contains the service to serve.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Do not add a Tailscale node to a stack only to make its HTTP endpoints private. Use Private App Access for that. Keep this stack when the node itself is the workload you want to deploy.
  • Deploying a node does not expose other app services and does not change the app environment's Access setting.
  • Removing Private App Access does not remove the node, and deleting the node service does not change Access.

See VPN providers for how nodes and Private App Access differ.

docs.title: TanStack Start stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby TanStack Start catalog stack runs a Node.js (TanStack Start) app service with optional PostgreSQL, Valkey, Mailpit, OpenSMTPD, and Gotenberg services. The app renders pages and runs server functions on a Node.js server. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-tanstack-start.

For a single-page app that uses TanStack Router without TanStack Start, use the React stack: it serves the static build with Nginx.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
Start from the TanStack Start Boilerplate, or connect your own compatible source repository. The app service is the only required service. The others are optional and not selected by default, so select the ones your application uses when you create the environment. The app service links to PostgreSQL for the database, Valkey for Redis, and Mailpit for mail. Change a link under Connections > Links on the app service.

The boilerplate includes a health endpoint at /healthz and checks it after each deployment.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
• The service's Dockerfile copies your build context, runs npm run build while the image is built, and starts the container with npm run start. package.json must define both scripts.
  • Build with TanStack Start's Node.js server output: add the nitro() plugin from nitro/vite to vite.config.ts, build with vite build, and start with node .output/server/index.mjs. The boilerplate is set up this way.
  • The Dockerfile does not install dependencies. Install them in your pipeline before the image is built, for example with wodby ci run -- npm ci, so that node_modules is part of the image. See CI/CD.
  • Runtime variables are not available to npm run build. That includes link variables and secrets. Read them in server functions, server routes, or middleware when a request is handled, not when a module loads.
  • The application must listen on port 3000, the Nitro server's default.
  • NODE_ENV is production in every environment type, including dev, because the container runs a production build. Do not set it to development for a deployed environment.
  • The image build keeps your repository's .gitignore. Keep .output listed in it: Tailwind CSS skips the files listed there, and without that entry a stylesheet imported with ?url can be linked under a name that does not exist. Importing the stylesheet with a plain import in the root route avoids this in any case.
  • Files written inside the container are lost when it is replaced.

docs.title: Connect the database, Valkey, and mail
docs.text:
Server functions and server routes read these variables from process.env. They do not reach the browser: only variables prefixed with VITE_ that exist at build time are compiled into client code. A variable is present only while its link exists and the linked service is enabled. The mail link carries no credentials.

Link Variables Database DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME (also DB_DATABASE), DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_DRIVER (also DB_CONNECTION) Valkey REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD Mail SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT

Valkey writes nothing to disk unless you add a data volume, and it can evict any key at its memory limit. For a job queue or sessions, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction on the Valkey service and size VALKEY_MAXMEMORY to fit.

Gotenberg has no link. Its address is http://gotenberg:3000; put it in your own configuration. See the Gotenberg guide.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Mailpit captures every message and delivers none, so use it for development and testing. Its public domains are protected by basic auth by default. Find the password under Endpoints > Auths, see Endpoints. Mailpit accepts SMTP without authentication or TLS, so configure the application's mail transport without them.

For real delivery, enable OpenSMTPD, point the app service's mail link to it, and attach an SMTP provider. See the OpenSMTPD guide.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, your application gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores data on a data volume of 10 GB. Its backups are gzipped SQL dumps of the environment's database. An import replaces the contents of the data volume. See Application backups and Application imports.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace:

  • Setup installs dependencies from the lockfile. Run setup again after you change dependencies.
  • The app service runs the Vite development server through Vite's API with your Vite configuration file, not with the dev script in package.json. Options in that script do not apply. vite must be a dependency of the project.
  • The server listens on port 3000. Do not change the port in your Vite configuration.
  • Vite rejects host names it does not know. Allow the environment's hosts in server.allowedHosts of your Vite configuration. WODBY_HOSTS holds them as a JSON array; the boilerplate's vite.config.ts reads it.
  • NODE_ENV is development. Saved files and new route files are picked up without a restart, and the route tree in src/routeTree.gen.ts is regenerated; keep that file in Git. The npm run build step does not run.
  • .output, .nitro, and .tanstack are kept out of Git status.
  • To start the server another way, set WORKSPACE_NODE_COMMAND on the app service. The command must listen on $HOST:$PORT and poll for file changes itself.

docs.title: Grafana Tempo stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby Grafana Tempo catalog stack collects and stores distributed traces from your applications. The OpenTelemetry Collector receives traces, Grafana Tempo stores them, and Grafana shows them. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-tempo.

To collect traces, metrics, and logs in one app, with links between them in Grafana, use the Observability stack.

docs.title: Choose services when you create the app
docs.text: Tempo and the OpenTelemetry Collector are required. Grafana is enabled by default as the stack's main interface, with Tempo provisioned as its default data source. You can exclude Grafana when you query Tempo from another Grafana.

docs.title: Send traces from your applications
docs.text:
Applications send traces to the Collector over OTLP. The Collector's HTTP port has a public HTTPS domain, listed under Endpoints for the app environment, so applications in other app environments, other clusters, or outside Wodby can use it.

Every request needs the Collector's ingest token. Open the Collector app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal ingest_token. See Tokens. Requests without the token are refused with 401.

Set the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables in the application that sends traces:

Variable Value OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT https://<Collector domain>, without a path OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL http/protobuf OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS Authorization=Bearer%20<ingest token> OTEL_SERVICE_NAME A name for the application, shown in Grafana

Store OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS as a secret variable. The space after Bearer is written as %20 because SDKs URL-decode header values. On Wodby, add the variables to the sending app service. See Environment variables.

The Collector accepts traces only. Set OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none and OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none for SDKs and agents that also export metrics or logs by default, such as the OpenTelemetry Java agent; otherwise those exports fail.

Inside the same app environment, services can also send to http://<Collector app service name>:4318, or over gRPC to port 4317, with the same token.

Apps from the Wodby application stacks can instead forward traces through their own Collector: set its Traces link to this app's Collector, listed with the other apps you can link to. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: View traces in Grafana
docs.text:
Open the Grafana domain listed under Endpoints. Open the Grafana app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal admin_username (admin) and admin_password. Grafana applies them once, on the first start with an empty data volume. See the Grafana guide.

Search traces with Explore and the Tempo data source, or with Drilldown > Traces. A trace can be opened by ID as soon as it arrives; it appears in search results a few seconds later.

docs.title: Change configuration
docs.text:
The Collector and Tempo each have a config file under their app service's Configuration > Configs tab: Collector config and Tempo config. See Configs tab. After a change, deploy the app service. Wodby restarts it so the new file takes effect.

Common changes:

  • Send traces to another backend as well. Add an exporter to the Collector config, for example otlp_http with the backend's endpoint and headers. In the traces pipeline, replace the exporter list ${env:OTLP_TRACES_EXPORTERS:-[nop]} with both exporters, [otlp_http/traces, otlp_http/<name>]. Put the backend's key in a secret environment variable of the Collector and refer to it as ${env:NAME} in the file.
  • Keep traces longer. Tempo deletes traces after 7 days. Change overrides.defaults.compaction.block_retention in the Tempo config, for example to 336h for 14 days, and increase the Tempo data volume to match.

Keep the token check on the Collector's receivers while its HTTP port has a public domain, and keep Tempo's listen ports and storage paths unchanged.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: The stack creates a 20 GB Tempo data volume for traces. Grafana has its own 10 GB volume with its dashboards, users, settings, and plugins. Wodby defines no backups or imports for these services.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Tempo runs as a single instance and is not scalable. It suits development environments and low to moderate trace volumes.
  • Tempo's ports are private: query Tempo through Grafana or from another service in the app environment.
  • The Collector can run several replicas with the default configuration. A tail-sampling configuration needs all spans of a trace on one replica, so keep one replica with it.

docs.title: Check that the services are ready
docs.text:
• Tempo: /ready on port 3200 answers when Tempo can accept requests.
  • Collector: port 13133 answers 200 when every pipeline has started.
  • Send a test request to the Collector domain with the token: a POST of {} with Content-Type: application/json to https://<Collector domain>/v1/traces returns 200.

docs.title: Valkey stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Valkey catalog stack runs a single Valkey service. The current composition and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-valkey.

docs.title: Connect an application
docs.text:
The Valkey service listens on port 6379 and speaks the Redis protocol, so Redis clients work unchanged. The service has no HTTP endpoint, so Wodby creates no route for it.

  1. Link your application's app service to the Valkey app service. See Links.
  2. Read the connection values from the environment variables your app service receives. The linking service chooses their names. They usually keep the Redis prefix, for example REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT and REDIS_PASSWORD, or a single REDIS_URL.

A password is always required. Wodby generates it as the password token. Open the Valkey app service's Configuration > Tokens tab to see it. Do not hardcode the host or copy the password into your repository.

docs.title: Choose cache or storage behavior
docs.text:
With the defaults, Valkey is a cache. It holds up to 128 MB (VALKEY_MAXMEMORY). After that it evicts any key, including keys without an expiry (VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY is allkeys-lru).

If you store a job queue, sessions or other data that must not disappear, set VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY to noeviction and raise VALKEY_MAXMEMORY. Otherwise Valkey drops data silently under memory pressure.

Set these variables on the Valkey app service under Configuration > Variables. See Environment variables. They apply on the next deployment. Do not edit the generated configuration file; it is rewritten on every start.

Variable Effect Default VALKEY_MAXMEMORY Memory limit 128m VALKEY_MAXMEMORY_POLICY Eviction policy allkeys-lru VALKEY_DATABASES Number of databases 16 VALKEY_TIMEOUT Idle client timeout, in seconds 300 VALKEY_NOTIFY_KEYSPACE_EVENTS Keyspace notifications empty

docs.title: Data and backups
docs.text:
The stack does not add the optional Data volume. Without it nothing is written to disk, and every restart or deployment starts with an empty Valkey. To keep data, add the volume under Runtime > Volumes on the Valkey app service and redeploy. Wodby then turns persistence on. Once added, the volume cannot be resized or removed. See Volumes.

The service has no backup or import support.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
Open a web terminal on the Valkey app service and run:

valkey-cli -a "$VALKEY_PASSWORD" ping

The answer is PONG. Use config get maxmemory-policy and config get appendonly to see the eviction policy and whether persistence is on. info stats shows evicted_keys.

docs.title: VictoriaMetrics stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby VictoriaMetrics catalog stack runs single-node VictoriaMetrics with Grafana as its interface. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-victoria-metrics.

To collect traces, metrics, and logs in one app, with links between them in Grafana, use the Observability stack.

docs.title: Choose services when you create the app
docs.text: VictoriaMetrics is required. Grafana is enabled by default and is the stack's public interface. Its VictoriaMetrics data source is provisioned for you. The OpenTelemetry Collector is enabled by default as the public endpoint that applications send metrics to. You can exclude it when only services in the same app environment write metrics.

docs.title: Sign in to Grafana
docs.text: Open the Grafana app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal admin_username (admin) and admin_password. Grafana applies them once, on the first start with an empty data volume. Changing the tokens later does not change the existing account. See Tokens and the Grafana guide.

docs.title: Send metrics from your applications
docs.text:
Applications send metrics to the OpenTelemetry Collector over OTLP. The Collector's HTTP port has a public HTTPS domain, listed under Endpoints for the app environment, so applications in other app environments, other clusters, or outside Wodby can use it. Every request needs the Collector's ingest token: open the Collector app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal ingest_token. See Tokens.

Set the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables in the application that sends metrics:

Variable Value OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT https://<Collector domain>, without a path OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL http/protobuf OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS Authorization=Bearer%20<ingest token>, stored as a secret OTEL_SERVICE_NAME A name for the application OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER otlp OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER, OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER none, because this Collector accepts metrics only

The Collector forwards metrics to VictoriaMetrics. VictoriaMetrics keeps OpenTelemetry attribute names, so queries quote them in label filters, for example {"service.name"="api"}. To change what the Collector does, edit its Collector config under Configuration > Configs and deploy the service. See Configs tab.

Apps from the Wodby application stacks can instead forward metrics through their own Collector: set its Metrics link to this app's Collector, listed with the other apps you can link to. See OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Send and query metrics
docs.text:
VictoriaMetrics listens on port 8428. The port is private, so Wodby creates no public route for it. Other services in the app environment reach it at http://<VictoriaMetrics app service name>:8428. No authentication is configured.

The same port serves:

  • the Prometheus-compatible query API (/api/v1/query, /api/v1/query_range), which Grafana uses
  • Prometheus remote write (/api/v1/write)
  • the built-in interface (/vmui)

Wodby sets no scrape configuration. Metrics arrive only when something writes them: the Collector, or a service in the same app environment.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Retention is the upstream default. Wodby sets none.
  • VictoriaMetrics has no settings, links, or config files in Wodby. Environment variables are not read as flags, so you cannot change its flags this way.
  • It is not scalable.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: The stack creates a 20 GB VictoriaMetrics data volume, mounted at /victoria-metrics-data. Grafana has its own 10 GB volume. Wodby defines no backups or imports for these services.

docs.title: Check that it is ready
docs.text: /-/ready and /-/healthy on port 8428 are the readiness and liveness endpoints.

docs.title: vLLM stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby vLLM catalog stack runs one vLLM service that serves a Hugging Face model through an OpenAI-compatible API. The current composition and defaults are in wodby/stack-vllm.

This stack is a preview release. End-to-end GPU inference and private-access validation are still required before production use.

docs.title: Before you create the app
docs.text:
• GPU capacity. The cluster needs GPU nodes that vLLM can use. Each replica requests one GPU and runs only on Linux amd64 nodes. See GPU node pools for the supported managed clusters.
  • Private access. The stack requires Private App Access with the Private network type for the entire app. Select a compatible Private App Access integration when you create the app. This needs an active paid subscription and a cluster that uses managed app routing. vLLM's API key does not protect all of its management and metrics routes, so the stack does not publish a public route.

docs.title: Choose a model
docs.text:
Set these on the vLLM app service. Change the model and its revision together.

Setting Default Notes Hugging Face model Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B A small model for a first test, not a production target Model revision A pinned commit A commit, tag, or branch of the model API model name model The name clients use, not the Hugging Face name Maximum context length 4096 Input and output tokens per request. A higher value needs more VRAM GPUs used by each replica 1 Also set the container's GPU count to this value. The GPUs must be on one node Fraction of GPU memory used by vLLM 0.9 Hugging Face token Empty Optional secret for private or gated models. Accept the model's license separately

Check which model architectures vLLM supports before you pick another model. A model needs enough VRAM on the node. Raise the app service's CPU and memory resources for a larger model.

docs.title: Call the API
docs.text:
Use the private address that Private App Access reports for the app, with /v1 appended. Services in the same environment can use http://<app service name>:8000/v1.

Open the vLLM app service's Configuration > Tokens tab and reveal api_key. Clients send it as a Bearer token. Request /v1/models to list the served model name. See Tokens.

The key protects the /v1 routes. /health and /metrics answer without it, so keep the whole app private. /health answers when the model is loaded.

docs.title: Replicas and updates
docs.text:
• The stack starts with one replica. Each replica needs its own GPUs. Three replicas at two GPUs each need six GPUs.
  • An update stops a replica before it starts the replacement, so it needs no extra GPU. A single replica is unavailable during an update.
  • Startup includes the model download and can take up to 29 minutes before Wodby treats the pod as failed.

docs.title: Model cache
docs.text:
By default, the model cache is per pod and limited to 20 GiB. It survives a container restart but is lost when the pod is replaced, and every replica downloads its own copy.

The optional Model cache volume (50 GiB by default) keeps the cache across pod replacements, so the model is not downloaded again. Its claim attaches to one node, so use it with a single replica. Add it from the app service's volumes, or give it a size in the stack.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The stack does not provision machines, install GPU drivers, or buy external GPU capacity.
  • Remote model code is not enabled.
  • KServe, external GPU providers, Wodby Cloud GPU billing, and token-aware scaling are not part of this stack.
  • AMD, CPU-only inference, MIG configuration, multi-node tensor parallelism, and GPU sharing are not part of this stack.

For client examples, see wodby/llm-inference-boilerplate.

docs.title: Vue stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Vue catalog stack serves a built Vue application with Nginx. The current service and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-vue.

docs.title: Build and deployment
docs.text:
Start from the Vue boilerplate or connect your own repository. The deployed app service runs no Node.js process. The pipeline installs dependencies, runs the production build, and builds the image from the output directory only (dist in the boilerplate). Source files and node_modules are not in the image.

If you change the name or location of the build output, change the pipeline's wodby ci build --from step too. Otherwise the image is built from the wrong directory. See Application Builds.

Nginx answers requests for paths that are not files with index.html, so client-side routes work without extra configuration. /.healthz returns status 204.

docs.title: Configuration reaches the build, not the browser
docs.text: The application runs in the browser. Environment variables of the app service, including WODBY_*, do not reach it at run time. Put the values it needs into the build, or have the application fetch them from an API.

docs.title: Web server settings
docs.text: Set NGINX_* environment variables on the app service to change Nginx, such as NGINX_HEADERS_CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY or NGINX_STATIC_EXPIRES. Do not add an nginx.conf to the repository. Changes apply with the next deployment.

docs.title: Development workspace
docs.text:
In a development workspace, the app service runs the Vite development server in a Node.js image instead of Nginx. Expect these differences:

  • Setup installs dependencies from the lockfile. Run setup again after you change dependencies.
  • The server starts through Vite's API with your Vite configuration file, not with the dev script in package.json. Options in that script do not apply. vite must be a dependency of the project.
  • The server listens on port 8080 and the container's health checks probe that port. Do not change the port.
  • Vite rejects host names it does not know. Allow the environment's hosts in server.allowedHosts of your Vite configuration.
  • To start the server another way, set WORKSPACE_NODE_COMMAND on the app service. The command must listen on $HOST:$PORT and poll for file changes itself.

docs.title: WordPress stack guide
docs.text:
The Wodby WordPress catalog stack combines a WordPress PHP runtime with its web, database, shared-storage, cache, mail, and optional utility services. The current composition and version choices are documented in wodby/stack-wordpress.

Start with the Vanilla WordPress boilerplate offered by the stack or connect a compatible Composer-based repository. The default WordPress root subdirectory is web; change the PHP app service's WordPress root subdirectory setting when your repository uses another layout.

docs.title: Runtime configuration
docs.text:
The WordPress PHP runtime generates wodby.wp-config.php from the current app environment and linked services. It provides:

  • WP_HOME and WP_SITEURL from the app environment's primary URL
  • database credentials from the selected database link
  • stable generated WordPress authentication keys and salts
  • the table prefix from WP_TABLE_PREFIX, with wp_ as the default
  • Valkey or Redis connection constants when a cache service is linked
  • reverse-proxy handling for HTTPS and the original client address

The Wodby-provided wp-config.php includes this file automatically. If your repository supplies its own wp-config.php, include the generated configuration before wp-settings.php:

require_once getenv('CONF_DIR') . '/wodby.wp-config.php';

Define application-specific constants before or after that include as appropriate. Do not edit the generated file in a running container because it is recreated from the app configuration.

docs.title: Code and shared content
docs.text:
Treat WordPress core, plugins, and themes as build inputs. Manage them in the source repository and rebuild the app so deployments remain reproducible. Changes written only to a running container do not become part of the next build.

The stack provides shared persistent storage for WordPress content. Use application imports for supported service-volume content and database imports for SQL data.

docs.title: Cache, mail, and cron
docs.text:
When the Valkey service is linked, Wodby exposes it through the standard WP_REDIS_* constants used by compatible WordPress object-cache plugins.

Mailpit is suitable for inspecting mail in non-production environments. For production delivery, enable OpenSMTPD and attach an SMTP provider integration.

The WordPress PHP service defines an hourly schedule for due WordPress cron events using the app environment's primary URL. Change the schedule or run it manually from the app environment's Cron page.

docs.title: Traces, metrics, and logs
docs.text: The stack includes an OpenTelemetry Collector, disabled by default. When you enable it and set where it forwards data, the PHP service gets the standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables that point to it. Add the OpenTelemetry PHP SDK with Composer; it then starts without code changes. To trace requests, also add open-telemetry/opentelemetry-auto-wordpress. See PHP applications and OpenTelemetry Collector in application stacks.

docs.title: Zammad stack guide
docs.text: The Wodby Zammad catalog stack runs the Zammad helpdesk with PostgreSQL, Redis, Memcached, Elasticsearch, and an OpenSMTPD mail relay. The current services and defaults are documented in wodby/stack-zammad.

docs.title: Before you create the app
docs.text:
• Zammad, PostgreSQL, Redis, and Memcached are required. Elasticsearch and OpenSMTPD are optional and selected by default.
